The motif of the shepherd-king frames the angel's proclamation of a 'Savior... in the city of David'; coherence is high, though the link is conceptual rather than quoted.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.
echoes.note: 'The glory of the LORD shone around them' renders the Septuagintal doxa kyriou, the visible Sinai/tabernacle glory that settled and shone. Luke uses the technical theophany vocabulary, giving real volume; coherence is high as the kabod now attends the announcement of salvation.

echoes.text: For to us a child is born. To us a son is given; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
echoes.note: The angel announces a child born 'this day' who is 'Savior... Christ the Lord' bringing 'great joy' and 'peace,' the cluster of Isaiah's oracle of the child born to us, called the Prince of Peace, on whose shoulder the government rests. Coherence is exact (birth, joy, peace, Davidic rule) and the theme recurs across the infancy account, giving strong volume despite no formula quotation.

echoes.text: You have multiplied the nation. You have increased their joy. They rejoice before you according to the joy in harvest, as men rejoice when they divide the plunder.
echoes.note: 'Good news of great joy' echoes Isaiah's 'they rejoice before you... as men rejoice when they divide the spoil,' the joy attending the breaking of the oppressor's yoke in the same Immanuel oracle that names the child. The joy-language strengthens the broader Isaiah 9 allusion in this pericope.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The angel 'brings good news' (euangelizomai) of peace and salvation, the very verb-and-content of Isaiah's herald who publishes peace and announces 'your God reigns.' Septuagintal availability is direct and the salvation/peace coherence is strong; Luke universalizes it to 'all the people.'

echoes.text: Yahweh will give strength to his people. Yahweh will bless his people with peace.
echoes.note: The Gloria's 'on earth peace' set beside the heavenly host's praise recalls the psalm in which the LORD enthroned amid the heavenly beings 'gives strength to his people' and 'blesses his people with peace.' The host-of-heaven plus peace pairing is coherent though the verbal contact is thin, so it is a faint supporting echo.

echoes.text: One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
echoes.note: The 'multitude of the heavenly army' crying 'Glory to God in the highest' resembles the seraphim antiphon 'Holy... the whole earth is full of his glory,' a heavenly liturgy proclaiming God's glory over the earth. The pattern (angelic chorus, glory, earth) is coherent though Luke's wording is independent.

echoes.text: Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh from the heavens! Praise him in the heights! Praise him, all his angels! Praise him, all his army!
echoes.note: 'Glory to God in the highest' with the angelic host praising parallels the psalm's call to 'praise him in the heights... praise him, all his hosts/angels.' The heights/host/praise vocabulary is coherent, supplying a plausible liturgical backdrop to the Gloria, though faint as direct source.

echoes.text: Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brothers: and the Spirit of Yahweh came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up, and went to Ramah.
echoes.note: Naming Jesus 'Savior... Christ (anointed) the Lord' in David's city recalls the anointing of David at Bethlehem when the Spirit rushed upon him. The christos-David-Bethlehem nexus is coherent within the chapter's Davidic frame, though no verbal echo is pressed.

pericopes.text: When the angels went away from them into the sky, the shepherds said one to another, “Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” They came with haste, and found both Mary and Joseph, and the baby was lying in the feeding trough. When they saw it, they publicized widely the saying which was spoken to them about this child. All who heard it wondered at the things which were spoken to them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart. The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as it was told them.

echoes.text: His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind.
echoes.note: 'Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart' resembles Jacob who 'kept the saying in mind' after Joseph's dreams (LXX: dieterei to rhema). The verbal pattern (keeping/treasuring a rhema) is close and recurs at 2:51, giving recurrence, though the motif is also a general wisdom convention, so the specific source is contested.

echoes.text: Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts much troubled me, and my face was changed in me: but I kept the matter in my heart.
echoes.note: Mary's treasuring the matter 'in her heart' parallels Daniel who 'kept the matter in my heart' (LXX) after a revelation he did not fully grasp. The apocalyptic reticence-and-treasuring motif coheres with Luke's portrayal of a not-yet-understood revelation, but the link is faint.

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: The shepherds 'returned, glorifying and praising God' and publishing the saying recalls the psalmist's vow to 'declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will praise you.' The proclaim-and-praise pattern is coherent but generic, so a faint echo at best.

pericopes.text: When eight days were fulfilled for the circumcision of the child, his name was called Jesus, which was given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

echoes.text: He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.
echoes.note: Jesus is circumcised 'when eight days were fulfilled,' the precise Abrahamic stipulation that every male be circumcised on the eighth day as the sign of the covenant. Volume is high (the eighth-day specification) and coherence exact: Jesus is incorporated into the covenant of Abraham.

echoes.text: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
echoes.note: The eighth-day circumcision restates the Mosaic legislation, 'on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised,' which also frames the purification timeline taken up in the next pericope. Direct legal availability and exact coherence make this a strong allusion.

echoes.text: God said, “No, but Sarah, your wife, will bear you a son. You shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant for his seed after him.
echoes.note: That the child's 'name was called' as commanded by the angel before conception echoes the divine naming of Isaac ('you shall call his name Isaac') announced before his birth. The angel-given name-before-birth pattern is coherent with the Isaac annunciation type-scene Luke is reworking.

pericopes.text: When the days of their purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him up to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”), and to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, “A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.”

echoes.text: “‘When the days of her purification are completed, for a son, or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the door of the Tent of Meeting, a year old lamb for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon, or a turtledove, for a sin offering:
echoes.note: 'The days of their purification according to the law of Moses' are exactly Leviticus 12's prescription for the mother's purification after childbirth, culminating in a burnt offering and a sin offering. Volume and availability are maximal since Luke is paraphrasing the statute; coherence is total.

echoes.text: If she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves, or two young pigeons; the one for a burnt offering, and the other for a sin offering: and the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean.’”
echoes.note: Luke quotes the offering 'a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,' the Levitical concession for those who cannot afford a lamb. This is the explicit nearer source of v. 24's citation and signals the holy family's poverty; it is a near-verbatim quotation introduced by 'as is said in the law.'

echoes.text: “Sanctify to me all of the firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of animal. It is mine.”
echoes.note: 'Every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord' renders the consecration of the firstborn, 'sanctify to me every firstborn that opens the womb.' Luke marks it 'as it is written,' so this is a formal quotation; the firstborn-belongs-to-God theme tracks the prototokos of v. 7.

echoes.text: that you shall set apart to Yahweh all that opens the womb, and every firstborn which you have that comes from an animal. The males shall be Yahweh’s. Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb; and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck; and you shall redeem all the firstborn of man among your sons. It shall be, when your son asks you in time to come, saying, ‘What is this?’ that you shall tell him, ‘By strength of hand […]
echoes.note: The presentation of the firstborn to the Lord enacts the Exodus mandate to set apart every firstborn that opens the womb because the LORD spared Israel's firstborn at the Passover. Coherence is exact and the redemptive backstory (firstborn spared by blood) resonates with Luke's larger soteriology.

echoes.text: Everything that opens the womb, of all flesh which they offer to Yahweh, both of man and animal shall be yours. Nevertheless, you shall surely redeem the firstborn of man, and you shall redeem the firstborn of unclean animals. You shall redeem those who are to be redeemed of them from a month old, according to your estimation, for five shekels of money, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which weighs twenty gerahs.
echoes.note: The redemption of the firstborn human (to be redeemed at a set price) underlies bringing Jesus 'to present him to the Lord'; Numbers spells out that every firstborn is the LORD's and must be redeemed. This is the priestly legislation completing the Exodus firstborn command Luke invokes.

echoes.text: When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him to Yahweh’s house in Shiloh. The child was young. They killed the bull, and brought the child to Eli. She said, “Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to Yahweh. For this child I prayed; and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore also I have granted him […]
echoes.note: Bringing the child up to the sanctuary and presenting him 'to the Lord' strongly recalls Hannah bringing Samuel and 'lending' him to the LORD; Luke's whole infancy narrative is patterned on 1 Samuel (Magnificat on Hannah's song). Recurrence of the Samuel template gives this real weight beyond the bare legal citations.

echoes.text: “All that opens the womb is mine; and all your livestock that is male, the firstborn of cow and sheep. The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb: and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. No one shall appear before me empty.
echoes.note: The restated covenant law that 'all that opens the womb is mine' and the firstborn must be redeemed reinforces v. 23's quotation; the doublet across Exodus 13 and 34 supplies recurrence for the firstborn-consecration theme Luke foregrounds.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: When 'they brought him up to Jerusalem... to the temple,' Luke begins to stage Malachi's promise that 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple,' a theme that climaxes in Simeon and Anna meeting him there. The temple-arrival coherence is strong and recurs through vv. 25-38, though it is set up rather than quoted here.

pericopes.text: Behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, looking for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was on him. It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. He came in the Spirit into the temple. When the parents brought in the child, Jesus, that they might do concerning him according to the custom of the law, then he received him into his arms, and blessed God, and said, “Now you are releasing your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples; a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.” Joseph and his mother were marveling at the things which were spoken concerning him, and Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary, his mother, “Behold, this child is set for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which is spoken against. Yes, a sword will pierce through your own soul, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

echoes.text: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
echoes.note: Simeon is 'looking for the consolation (paraklesis) of Israel,' the exact Septuagintal keynote of Isaiah's 'Comfort, comfort my people.' Volume is high (the noun consolation), the Isaiah background recurs throughout the Nunc Dimittis, and coherence is exact: the end of exile-comfort arrives in the child.

echoes.text: but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried in a good old age.
echoes.note: 'Now you are releasing your servant... in peace; for my eyes have seen...' draws on the promise that Abraham would 'go to his fathers in peace' once God's word was fulfilled. The depart-in-peace-after-seeing-the-promise pattern is coherent, supplying the form of Simeon's release.

echoes.text: Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.”
echoes.note: Simeon's readiness to die having seen salvation closely parallels Jacob: 'Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.' The see-then-ready-to-die formula is verbally and thematically close, a strong candidate alongside Genesis 15:15 for the source of the Nunc Dimittis opening.

echoes.text: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
echoes.note: 'My eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples' renders Isaiah's 'all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God,' where the LORD bares his arm 'before all the nations.' The seeing-of-God's-salvation-before-all-nations cluster is verbally and thematically exact.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'A light for revelation to the nations (Gentiles), and the glory of your people Israel' fuses the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' with Israel's restoration. Volume and coherence are very high; this is among the clearest OT echoes in the chapter.

echoes.text: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations;
echoes.note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations' (and a covenant to the people) directly informs Simeon's 'light for revelation to the nations.' The doublet with Isaiah 49:6 supplies recurrence; the universal-light-of-salvation theme coheres exactly with Luke's program of salvation reaching the Gentiles.

echoes.text: I bring near my righteousness, it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not wait; and I will place salvation in Zion for Israel my glory.
echoes.note: 'I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory' supplies the second half of Simeon's couplet, 'the glory of your people Israel,' pairing salvation with Israel's glory. The salvation-and-glory-of-Israel coherence and Septuagintal availability make this a solid supporting allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together; for the mouth of Yahweh has spoken it.”
echoes.note: Simeon's 'my eyes have seen your salvation... before the face of all peoples' echoes 'the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.' The universal-seeing-of-revealed-glory theme reinforces the broader Isaiah 40-55 matrix of the Nunc Dimittis.

echoes.text: It shall be said in that day, “Behold, this is our God! We have waited for him, and he will save us! This is Yahweh! We have waited for him. We will be glad and rejoice in his salvation!”
echoes.note: 'This is our God; we have waited for him... let us be glad in his salvation' parallels the waiting Simeon who finally sees God's salvation. The wait-then-rejoice-in-salvation pattern is coherent, though it is a faint supporting echo within the strong Isaianic cluster.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: Simeon's oracle that the child is 'set for the falling and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against' draws on Isaiah's stone that becomes 'a sanctuary, but a stone of offense... many shall stumble and fall.' The fall/rise division of Israel over the sign is verbally and thematically coherent, a key prophetic warrant for Luke's divided-Israel theme.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'sign spoken against' over which many fall and rise also draws on the tested cornerstone laid in Zion, which becomes the criterion of standing or stumbling. Paired with Isaiah 8 this supplies the stone-of-decision motif; coherence is strong though Luke does not quote it.

echoes.text: Or if I bring a sword on that land, and say, Sword, go through the land; so that I cut off from it man and animal;
echoes.note: The 'sword' that 'will pierce through your own soul' has been linked to Ezekiel's recurring 'a sword shall pass through the land,' a figure of sifting judgment that divides. The sword-of-division imagery coheres with the falling-and-rising oracle, though the application to Mary's soul is distinctively Lukan, so the source is faint.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: The piercing 'sword' anticipating grief over the child has been read against Zechariah's 'they shall look on me whom they have pierced, and mourn,' associated with a future piercing of the LORD's chosen. The piercing-and-mourning link is suggestive but indirect here, hence a contested faint echo.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

echoes.text: Their sword shall enter into their own heart. Their bows shall be broken.
echoes.note: 'A sword will pierce through your own soul' may color itself with the psalm's idiom that the wicked's 'sword shall enter their own heart.' The sword-into-the-soul phrasing offers verbal contact, but the sense differs (Mary's anguish vs. the wicked's self-destruction), so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Simeon meets the child precisely in the temple, fulfilling 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple,' which Malachi pairs with a refining that tests Israel, coherent with the falling-and-rising oracle. The temple-coming-as-test theme recurs with Anna in the next pericope, giving it recurrence.

pericopes.text: There was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher (she was of a great age, having lived with a husband seven years from her virginity, and she had been a widow for about eighty-four years), who didn’t depart from the temple, worshiping with fastings and petitions night and day. Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of him to all those who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem.

echoes.text: Judith was a widow in her house three years and four months. She made herself a tent upon the roof of her house, and put on sackcloth upon her loins. The garments of her widowhood were upon her. And she fasted all the days of her widowhood, except the eves of the Sabbaths, the Sabbaths, the eves of the new moons, the new moons, and the feasts and joyful days of the house of Israel. She was of a goodly countenance, and exceeding beautiful to behold. Her […]
echoes.note: Anna, a long-widowed woman of great age devoted to fasting and prayer, closely matches Judith, a widow who lived chastely many years, fasted often, and feared God greatly. The pious-aged-widow type is coherent and the fasting-and-prayer detail gives real volume; Luke seems to draw on the Second-Temple ideal Judith exemplifies.

echoes.text: Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dances.
echoes.note: Anna is introduced as 'a prophetess' (prophetis), the same title and role given to Miriam who leads Israel's praise. The prophetess-who-leads-thanksgiving pattern is coherent, situating Anna in the line of Israel's women prophets.

echoes.text: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, she judged Israel at that time.
echoes.note: Anna 'the prophetess' also recalls Deborah, 'a prophetess... judging Israel,' another woman bearing the prophetic office at a hinge of salvation history. The title link is real but generic across the female-prophet category, so it is a faint supporting echo to Miriam.

echoes.text: Break out into joy, sing together, you waste places of Jerusalem; for Yahweh has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.
echoes.note: Anna speaks of the child 'to all who were looking for the redemption (lytrosis) of Jerusalem,' echoing Isaiah's 'the LORD has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.' The redemption-of-Jerusalem phrase has direct Septuagintal availability and pairs with Simeon's 'consolation of Israel,' giving the pericope a strong Isaianic frame.

echoes.text: “Speak comfortably to Jerusalem; and call out to her that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received of Yahweh’s hand double for all her sins.”
echoes.note: 'Looking for the redemption of Jerusalem' also resonates with Isaiah's address to Jerusalem that her warfare is ended and iniquity pardoned. It belongs to the same Isaiah 40-52 consolation matrix as Simeon's oracle; faint as an independent source but coherent with the cluster.

echoes.text: She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me, and not forget your handmaid, but will give to your handmaid a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”
echoes.note: Anna's name is the Greek form of Hannah, and her temple devotion of fasting and prayer mirrors Hannah's vow and worship at the sanctuary; Luke's infancy narrative is steeped in the Hannah/Samuel story. The onomastic and devotional link is suggestive though not pressed, so a faint echo.

pericopes.text: When they had accomplished all things that were according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth. The child was growing, and was becoming strong in spirit, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.

echoes.text: The child Samuel grew on, and increased in favor both with Yahweh, and also with men.
echoes.note: 'The child was growing, and was becoming strong... filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him' closely follows the boy Samuel who 'continued to grow... in favor with the LORD and with men.' The growth-and-favor formula is verbally and structurally parallel, and recurs at v. 52, giving strong recurrence within the chapter.

echoes.text: The woman bore a son, and named him Samson: and the child grew, and Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: 'The child grew, and the LORD blessed him' (Samson) supplies the same OT growth-of-the-promised-child notice that Luke reuses; together with 1 Samuel 2:26 it shows the type-scene of the divinely favored child maturing. Coherence with the annunciation-and-birth pattern is high.

echoes.text: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’”
echoes.note: That the child is 'filled with wisdom' and grows under God's grace faintly recalls the Nazirite child set apart to God from the womb in the Samson cycle; the link is the consecrated-child motif, supportive of the Samson allusion but not independently strong.

pericopes.text: His parents went every year to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover. When he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, and when they had fulfilled the days, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. Joseph and his mother didn’t know it, but supposing him to be in the company, they went a day’s journey, and they looked for him among their relatives and acquaintances. When they didn’t find him, they returned to Jerusalem, looking for him. After three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, both listening to them, and asking them questions. All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers. When they saw him, they were astonished, and his mother said to him, “Son, why have you treated us this way? Behold, your father and I were anxiously looking for you.” He said to them, “Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” They didn’t understand the saying which he spoke to them. And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

echoes.text: You shall observe the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib (for in it you came out of Egypt), and no one shall appear before me empty.
echoes.note: The family's annual Passover pilgrimage to Jerusalem enacts the Torah requirement that all appear before the LORD at the appointed feasts, the first being Unleavened Bread/Passover. The pilgrimage-feast obligation gives the scene its legal frame and coherence with Luke's law-observant family.

echoes.text: Observe the month of Abib, and keep the Passover to Yahweh your God; for in the month of Abib Yahweh your God brought you out of Egypt by night. You shall sacrifice the Passover to Yahweh your God, of the flock and the herd, in the place which Yahweh shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there. You shall eat no leavened bread with it. You shall eat unleavened bread with it seven days, even the bread of affliction; for you came out of the land of Egypt […]
echoes.note: Going up 'every year to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover' follows the Deuteronomic centralization of Passover at the place the LORD chooses, i.e., Jerusalem. Availability is direct and coherence exact for the pilgrimage detail in vv. 41-42.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: The explicit Passover setting frames Jesus' first recorded words against the founding redemption feast, a figural touch given Luke's later Passion-Passover. The connection is contextual rather than verbal here, so a faint echo at this point in the narrative.

echoes.text: The child Samuel grew on, and increased in favor both with Yahweh, and also with men.
echoes.note: The closing 'Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men' restates Samuel's growth 'in favor with the LORD and with men,' an inclusio with v. 40. Strong verbal parallel and double recurrence make this the chapter's clearest growth-formula allusion.

echoes.text: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction, and be wise. Don’t refuse it. Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts. For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh.
echoes.note: The boy 'filled with wisdom,' astonishing the teachers and increasing 'in wisdom,' is colored by Wisdom's call to the children who keep her ways and find favor from the LORD. The wisdom-and-favor coherence is real but the sapiential coloring is diffuse, so a faint echo.

echoes.text: Now I was a child of parts, and a good soul fell to my lot; Nay rather, being good, I came into a body undefiled. But perceiving that I could not otherwise possess wisdom except God gave her me (Yes and to know by whom the grace is given, this too came of understanding), I pleaded with the Lord and implored him, and with my whole heart I said,
echoes.note: The precociously wise child amazing his elders resembles the ideal in Wisdom where the speaker, 'a child of good parts,' receives wisdom as a gift sought in the sanctuary. The early-wisdom motif is coherent within Second-Temple thought, though not a verbal source.

echoes.text: Stand you in the multitude of the elders; And whoso is wise, cleave you to him. Be willing to listen to every godly discourse; And don’t let the proverbs of understanding escape you. If you see a man of understanding, get you betimes to him, And let your foot wear out the steps of his doors. Let your mind dwell upon the ordinances of the Lord, And meditate continually in his commandments: He will establish your heart, And your desire of wisdom will be […]
echoes.note: Jesus 'sitting in the midst of the teachers, both listening and asking questions' embodies Ben Sira's counsel to stand in the assembly of elders, attach oneself to the wise, and meditate on the law. The disciple-among-the-sages image coheres, but the link is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Jesus is found in the temple declaring he 'must be in my Father's house,' the Lord present in his own temple as Malachi foretold and as Simeon's temple-encounter anticipated. The temple-claim coheres with the Father-Son relation Luke develops and recurs across the chapter's temple scenes.

echoes.text: One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after, that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.
echoes.note: Jesus' devotion to being 'in my Father's house' resonates with the psalmist's one desire 'to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life.' The longing-for-God's-house theme is coherent but generic, hence a faint supporting echo.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After three days they found him' has occasionally been read against Hosea's 'on the third day he will raise us up,' a figural foreshadowing of the resurrection found-on-the-third-day. The three-days detail offers verbal contact, but the application is debated, so a contested faint echo.

pericopes.text: Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, in the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness.

echoes.text: The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin: to whom Yahweh’s word came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.
echoes.note: "The word of God came to John" replicates the prophetic-call superscription formula of Jeremiah 1:1-2, which likewise dates a prophet's commission by regnal year and names the priestly father. The verbal correspondence (logos egeneto ... epi/pros) and the structural pairing of a dated regnal synchronism with the coming of the word give this high Volume; Luke's deliberate sevenfold dating frame imitates the prophetic-book convention.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word that came to Hosea the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.
echoes.note: Hosea 1:1 ("the word of the LORD that came to Hosea ... in the days of" the kings) is the closest LXX analogue to Luke's construction, anchoring John's call in the classic prophetic-word-reception formula. The combination of named rulers plus the coming of the divine word marks John as a prophet in the canonical mold; recurrence of this formula across the prophets reinforces Coherence.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh’s word came to Isaiah, saying,
echoes.note: "Then came the word of the LORD to Isaiah" supplies another instance of the egeneto-logos idiom that Luke draws on for John. Lower Volume than Jeremiah/Hosea since it lacks the dated-superscription shape, but it belongs to the same prophetic word-event pattern available to Luke.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came expressly to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar; and the hand of Yahweh was there on him.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's call ("the word of the LORD came expressly to Ezekiel ... the son of Buzi the priest") combines the word-event formula with a named priestly lineage in the wilderness/exile, paralleling John "son of Zacharias" the priest in the wilderness. The priest-prophet pairing adds Coherence to Luke's portrait of John as Ezekiel-like prophet.

echoes.text: And there came forth out of them a sinful root, Antiochus Epiphanes, son of Antiochus the king, who had been a hostage at Rome, and he reigned in the hundred and thirty and seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks.
echoes.note: 1 Maccabees opens its narrative with a precise regnal-year dating of a ruler as historiographical frame, a Second-Temple convention Luke shares in synchronizing John's appearance with Tiberius's fifteenth year. Faint and generic, marked low; the parallel is one of historiographical method rather than verbal echo.

pericopes.text: He came into all the region around the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for remission of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make ready the way of the Lord. Make his paths straight. Every valley will be filled. Every mountain and hill will be brought low. The crooked will become straight, and the rough ways smooth. All flesh will see God’s salvation.’”

echoes.text: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. The uneven shall be made level, and the rough places a plain. Yahweh’s glory shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together; for the mouth of Yahweh has spoken it.”
echoes.note: Luke gives the fullest NT citation of Isaiah 40:3-5, uniquely extending the quotation through v.5 to "all flesh shall see the salvation of God," following the LXX (which reads "the salvation of God" where MT has "the glory of the LORD"). The explicit citation formula ("as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah") and verbatim LXX wording give maximal Volume; the extension serves Luke's universal-salvation theme.
echoes.lxxText: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low: and all the crooked ways shall become straight, and the rough places plains. And the glory of the Lord shall appear, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God: for the Lord has spoken it.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The preparing-the-way motif fuses Isaiah 40 with Malachi 3:1 ("I send my messenger to prepare the way before me"), the standard conflation underlying the John-as-forerunner tradition. Coherence is strong across the gospel tradition even though Luke here cites only Isaiah by name.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you by the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.
echoes.note: Exodus 23:20 LXX ("I send my angel before you to guard you on the way") feeds the "prepare the way" messenger tradition behind Mark's conflated citation, available to Luke's forerunner theme. Faint here since Luke names only Isaiah; marked low and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
echoes.note: "All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God" (Isaiah 52:10 LXX) closely parallels Luke's extended clause "all flesh shall see the salvation of God," reinforcing the universal-salvation reading. Likely a reinforcing intratextual Isaianic resonance Luke exploits rather than a separate citation; low and contested.

pericopes.text: He said therefore to the multitudes who went out to be baptized by him, “You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance, and don’t begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father;’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones! Even now the ax also lies at the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down, and thrown into the fire.”

echoes.text: They hatch adders’ eggs, and weave the spider’s web: he who eats of their eggs dies; and that which is crushed breaks out into a viper.
echoes.note: "Offspring of vipers" draws on the prophetic image of the wicked hatching adders' eggs (Isaiah 59:5), where viper-brood imagery signals deadly, deceitful evildoers under judgment. Coherence with John's judgment oracle is strong; the serpent-progeny metaphor is distinctly prophetic.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: The "offspring of vipers" may evoke the serpent's seed of Genesis 3, casting the unrepentant as children of the primeval serpent in opposition to God. Faint and figural; marked low since the immediate force is prophetic invective rather than a Genesis citation.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.
echoes.note: "God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones" plays on Isaiah 51:1-2, which calls Israel to "look to the rock from which you were hewn ... to Abraham your father," the rock-Abraham-descendants nexus John inverts. The shared Abraham-from-stone logic gives this real Volume; possible Hebrew wordplay (banim/abanim, children/stones) strengthens the link.

echoes.text: Behold, the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will lop the boughs with terror. The tall will be cut down, and the lofty will be brought low. He will cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon will fall by the Mighty One.
echoes.note: "The axe lies at the root of the trees" and trees cut down echoes Isaiah 10:33-34, where the LORD lops the boughs and hews down the forest of the arrogant in judgment. The arboreal-judgment imagery and verb of cutting give solid Coherence with John's eschatological warning.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: Trees that bear no good fruit being "cut down and thrown into the fire" coheres with Malachi 4:1 (3:19 MT), where the day comes burning like an oven, leaving the wicked neither root nor branch. The root/branch and burning-judgment vocabulary reinforce the eschatological-fire theme John develops in v.17.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, what is the vine tree more than any tree, the vine-branch which is among the trees of the forest? Will wood be taken of it to make anything? Will men take a pin of it to hang any vessel on it? Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire has devoured both its ends, and its midst is burned: is it profitable for any work? Behold, when it was whole, it was meet for no work: how much less, when the fire has […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's parable of the useless vine fit only for the fire parallels the unfruitful tree consigned to burning. A reinforcing instance of the prophetic fruitless-wood-to-fire judgment topos; low and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh called your name, A green olive tree, beautiful with goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he has kindled fire on it, and its branches are broken. For Yahweh of Armies, who planted you, has pronounced evil against you, because of the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they have worked for themselves in provoking me to anger by offering incense to Baal.
echoes.note: Jeremiah likens Israel to a once-green tree the LORD sets on fire and whose branches are broken for evil done, matching John's unfruitful-tree-cast-into-fire image. Faint reinforcing echo within the prophetic tree-judgment field; low.

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: The fruit-bearing-tree-versus-judgment contrast inverts Psalm 1's tree that yields fruit in season; John warns that fruitlessness ends in fire. Thematic and faint; the Volume is low and the link is contested.

pericopes.text: The multitudes asked him, “What then must we do?” He answered them, “He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none. He who has food, let him do likewise.” Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what must we do?” He said to them, “Collect no more than that which is appointed to you.” Soldiers also asked him, saying, “What about us? What must we do?” He said to them, “Extort from no one by violence, neither accuse anyone wrongfully. Be content with your wages.”

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: John's practical ethics of justice and mercy (share clothing/food, no extortion, no false accusation) embody Micah 6:8's demand to do justice and love mercy as the true fruit of repentance. The prophetic reduction of repentance to concrete social righteousness gives strong Coherence with John's program.

echoes.text: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke, and to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke? Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
echoes.note: "He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none ... he who has food" closely matches Isaiah 58:7's true fast: share bread with the hungry and cover the naked. The verbal pairing of clothing and food for the destitute gives this real Volume as the prophetic template for John's instruction.

echoes.text: But if a man is just, and does that which is lawful and right, and has not eaten on the mountains, neither has lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, neither has defiled his neighbor’s wife, neither has come near to a woman in her impurity, and has not wronged any, but has restored to the debtor his pledge, has taken nothing by robbery, has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment; he who has not lent on […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel 18's portrait of the righteous man (gives bread to the hungry, covers the naked, takes no usury/extortion, returns the pledge) directly parallels John's checklist of repentant conduct. The catalog of just deeds as the mark of the one who lives gives strong Coherence with John's "fruits worthy of repentance."

echoes.text: “‘You shall not steal. “‘You shall not lie. “‘You shall not deceive one another. “‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh. “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
echoes.note: John's charges to soldiers and tax collectors not to extort, defraud, or accuse falsely echo the Holiness Code's prohibitions of robbery, fraud, and oppression of the wage-laborer (Lev 19:11-13). A reinforcing legal substratum for John's ethic; low and contested.

echoes.text: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, her have I guided from my mother’s womb); if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece;
echoes.note: Job's oath of innocence (he did not withhold bread from the poor or let any perish for lack of clothing) parallels John's clothing-and-food charity. Part of the wider OT righteousness-as-mercy field; faint and low.

pericopes.text: As the people were in expectation, and all men reasoned in their hearts concerning John, whether perhaps he was the Christ, John answered them all, “I indeed baptize you with water, but he comes who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to loosen. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire, whose fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, and will gather the wheat into his barn; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.” Then with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people,

echoes.text: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and refine them as gold and silver; and they shall offer to Yahweh offerings in righteousness.
echoes.note: The Coming One who baptizes "with the Holy Spirit and fire" and refines/purges directly answers Malachi 3:2-3, where the messenger of the covenant is like a refiner's fire purifying the sons of Levi. The pairing of fire with purgative judgment-and-cleansing gives high Coherence with John's contrast between the mightier one and himself.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: The winnowing fork separating wheat from chaff to be burned with unquenchable fire mirrors Malachi 4:1 (3:19 MT), where the day burns like a furnace and the wicked are stubble. The threshing-floor/chaff-versus-grain judgment and the inextinguishable fire give this strong Volume.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: "Unquenchable fire" (pyr asbeston) echoes Isaiah 66:24, where the fire upon the rebels' corpses is not quenched, the OT locus for everlasting judgment-fire. The precise eschatological-fire vocabulary gives this real Volume within John's threshing-floor oracle.

echoes.text: I have winnowed them with a fan in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them of children, I have destroyed my people; they didn’t return from their ways.
echoes.note: "I have winnowed them with a fan in the gates of the land" (Jeremiah 15:7) supplies the divine-winnowing image of separating people for judgment that underlies John's fan and threshing floor. The agricultural-judgment metaphor (winnow/scatter the unfaithful) gives solid Coherence.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: The promise that the Coming One "will baptize you in the Holy Spirit" resonates with Joel's outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, a text Luke develops at Pentecost. Faint here, foreshadowing the Lukan Spirit theme; low and contested as the immediate image is refining fire.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: Spirit-baptism that purifies recalls Ezekiel 36:25-27, where God sprinkles clean water and puts a new Spirit within his people. A reinforcing prophetic Spirit-and-cleansing background for the contrast between water and Spirit baptism; low.

echoes.text: Behold, I have made you into a new sharp threshing instrument with teeth. You will thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and will make the hills like chaff. You will winnow them, and the wind will carry them away, and the whirlwind will scatter them. You will rejoice in Yahweh. You will glory in the Holy One of Israel.
echoes.note: Isaiah 41:15-16 makes Israel a threshing sledge that winnows mountains so the wind carries them off, another winnowing-judgment image feeding John's fan and chaff. Faint reinforcing echo within the OT threshing-floor field; low and contested.

pericopes.text: but Herod the tetrarch, being reproved by him for Herodias, his brother’s wife, and for all the evil things which Herod had done, added this also to them all, that he shut up John in prison.

echoes.text: When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, “Is that you, you troubler of Israel?” He answered, “I have not troubled Israel; but you, and your father’s house, in that you have forsaken the commandments of Yahweh, and you have followed the Baals.
echoes.note: John reproving Herod for his evil and being imprisoned casts John in the Elijah role confronting a wicked king (and queen Herodias as a Jezebel figure), recalling Elijah's rebuke of Ahab. Coherence with Luke's Elijah typology for John is real but the link here is thematic, not verbal; low.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife. It is your brother’s nakedness.
echoes.note: Herod's offense of taking his brother's wife is the very union forbidden by Leviticus 18:16 / 20:21, the legal basis of John's reproof. The Torah prohibition underlies the charge even though Luke does not cite it; low and contested.

pericopes.text: Now when all the people were baptized, Jesus also had been baptized, and was praying. The sky was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form as a dove on him; and a voice came out of the sky, saying “You are my beloved Son. In you I am well pleased.”

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The heavenly voice "You are my beloved Son" draws on Psalm 2:7's royal-messianic decree, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you," identifying Jesus as the enthroned Davidic king. The verbal core ("You are my Son") gives high Volume, and Luke's western text-tradition at this verse even cites Psalm 2:7 in full.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: "In you I am well pleased" with the Spirit descending fulfills Isaiah 42:1, the Servant on whom God puts his Spirit and "in whom my soul delights." The fusion of beloved-Son with the Spirit-endowed Servant gives strong Coherence with Luke's portrayal of Jesus' anointing for mission.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: "Beloved Son" (ho agapetos) echoes the LXX of Genesis 22:2, where God names Isaac "your beloved son" before the Akedah, layering sacrificial-son overtones onto Jesus' designation. The distinctive agapetos vocabulary gives this real Volume beyond the Psalm 2 base.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The Spirit descending over the waters of baptism evokes Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit of God hovers over the waters at creation, framing the baptism as a new-creation moment. Coherence with the Spirit-over-water motif is strong though the dove form is not in Genesis; medium.

echoes.text: He himself sent out a dove to see if the waters were abated from the surface of the ground, but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him into the ship, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship. He waited yet another seven days; and again he sent the dove out of the ship. The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly […]
echoes.note: The Spirit "as a dove" recalls Noah's dove over the floodwaters (Genesis 8), suggesting baptism as a new beginning after judgment-by-water. The dove-over-water imagery gives this medium Volume; the symbol is widely read against the flood narrative.

echoes.text: Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence,
echoes.note: "The sky was opened" answers Isaiah 64:1's plea, "O that you would rend the heavens and come down," the prophetic hope of God breaking in. Faint but coherent with Luke's theophany framing; low and contested.

echoes.text: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.
echoes.note: The opened heaven and Spirit-vision recalls Ezekiel 1:1 ("the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God"), the prophetic-call theophany formula. Reinforcing the heaven-opened motif; low.

pericopes.text: Jesus himself, when he began to teach, was about thirty years old, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph, the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Joseph, the son of Judah, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmodam, the son of Er, the son of Jose, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonan, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menan, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David, the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Salmon, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Aram, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor, the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

echoes.text: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
echoes.note: The genealogy's primeval span from Adam through Seth, Enosh, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, and on to Abraham reproduces the genealogical line of 1 Chronicles 1:1-27, Luke's evident source for the antediluvian and postdiluvian names. The sustained sequence of names gives maximal Volume as direct genealogical dependence.

echoes.text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness. He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them “Adam”. Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he became the father of other sons and […]
echoes.note: Adam-Seth-Enosh-Kenan-Mahalalel-Jared-Enoch-Methuselah-Lamech-Noah follows the toledot of Genesis 5 in reverse order, the canonical line from Adam to Noah. Verbal correspondence of the name-chain is exact, giving high Volume.

echoes.text: This is the history of the generations of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old and became the father of Arpachshad two years after the flood. Shem lived five hundred years after he became the father of Arpachshad, and became the father of sons and daughters. Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and became the father of Shelah. Arpachshad lived four hundred three years after he became the father of Shelah, and became the father of sons and daughters. Shelah […]
echoes.note: Shem-Arphaxad-(Cainan)-Shelah-Eber-Peleg-Reu-Serug-Nahor-Terah-Abraham tracks the Shemite genealogy of Genesis 11:10-26; the extra "Cainan" between Arphaxad and Shelah follows the LXX, confirming Luke's use of the Greek text. High Volume as direct genealogical dependence.

echoes.text: Now this is the history of the generations of Perez: Perez became the father of Hezron, and Hezron became the father of Ram, and Ram became the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab became the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon became the father of Salmon, and Salmon became the father of Boaz, and Boaz became the father of Obed, and Obed became the father of Jesse, and Jesse became the father of David.
echoes.note: Perez-Hezron-Ram(Aram)-Amminadab-Nahshon-Salmon-Boaz-Obed-Jesse-David exactly reproduces the closing genealogy of Ruth 4:18-22, the Davidic line through Judah. The verbatim ten-name sequence gives maximal Volume.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: Placed immediately after the baptismal "beloved Son," the genealogy's anchoring in Abraham reactivates the Abraham-Isaac promise line as the channel of blessing for all nations. Faint and structural; low.

echoes.text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness. He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them “Adam”.
echoes.note: Terminating the line at "Adam, the son of God" reads Genesis 5:1-2's "likeness of God" / Genesis 2:7's God-breathed Adam as divine sonship, framing Jesus the Son of God as the new Adam over against the first. The figural pairing with the baptismal Son-declaration gives this medium Coherence within Luke's Adam-Christ structure.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: "Adam, the son of God" presupposes the special creation of Genesis 2:7, where God forms Adam and breathes life into him, grounding the divine-sonship language of the genealogy's terminus. Reinforcing the new-Adam reading; low and contested.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: Routing the line through David and his son Nathan invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting royal seed (2 Samuel 7), the messianic substructure of the genealogy. Thematic rather than verbal here; low and contested.

echoes.text: The sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son, and Malchiram, and Pedaiah, and Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah. The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel, and Shimei. The sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam, and Hananiah; and Shelomith was their sister;
echoes.note: Shealtiel-Zerubbabel in the post-exilic segment corresponds to the Davidic descendants listed in 1 Chronicles 3:17-19, tying Jesus' line to the returned royal house. The shared distinctive post-exilic names give this medium Volume.

pericopes.text: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. He ate nothing in those days. Afterward, when they were completed, he was hungry. The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.” Jesus answered him, saying, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.’” The devil, leading him up on a high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. The devil said to him, “I will give you all this authority, and their glory, for it has been delivered to me; and I give it to whomever I want. If you therefore will worship before me, it will all be yours.” Jesus answered him, “Get behind me Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’” He led him to Jerusalem, and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down from here, for it is written, ‘He will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you;’ and, ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone.’” Jesus answering, said to him, “It has been said, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’” When the devil had completed every temptation, he departed from him until another time.

echoes.text: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not. He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of […]
echoes.note: Jesus' reply 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God' quotes Deuteronomy 8:3 (LXX). The forty days of fasting and testing in the wilderness deliberately recapitulate Israel's forty years where God humbled them with hunger and fed them manna 'that he might teach you that man does not live by bread alone.' Maximal Volume and Coherence: the whole temptation is framed as a re-run of Israel's wilderness test.

echoes.text: You shall fear Yahweh your God; and you shall serve him, and shall swear by his name.
echoes.note: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only' renders Deuteronomy 6:13 (LXX, which adds 'worship/proskyneo' and 'only/mono'). High Volume verbatim citation; the Shema context (Deut 6) anchors the second/third temptation answers in Israel's covenant loyalty.

echoes.text: You shall not tempt Yahweh your God, as you tempted him in Massah.
echoes.note: 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God' quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 (LXX), which itself recalls Israel's testing of God at Massah (Exod 17:1-7). Verbatim citation answering the pinnacle temptation; strong Recurrence with the other Deuteronomy quotations in the pericope.

echoes.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up in their hands, so that you won’t dash your foot against a stone.
echoes.note: The devil quotes 'He will put his angels in charge of you... on their hands they will bear you up, lest you dash your foot against a stone' from Psalm 91:11-12 (LXX 90). High Volume verbatim citation, placed in Satan's mouth as a misuse of Scripture; the Deuteronomy reply rebuts it.

echoes.text: He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.
echoes.note: The forty-day fast echoes Moses on Sinai, forty days and nights without bread or water (Exod 34:28; cf. Deut 9:9). Coherence with Jesus as new Moses/Israel; Availability strong, though the dominant frame is Israel's forty years rather than Moses' forty days.

echoes.text: He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the Mount of God.
echoes.note: Elijah's forty-day fast journey to Horeb is a secondary candidate for the forty-day motif. Lower Volume than the Exodus/Deuteronomy frame, but Luke's special interest in Elijah later in this very chapter (vv.25-26) raises its Coherence.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: Jesus tested over food by the tempter/serpent inverts Adam and Eve's failure under the same kind of test; figural Adam-Christ logic latent in Luke's genealogy ending at Adam (3:38) immediately before. Faint Volume but coherent within Luke's structure.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The devil's offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world... all this authority and their glory' contrasts with the authority, glory, and kingdom rightly given to the one like a son of man in Daniel 7:14. Contested and faint; the irony works only if the Danielic gift of dominion is in view.

pericopes.text: Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and news about him spread through all the surrounding area. He taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: 'Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit' anticipates the Spirit-anointing announced in the Nazareth quotation that follows (vv.18-19, Isa 61:1). Faint as a standalone allusion here but coherent with Luke's Spirit-Christology drawn from Isaiah.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

pericopes.text: He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and stood up to read. The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He opened the book, and found the place where it was written, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” He closed the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him. He began to tell them, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
echoes.note: The Nazareth scroll reading 'The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor... release to the captives... recovering of sight to the blind... to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' is a formal citation of Isaiah 61:1-2 (LXX). Highest Volume in the chapter; explicitly introduced as 'the book of the prophet Isaiah.'
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn;

echoes.text: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke, and to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke?
echoes.note: The clause 'to deliver/set at liberty those who are crushed (oppressed)' is spliced in from Isaiah 58:6 (LXX 'aphesei tethrausmenous'), not part of Isa 61. The deliberate conflation of two 'release/aphesis' texts is a recognized Lukan composite citation; high Volume and verbatim LXX wording.

echoes.text: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.
echoes.note: 'To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' and 'release/aphesis' evoke the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, when liberty is proclaimed and debts/captives released. Isaiah 61 itself draws on Jubilee language; Luke makes the year-of-release motif programmatic, giving strong Coherence and Availability.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: 'Recovering of sight to the blind' and 'release to the captives' resonate with the Servant's task in Isaiah 42:7 ('to open blind eyes, to bring out prisoners'). Recurrence of the Isaianic Servant/blindness motif strengthens this, though the wording is closest to Isa 61/LXX.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: The opening of blind eyes and hearing of the deaf in Isaiah 29:18 belongs to the cluster of Isaianic restoration texts Luke draws on for sight-to-the-blind. Faint and secondary to Isa 61, but coherent with Luke's Isaianic program.

pericopes.text: All testified about him, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth, and they said, “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?” He said to them, “Doubtless you will tell me this parable, ‘Physician, heal yourself! Whatever we have heard done at Capernaum, do also here in your hometown.’” He said, “Most certainly I tell you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.

echoes.text: You are the most excellent of the sons of men. Grace has anointed your lips, therefore God has blessed you forever.
echoes.note: The crowd's wonder at the 'gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth' faintly echoes Psalm 45:2 (LXX 44:3), 'grace is poured upon your lips.' Low Volume; the verbal overlap (grace + mouth/lips) is suggestive but the connection is contested.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;
echoes.note: 'No prophet is acceptable in his hometown,' and the townsmen's coming murderous rejection, reflects the prophet-rejected-by-his-own pattern, e.g. Jeremiah's own people of Anathoth seeking his life (Jer 11:21). Faint, pattern-level allusion rather than verbal citation.

pericopes.text: But truly I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut up three years and six months, when a great famine came over all the land. Elijah was sent to none of them, except to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. There were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, yet not one of them was cleansed, except Naaman, the Syrian.”

echoes.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
echoes.note: 'When the sky was shut up three years and six months... a great famine' summarizes Elijah's drought announced in 1 Kings 17:1 (and ended in 18:1). Jesus names the era explicitly ('in the days of Elijah'); high Volume narrative citation.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: 'Elijah was sent... to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow' directly retells 1 Kings 17:8-16, the widow of Zarephath. Explicit naming of place and figure makes this a high-Volume citation deployed as Gentile-inclusion precedent.

echoes.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]
echoes.note: 'Naaman, the Syrian' cleansed of leprosy by Elisha retells 2 Kings 5:1-14. Named figure and event; high Volume, paired with the Zarephath widow to ground Jesus' point that prophets are sent to Gentiles when Israel rejects them.

pericopes.text: They were all filled with wrath in the synagogue, as they heard these things. They rose up, threw him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill that their city was built on, that they might throw him off the cliff. But he, passing through their midst, went his way.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: The synagogue's murderous rage and attempt to throw Jesus off the cliff continues the rejected-prophet motif (cf. Israel killing the prophets, 1 Kings 19:10,14). Pattern-level echo reinforcing the Elijah framing just invoked; faint verbal contact.

pericopes.text: He came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. He was teaching them on the Sabbath day, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word was with authority. In the synagogue there was a man who had a spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Ah! what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us?
