I know you who you are: the Holy One of God!” Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” When the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. Amazement came on all, and they spoke together, one with another, saying, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” News about him went out into every place of the surrounding region.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: The demon's title 'the Holy One of God' (ho hagios tou theou) draws on the OT 'holy one' (LXX hosios) of Psalm 16:10 (LXX 15:10), a text Luke applies messianically in Acts 2:27. Coherence with Lukan Christology; medium because 'Holy One' also has wider OT roots (e.g. consecrated figures).

echoes.text: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’”
echoes.note: 'Holy one of God' may also echo the Nazirite consecration language ('a Nazirite/holy one of God', Judg 13:7 LXX), faintly punning on Jesus 'of Nazareth' in the demon's cry. Faint and contested but available in the LXX tradition.

pericopes.text: He rose up from the synagogue, and entered into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was afflicted with a great fever, and they begged him for her. He stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her. Immediately she rose up and served them. When the sun was setting, all those who had any sick with various diseases brought them to him; and he laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them. Demons also came out of many, crying out, and saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of God!” Rebuking them, he didn’t allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: Healings gathered 'when the sun was setting' may evoke Malachi 4:2 (LXX 3:20), 'the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings.' Faint and contested word-play on sun + healing; Luke's sunset detail is plausibly incidental, hence low confidence.

pericopes.text: When it was day, he departed and went into an uninhabited place, and the multitudes looked for him, and came to him, and held on to him, so that he wouldn’t go away from them. But he said to them, “I must preach the good news of the Kingdom of God to the other cities also. For this reason I have been sent.” He was preaching in the synagogues of Galilee.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: 'I must preach the good news of the Kingdom of God... for this reason I have been sent' echoes the commissioning of the Isaiah 61:1 herald ('he has sent me to preach good news') that opened the chapter. Inclusio-like Recurrence binding the chapter to its Isaianic program; faint as a standalone allusion.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

pericopes.text: Now while the multitude pressed on him and heard the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret. He saw two boats standing by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them, and were washing their nets. He entered into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. He sat down and taught the multitudes from the boat. When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.” Simon answered him, “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.” When they had done this, they caught a great multitude of fish, and their net was breaking. They beckoned to their partners in the other boat, that they should come and help them. They came, and filled both boats, so that they began to sink. But Simon Peter, when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” For he was amazed, and all who were with him, at the catch of fish which they had caught; and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Jesus said to Simon, “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.” When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything, and followed him.

echoes.text: Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!”
echoes.note: Peter's reaction, falling at Jesus' knees and crying 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man,' replays the prophet's response to theophany: confrontation with the holy provokes confession of uncleanness ('Woe is me, for I am a man of unclean lips'). Both join recognition of divine presence to commissioning ('Don't be afraid... you will be catching people'). High volume and coherence with the call-narrative form.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send for many fishermen, says Yahweh, and they shall fish them up; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.
echoes.note: The 'catching people alive' commission draws on the prophetic image of God sending fishermen to gather Israel ('I will send for many fishers, and they shall fish them'). The shared metaphor of human fishers as agents of God's ingathering gives volume; the call setting supplies coherence, though Jeremiah's image is originally one of judgment.

echoes.text: It shall happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, shall live; and there shall be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the river comes. It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's temple-river vision teems with fish and stations fishers from Engedi to Eneglaim, a figure of eschatological abundance and life flowing outward. The miraculous superabundant catch may echo this image of overflowing life as a sign of the new creation, though the verbal links are faint.

echoes.text: and make men like the fish of the sea, like the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? He takes up all of them with the hook. He catches them in his net, and gathers them in his dragnet. Therefore he rejoices and is glad.
echoes.note: Habakkuk likens people gathered by the conqueror to fish caught in a net and hauled up. The fishers-of-men motif may invert this image of catching for destruction into one of catching for life. Faint and contested; offered for the recurrence of the fish-net-people complex in the prophets.

echoes.text: Abraham answered, “See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, who am but dust and ashes.
echoes.note: Abraham's self-deprecation before the LORD ('I am but dust and ashes') models the creature's recognition of unworthiness in the divine presence, paralleling Peter's 'I am a sinful man.' The motif of the human cowering before manifest holiness is widely attested; low volume here.

echoes.text: Gideon saw that he was Yahweh’s angel; and Gideon said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh! Because I have seen Yahweh’s angel face to face!” Yahweh said to him, “Peace be to you! Don’t be afraid. You shall not die.”
echoes.note: Gideon's fear at having seen the angel of the LORD face to face, answered by 'Peace, do not fear,' parallels the theophanic-fear-and-reassurance pattern (Jesus' 'Don't be afraid'). The form is recurrent across call narratives, lending coherence though the link to Luke 5 is general.

pericopes.text: While he was in one of the cities, behold, there was a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face, and begged him, saying, “Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean.” He stretched out his hand, and touched him, saying, “I want to. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him. He commanded him to tell no one, “But go your way, and show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing according to what Moses commanded, for a testimony to them.” But the report concerning him spread much more, and great multitudes came together to hear, and to be healed by him of their infirmities. But he withdrew himself into the desert, and prayed.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “When a man shall have a rising in his body’s skin, or a scab, or a bright spot, and it becomes in the skin of his body the plague of leprosy, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons, the priests: and the priest shall examine the plague in the skin of the body: and if the hair in the plague has turned white, and the appearance of the plague is deeper than the body’s skin, it is the […]
echoes.note: The 'man full of leprosy' invokes the priestly diagnosis of skin disease and the resulting state of ritual uncleanness and exclusion. Luke's scene presupposes this legal world; the leper's plea 'you can make me clean' uses Levitical cleanness language directly.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper, then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop. The priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in […]
echoes.note: Jesus' command to 'show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing according to what Moses commanded' explicitly cites the Levitical rite for cleansing the leper (Lev 14:2-32). High volume: a near-direct reference to Mosaic legislation by name.

echoes.text: Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
echoes.note: Naaman the Syrian's cleansing from leprosy is the paradigmatic OT leprosy-healing and is explicitly invoked by Luke at 4:27, just before this scene. The healing of the leper here coheres with that recently activated narrative; Naaman's restored flesh and the prophet's mediation supply the type.

echoes.text: The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned. Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” Yahweh […]
echoes.note: Miriam's leprosy and Moses' intercessory plea ('Heal her, O God') present another instance where leprosy is removed by divine power at a mediator's word. Recurrence of the leprosy-healing motif gives some coherence, though no verbal contact with Luke.

echoes.text: Now there were four leprous men at the entrance of the gate. They said one to another, “Why do we sit here until we die?
echoes.note: The lepers outside Samaria's gate exemplify the social exclusion of the leper that frames Luke's scene. Faint, contextual only.

pericopes.text: On one of those days, he was teaching; and there were Pharisees and teachers of the law sitting by, who had come out of every village of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. The power of the Lord was with him to heal them. Behold, men brought a paralyzed man on a cot, and they sought to bring him in to lay before Jesus. Not finding a way to bring him in because of the multitude, they went up to the housetop, and let him down through the tiles with his cot into the midst before Jesus. Seeing their faith, he said to him, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” The scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, “Who is this that speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins, but God alone?” But Jesus, perceiving their thoughts, answered them, “Why are you reasoning so in your hearts? Which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you;’ or to say, ‘Arise and walk?’ But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (he said to the paralyzed man), “I tell you, arise, and take up your cot, and go to your house.” Immediately he rose up before them, and took up that which he was laying on, and departed to his house, glorifying God. Amazement took hold on all, and they glorified God. They were filled with fear, saying, “We have seen strange things today.”

echoes.text: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
echoes.note: 'I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake' grounds the scribes' premise that God alone forgives sins. Jesus' pronouncement of forgiveness, and the controversy it provokes, presuppose this divine prerogative; strong coherence with the second-Isaiah claim that pardon is God's act.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”
echoes.note: The covenantal self-revelation of the LORD as the one 'forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin' is the foundational scriptural warrant for God's sole authority to pardon. The scribes' objection ('who can forgive sins but God alone?') rests on this confession. Medium volume; thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: who forgives all your sins; who heals all your diseases;
echoes.note: 'Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases' yokes forgiveness and healing exactly as Jesus does ('which is easier: your sins are forgiven, or arise and walk?'). The Psalm's pairing supplies the logic that healing demonstrates the authority to forgive.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Jesus' self-designation 'the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins' draws on the one like a son of man to whom dominion and authority are given. The claim of authority bound to the Son of Man title gives volume and coherence with the Danielic vision.

echoes.text: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
echoes.note: 'Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow' offers the prophetic promise of divine cleansing of sin that underlies the forgiveness pronounced here. Thematic only; low volume.

echoes.text: Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness. He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
echoes.note: 'Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity... he will subdue our iniquities; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea' echoes the rhetorical 'who can forgive but God?' and the pardon motif. Faint; offered for recurrence of the God-alone-pardons theme.

pericopes.text: After these things he went out, and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax office, and said to him, “Follow me!” He left everything, and rose up and followed him. Levi made a great feast for him in his house. There was a great crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining with them. Their scribes and the Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus answered them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice' is the prophetic warrant for Jesus' table-fellowship with tax collectors and sinners against the Pharisees' purity objection. Though the explicit citation appears in Matthew's parallel, the same logic of mercy over ritual separation governs Luke's controversy; medium coherence.

echoes.text: Is there no balm in Gilead? is there no physician there? why then isn’t the health of the daughter of my people recovered?
echoes.note: 'Is there no balm in Gilead? is there no physician there?' supplies the physician imagery Jesus turns on his critics ('those who are sick need a physician'). The prophetic lament over an unhealed people lends thematic depth; verbal contact is the shared 'physician' figure.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: The LORD as shepherd who seeks the lost, binds the broken, and strengthens the sick coheres with Jesus' coming to call sinners rather than the righteous. The seek-the-sick/lost motif gives some coherence to the mission statement; low volume.

echoes.text: Honor a physician according to your need of him with the honors due to him: For verily the Lord has created him. For from the Most High comes healing; And from the king he shall receive a gift.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's praise of the physician, whose healing comes from the Most High, belongs to the Second-Temple physician imagery Jesus deploys. Availability within the deuterocanon; faint and contested.

pericopes.text: They said to him, “Why do John’s disciples often fast and pray, likewise also the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink?” He said to them, “Can you make the friends of the bridegroom fast, while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them. Then they will fast in those days.” He also told a parable to them. “No one puts a piece from a new garment on an old garment, or else he will tear the new, and also the piece from the new will not match the old. No one puts new wine into old wine skins, or else the new wine will burst the skins, and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wine skins, and both are preserved. No man having drunk old wine immediately desires new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’”

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: 'As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you' supplies the bridegroom imagery by which Jesus interprets the festal joy of his presence as incompatible with fasting. The prophetic figure of God as bridegroom of his people grounds the metaphor; medium coherence.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.
echoes.note: The LORD's betrothal of Israel 'in righteousness... in lovingkindness' is a primary scriptural source of the divine-bridegroom motif underlying Jesus' saying. The wedding/betrothal frame coheres with the bridegroom-present logic of the fasting question.

echoes.text: “Yet even now,” says Yahweh, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity. Who knows? He may turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, even a meal offering and a drink offering to Yahweh, your God. Blow the trumpet in […]
echoes.note: Joel's call to fasting and solemn assembly, which summons even 'the bridegroom out of his chamber,' joins fasting and bridegroom imagery in one passage. The juxtaposition makes it a plausible backdrop to Jesus' bridegroom-and-fasting saying, though the use is allusive and faint.

echoes.text: For your Maker is your husband; Yahweh of Armies is his name: and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer; the God of the whole earth shall he be called.
echoes.note: 'Your Maker is your husband' reinforces the prophetic divine-spouse motif that the bridegroom saying presupposes. Recurrence with Isa 62 and Hosea; low independent volume.

echoes.text: Behold, my breast is as wine which has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst.
echoes.note: Elihu's 'my belly is as wine which has no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles' is the closest OT parallel to the new-wine-bursting-old-skins parable. Shared imagery of new wine straining fresh versus old skins gives notable volume to the figure.

echoes.text: Therefore you shall speak to them this word: Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, Every bottle shall be filled with wine: and they shall tell you, Do we not certainly know that every bottle shall be filled with wine?
echoes.note: 'Every bottle shall be filled with wine' belongs to the prophetic wineskin imagery and is offered for recurrence of the wineskin figure; the connection to the new/old contrast is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: Forsake not an old friend; For the new is not comparable to him: As new wine, so is a new friend; If it become old, you will drink it with gladness.
echoes.note: 'A new friend is as new wine; when it is old, you shall drink it with pleasure' uniquely parallels Jesus' closing maxim 'the old is better.' The shared old-wine-is-preferred proverb gives this Second-Temple text real coherence with v.39, though verbal contact is partial.

pericopes.text: Now on the second Sabbath after the first, he was going through the grain fields. His disciples plucked the heads of grain, and ate, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said to them, “Why do you do that which is not lawful to do on the Sabbath day?” Jesus, answering them, said, “Haven’t you read what David did when he was hungry, he, and those who were with him; how he entered into God’s house, and took and ate the show bread, and gave also to those who were with him, which is not lawful to eat except for the priests alone?” He said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.”

echoes.text: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?” David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has commanded me a business, and has said to me, ‘Let no man know anything of the business about which I send you, and what I have commanded you; and I have appointed the young men to such and such a place.’ Now therefore what is under your hand? Give me five loaves […]
echoes.note: Jesus explicitly cites David eating the consecrated bread of the Presence when hungry, with his companions. The verbal and narrative dependence is direct (named figure, the showbread, eating what is 'not lawful except for the priests'), satisfying Volume and Availability decisively.

echoes.text: “You shall take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes of it: two tenth parts of an ephah shall be in one cake. You shall set them in two rows, six on a row, on the pure gold table before Yahweh. You shall put pure frankincense on each row, that it may be to the bread for a memorial, even an offering made by fire to Yahweh. Every Sabbath day he shall set it in order before Yahweh continually. It is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting […]
echoes.note: This is the legal basis for Jesus' phrase 'which is not lawful to eat except for the priests alone' — Leviticus prescribes the showbread and reserves it for Aaron and his sons. Luke's halakhic argument presupposes this statute, giving high Coherence with the David citation.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The whole controversy is over what is 'lawful to do on the Sabbath day,' which presupposes the Decalogue Sabbath command. Jesus' claim that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath answers directly to this prohibition of work, a strong thematic echo.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic restatement of the Sabbath command frames it humanely (rest, mercy, deliverance), coherent with Jesus' merciful reading of Sabbath law over the plucking of grain. Lower volume than Exodus 20 since Luke does not quote, but the humanitarian rationale is apt.

echoes.text: When you come into your neighbor’s standing grain, then you may pluck the ears with your hand; but you shall not move a sickle to your neighbor’s standing grain.
echoes.note: The Torah explicitly permits plucking heads of grain by hand from a neighbor's standing crop; the disciples' act is lawful in itself, so the dispute is purely about the Sabbath. This statute is the unspoken Availability that makes the Pharisees' objection narrowly Sabbatarian.

echoes.text: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
echoes.note: God's own Sabbath rest at creation is the root of Sabbath theology behind the pericope and the 'lord of the Sabbath' claim. The connection is theological rather than verbal, so confidence is low and the link is figural-conceptual.

pericopes.text: It also happened on another Sabbath that he entered into the synagogue and taught. There was a man there, and his right hand was withered. The scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, that they might find an accusation against him. But he knew their thoughts; and he said to the man who had the withered hand, “Rise up, and stand in the middle.” He arose and stood. Then Jesus said to them, “I will ask you something: Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good, or to do harm? To save a life, or to kill?” He looked around at them all, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He did, and his hand was restored as sound as the other. But they were filled with rage, and talked with one another about what they might do to Jesus.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: A second Sabbath controversy (healing the withered hand) again presupposes the Sabbath commandment; Jesus' question 'is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good?' directly engages the Decalogue prohibition of work. High Coherence with 6:1-5 and Recurrence within the chapter.

echoes.text: When the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar in Bethel, Jeroboam put out his hand from the altar, saying, “Seize him!” His hand, which he put out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back again to himself. The altar also was split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by Yahweh’s word. The king answered the man of God, “Now entreat the favor […]
echoes.note: Jeroboam's hand withers and is then restored at the prophet's word — the closest OT parallel to a withered (LXX exēranthē) hand being healed. The shared rare motif of a withered-then-restored hand gives moderate Volume despite no quotation.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: Jesus' antithesis 'to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill' echoes the Deuteronomic 'life and good, death and evil' set before Israel. Faint and conceptual, marked low.

pericopes.text: In these days, he went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God. When it was day, he called his disciples, and from them he chose twelve, whom he also named apostles: Simon, whom he also named Peter; Andrew, his brother; James; John; Philip; Bartholomew; Matthew; Thomas; James, the son of Alphaeus; Simon, who was called the Zealot; Judas the son of James; and Judas Iscariot, who also became a traitor.

echoes.text: Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, and rose up early in the morning, and built an altar under the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
echoes.note: Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars 'according to the twelve tribes of Israel.' Jesus' deliberate choice of twelve from his disciples evokes the constitution of Israel's twelve tribes, an act of eschatological restoration. Moderate Volume; the number twelve is the load-bearing link.

echoes.text: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his blessing.
echoes.note: The 'twelve tribes of Israel' as the patriarchal sons stand behind the symbolism of the Twelve apostles as a renewed Israel. The connection is typological rather than verbal, so confidence is medium.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain, and stay here, and I will give you the stone tablets with the law and the commands that I have written, that you may teach them.” Moses rose up with Joshua, his servant, and Moses went up onto God’s Mountain. He said to the elders, “Wait here for us, until we come again to you. Behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever is involved in a dispute can go to them.” Moses went up on the mountain, and the […]
echoes.note: Jesus goes up the mountain and spends the night in prayer before constituting the Twelve, recalling Moses ascending the mountain to commune with God before the covenant. The mountain-prayer setting gives a faint figural echo.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses asks God to appoint a leader 'over the congregation' so Israel is not 'as sheep without a shepherd'; Jesus' night of prayer before appointing leaders echoes that pattern of God-directed appointment. Low Volume, conceptual only.

pericopes.text: He came down with them, and stood on a level place, with a crowd of his disciples, and a great number of the people from all Judea and Jerusalem, and the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases; as well as those who were troubled by unclean spirits, and they were being healed. All the multitude sought to touch him, for power came out of him and healed them all.

echoes.text: Don’t rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, because the rod that struck you is broken; for out of the serpent’s root an adder will emerge, and his fruit will be a fiery flying serpent.
echoes.note: Crowds from Tyre and Sidon (Phoenicia) coming to be healed faintly recalls prophetic oracles concerning the nations' turning to Israel's God. The geographic detail evokes the inclusion of Gentile coastlands; low and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more.
echoes.note: 'Power came out of him and healed them all' loosely recalls the divine spirit/power resting on and going out from a mediator. Faint thematic echo of the OT idea of healing power proceeding from God's anointed.

pericopes.text: He lifted up his eyes to his disciples, and said, “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the Kingdom of God. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh. Blessed are you when men shall hate you, and when they shall exclude and mock you, and throw out your name as evil, for the Son of Man’s sake. Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven, for their fathers did the same thing to the prophets.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn; to appoint to those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of […]
echoes.note: The beatitudes for the poor, the mourning (who will laugh/rejoice), and the comforted directly draw on Isaiah's good-news-to-the-poor and comfort-for-mourners, which Luke programmatically makes Jesus' manifesto (cf. Luke 4:18). High Volume, Recurrence in Luke, and strong Coherence.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn; that there should be given to them that mourn in Sion glory instead of ashes, the oil of joy to the mourners, the garment of glory for the spirit of heaviness: and […]

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be disappointed; behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart, but you shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall wail for anguish of spirit.
echoes.note: Isaiah's eschatological reversal — God's servants will eat, rejoice and sing while the wicked hunger, are ashamed and wail — supplies the exact hunger/fullness and weeping/laughing antitheses structuring Luke's blessings and woes. Strong Coherence with the following woes section.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: 'Those who sow in tears shall reap with joyful shouting' is the Psalter's paradigm of weeping turned to joy, matching 'blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.' Moderate Volume via shared reversal motif.

echoes.text: For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.
echoes.note: 'He satisfies the hungry soul with good things' undergirds 'blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled.' Coherent with Luke's broader hunger-satisfaction theme (Magnificat, 1:53).

echoes.text: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: 'Their fathers did the same thing to the prophets' invokes the deuteronomistic tradition of Israel persecuting and killing the prophets, classically summarized in 2 Chronicles 36:16. High Coherence; Luke makes the persecuted-prophet typology explicit.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose trust Yahweh is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's macarism 'blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD' (tree planted by water) stands behind the OT beatitude form Luke adopts. The form-critical background gives a faint but real echo.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: The Psalter's opening 'Blessed is the man...' is the fountainhead of the beatitude genre Jesus employs, contrasting two ways with reward/judgment. Genre-level Availability, hence low confidence and figural.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Persecution endured 'for the Son of Man's sake,' with reward in heaven, draws the title and the vindication-of-the-righteous frame from Daniel's heavenly Son of Man. Coherent with Luke's pervasive Son of Man usage.

pericopes.text: “But woe to you who are rich! For you have received your consolation. Woe to you, you who are full now, for you will be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep. Woe,whenmen speak well of you, for their fathers did the same thing to the false prophets.

echoes.text: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come!
echoes.note: 'Woe to those who are at ease... the notable men' — Amos' woe against the complacent rich is the prophetic prototype of Jesus' 'woe to you who are rich.' Shared genre (prophetic woe-oracle) and target (the comfortable wealthy) give moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be disappointed; behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart, but you shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall wail for anguish of spirit.
echoes.note: The full/hungry and laughing/mourning reversals in the woes mirror Isaiah's oracle that the wicked who feast will hunger and those who rejoice will be put to shame and wail. Strong structural Coherence with the beatitudes that precede.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord Yahweh, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day. I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will make you wear sackcloth on all your bodies, and baldness on every head. I will make it like the mourning for an only son, and its end like a bitter day.
echoes.note: Amos turns feasting and songs into mourning and lamentation, paralleling 'you will mourn and weep' for those who now laugh. Faint thematic echo of prophetic reversal of revelry into grief.

echoes.text: The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority; and my people love to have it so. What will you do in the end of it?
echoes.note: 'The prophets prophesy falsely... and my people love it so' grounds 'their fathers did the same thing to the false prophets' — popular acclaim is the mark of the false prophet. Coherent with the deuteronomistic false-prophet tradition (cf. Micaiah, 1 Kings 22).

pericopes.text: “But I tell you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you. To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other; and from him who takes away your cloak, don’t withhold your coat also. Give to everyone who asks you, and don’t ask him who takes away your goods to give them back again. “As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Love your enemies' radicalizes and inverts the Holiness Code's 'love your neighbor as yourself,' which forbids vengeance and grudge-bearing. The love-command and its anti-retaliation logic are directly in view; high Coherence with vv.32-36.

echoes.text: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him, you shall surely help him with it.
echoes.note: The Torah already commands aiding an enemy's straying ox or fallen donkey — concrete enemy-love. This statute is the OT seedbed of 'do good to those who hate you,' giving strong Availability and Volume for the command.

echoes.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.
echoes.note: 'If your enemy is hungry, give him bread... ' is the wisdom tradition's enacted enemy-love, closely matching 'do good to those who hate you' and 'give to everyone who asks.' High Coherence with Leviticus 19 and Exodus 23.

echoes.text: And what you yourself hate, do to no man. Don’t drink wine to drunkenness, and don’t let drunkenness go with you on your way.
echoes.note: 'What you hate, do to no one' is the deuterocanonical negative Golden Rule, the nearest Second-Temple antecedent to 'as you would like people to do to you, do so to them.' Direct conceptual dependence; Availability within the OT/deuterocanon is secure.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me' is the proverbial renunciation of retaliation behind 'offer also the other cheek' and not demanding goods back. Moderate Volume; reinforces the anti-lex-talionis thrust.

echoes.text: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him; let him be filled full with reproach.
echoes.note: 'Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with reproach' is a striking verbal parallel to 'to him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other.' Notable Volume despite being a lament rather than a command.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The Servant 'gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pluck the beard' models nonretaliatory submission to assault, coherent with the cheek-turning saying. Figural link to the Suffering Servant pattern.

echoes.text: He that shows mercy will lend to his neighbor; And he that strengthens him with his hand keeps the commandments. Lend to your neighbor in time of his need; And pay you your neighbor again in due season.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's teaching on lending to a neighbor and showing mercy stands behind 'lend, expecting nothing back.' Faint wisdom-tradition echo of generous lending without calculation.

pericopes.text: If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive back as much. But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil. “Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.

echoes.text: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
echoes.note: 'Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful' is a deliberate reworking of the Holiness Code's imitatio Dei formula 'be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.' The imitation-of-God structure is unmistakable; Luke substitutes mercy for holiness. High Volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The defining self-revelation 'the LORD, a God merciful and gracious' supplies the content of the Father's mercy that disciples are to imitate, and 'kind toward the unthankful and evil' echoes God's compassion on the undeserving. Strong Coherence with the imitatio Dei.

echoes.text: Yahweh is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness. He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities. For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us. Like a father has compassion on his […]
echoes.note: 'The LORD is merciful and gracious... as a father has compassion on his children' joins divine mercy with fatherhood exactly as Luke does ('your Father is merciful'). Moderate Volume reinforcing Exodus 34.

echoes.text: All day long he deals graciously, and lends. His seed is blessed.
echoes.note: 'All day long he deals graciously and lends' commends the righteous lender who gives freely, undergirding 'lend, expecting nothing back.' Faint wisdom-Psalter echo, low confidence.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: The command to lend generously to the poor 'and your heart shall not be grieved' grounds open-handed lending without expectation of return. Coherent with Luke's generosity ethic; moderate Availability.

pericopes.text: Don’t judge, and you won’t be judged. Don’t condemn, and you won’t be condemned. Set free, and you will be set free. “Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you. For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you.”

echoes.text: your own iniquities, and the iniquities of your fathers together”, says Yahweh, “who have burned incense on the mountains, and blasphemed me on the hills; therefore will I first measure their work into their bosom.”
echoes.note: 'I will measure their former work into their bosom' supplies the measure-into-the-lap imagery behind 'good measure... running over, will be given into your bosom.' Faint but specific verbal contact with the lap/bosom measuring motif.

echoes.text: “‘You shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measures of length, of weight, or of quantity. You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin. I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: The Torah's demand for honest measures ('a just ephah') stands behind the just-recompense logic of 'with the measure you measure it will be measured back.' Conceptual echo of measure-for-measure justice.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay' captures the give-and-it-will-be-given reciprocity of v.38. Coherent with the surrounding generosity teaching; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man you will show yourself perfect. With the pure you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.
echoes.note: 'With the merciful you show yourself merciful... with the pure you show yourself pure' is the OT measure-for-measure principle of divine requital matching human conduct, behind 'with the measure you measure.' Low and contested.

pericopes.text: He spoke a parable to them. “Can the blind guide the blind? Won’t they both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. Why do you see the speck of chaff that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how can you tell your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck of chaff that is in your eye,’ when you yourself don’t see the beam that is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck of chaff that is in your brother’s eye.

echoes.text: His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge; they are all mute dogs, they can’t bark; dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.
echoes.note: Israel's leaders are 'blind watchmen' who cannot see — the prophetic image of blind guides directly informs 'can the blind guide the blind?' Strong Coherence between Jesus' polemic against the Pharisees and Isaiah's blind shepherds.

echoes.text: For those who lead this people lead them astray; and those who are led by them are destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Those who guide this people lead them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up' is a close conceptual match to blind guides and their followers both falling into a pit. Moderate Volume on the leaders-lead-astray motif.

echoes.text: Whoever digs a pit shall fall into it. Whoever rolls a stone, it will come back on him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever digs a pit will fall into it' supplies the pit-falling imagery of v.39. Faint proverbial echo, low confidence given how common the motif is.

pericopes.text: For there is no good tree that produces rotten fruit; nor again a rotten tree that produces good fruit. For each tree is known by its own fruit. For people don’t gather figs from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble bush. The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.

echoes.text: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.
echoes.note: 'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree; so the expression of a thought discloses the cultivation of a person's mind' is an almost exact deuterocanonical parallel to 'each tree is known by its own fruit' joined to speech from the heart's abundance. High Volume; nearest Second-Temple antecedent.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his fruit' fuses heart and fruit imagery exactly as Luke links the good treasure of the heart to good fruit. Coherent with the heart-fruit correspondence.

echoes.text: In the shaking of a sieve, the refuse remains; So the filth of man in his reasoning. The furnace will prove the potter’s vessels; And the trial of a man is in his reasoning. The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man. Praise no man before you hear him reason; For this is the trial of men.
echoes.note: The wider Sirach passage on sieving (chaff/refuse remaining) and a person revealed by speech, including 'do not praise anyone before he speaks,' undergirds 'out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.' Reinforces the high-confidence v.6 link.

echoes.text: A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth. The work of a man’s hands shall be rewarded to him.
echoes.note: 'From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good' connects mouth, fruit, and the good a person produces, a faint wisdom echo behind vv.44-45. Low confidence given the commonplace nature of fruit imagery.

pericopes.text: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say? Everyone who comes to me, and hears my words, and does them, I will show you who he is like. He is like a man building a house, who dug and went deep, and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house, and could not shake it, because it was founded on the rock. But he who hears, and doesn’t do, is like a man who built a house on the earth without a foundation, against which the stream broke, and immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

echoes.text: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash: tell those who plaster it with whitewash, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and you, great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall tear it. Behold, when the wall has fallen, shall it not be said to you, Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it? Therefore […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's wall, daubed without proper foundation, that the LORD breaks down with a flooding rain and storm until it falls, is the closest OT antecedent to the house without foundation swept away by the flood. High Volume and Coherence with the build/collapse imagery.

echoes.text: When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more; but the righteous stand firm forever.
echoes.note: 'When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever' is the proverbial two-outcomes saying behind the wise/foolish builders surviving or collapsing in the storm. Strong wisdom-tradition Coherence.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily. I will make justice the measuring line, and righteousness the plumb line. The hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters will overflow the hiding place.
echoes.note: The tested foundation stone in Zion, with judgment as a flooding waters that sweeps away the refuge of lies, supplies the rock-foundation-versus-flood contrast. Moderate Volume; the foundation/flood pairing is apt.

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper. The wicked are not so, but are like the chaff which the wind drives away. Therefore the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.
echoes.note: The two-ways conclusion — the righteous established versus the wicked driven away like chaff — frames the wise/foolish builders as the chapter's closing two-ways. Genre-level echo, low confidence.

echoes.text: The flood was forty days on the earth. The waters increased, and lifted up the ship, and it was lifted up above the earth. The waters rose, and increased greatly on the earth; and the ship floated on the surface of the waters. The waters rose very high on the earth. All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered. The waters rose fifteen cubits higher, and the mountains were covered. All flesh died that moved on the earth, including […]
echoes.note: The cataclysmic flood that sweeps away all not preserved supplies the eschatological-judgment overtone of the rising stream destroying the foundationless house. Faint figural echo of flood-as-judgment.

pericopes.text: After he had finished speaking in the hearing of the people, he entered into Capernaum. A certain centurion’s servant, who was dear to him, was sick and at the point of death. When he heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and save his servant. When they came to Jesus, they begged him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy for you to do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue for us.” Jesus went with them. When he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying to him, “Lord, don’t trouble yourself, for I am not worthy for you to come under my roof. Therefore I didn’t even think myself worthy to come to you; but say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I also am a man placed under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go!’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come!’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turned and said to the multitude who followed him, “I tell you, I have not found such great faith, no, not in Israel.” Those who were sent, returning to the house, found that the servant who had been sick was well.

echoes.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]
echoes.note: The healing of a Gentile military officer (Naaman, captain of Aram's army) at a distance through Israel's prophet supplies a strong typological precedent for the centurion whose servant Jesus heals from afar. Naaman's mediated request, his concern about the prophet's coming, and the wonder at faith found outside Israel cohere with Luke's emphasis on the believing Gentile. Recurrence is supported by Luke 4:27, where Jesus himself names Naaman as the paradigm of Gentile favor.

echoes.text: “Moreover concerning the foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, when he shall come out of a far country for your name’s sake (for they shall hear of your great name, and of your mighty hand, and of your outstretched arm); when he shall come and pray toward this house; hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and do according to all that the foreigner calls to you for; that all the peoples of the earth may know your name, to fear you, as do your people […]
echoes.note: Solomon's prayer that the foreigner who hears of God's name and comes toward the temple be answered frames the God-fearing Gentile who loves Israel and builds the synagogue. The elders' plea that the centurion is 'worthy' because 'he loves our nation' echoes the Deuteronomic ideal of the righteous resident foreigner. Faint and thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Also the foreigners who join themselves to Yahweh, to minister to him, and to love Yahweh’s name, to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath from profaning it, and holds fast my covenant; even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
echoes.note: The foreigner who joins himself to the LORD, loves his name, and is welcomed into the house of prayer resonates with the synagogue-building centurion. The coherence with Luke's Gentile-inclusion theme is strong even though there is no verbal contact, so this is a faint figural echo.

pericopes.text: Soon afterwards, he went to a city called Nain. Many of his disciples, along with a great multitude, went with him. Now when he drew near to the gate of the city, behold, one who was dead was carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. Many people of the city were with her. When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said to her, “Don’t cry.” He came near and touched the coffin, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, arise!” He who was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he gave him to his mother. Fear took hold of all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and, “God has visited his people!” This report went out concerning him in the whole of Judea, and in all the surrounding region.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: The raising of the widow of Nain's son is closely modeled on Elijah's raising of the widow of Zarephath's only son. Luke 7:15, 'he gave him to his mother,' reproduces 1 Kings 17:23 LXX nearly verbatim, and the shared motifs (a widow, a dead only son, a city gate, the crowd's recognition of a great prophet) give high volume and coherence. Zarephath lies near Nain's geography of Galilee/Sidon, and the Elijah-typology pervades Luke 7.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha's raising of the Shunammite woman's only son is the second prophetic resurrection paradigm behind Nain. The motif of a single beloved son restored to a grieving mother, and the prophet's bodily proximity to the corpse, reinforce the doubled Elijah/Elisha typology Luke deploys. Recurrence with 7:11-17 is strengthened by Luke 9:8,19 expectations of a returning prophet.

echoes.text: Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
echoes.note: The clause 'and he gave him to his mother' (kai edoken auton te metri autou) matches the LXX of 1 Kings 17:23 word-for-word, making this the strongest verbal anchor for the whole pericope. The near-citation in narrative voice signals deliberate Elijah modeling rather than coincidence.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The crowd's cry 'A great prophet has arisen among us' activates the expectation of an Elijah-like prophet whose coming Malachi promises before the Day of the LORD. Coherence with the deliberate Elijah typology of the resurrection scene makes this more than incidental, though the verbal link is to the popular prophetic-return hope rather than a citation.

echoes.text: Also there arose Elijah the prophet as fire, And his word burned like a torch: Who brought a famine upon them, And by his zeal made them few in number. By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven: Thrice did he thus bring down fire. How was you glorified, O Elijah, in your wondrous deeds! And who shall glory like to you? Who did raise up a dead man from death, And from the place of the dead, by the word of the Most High: Who brought down kings to […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's praise of Elijah explicitly celebrates that he 'raised a corpse from death' (Sir 48:5), the same deed Jesus performs at Nain, making the deuterocanonical encomium a Second-Temple lens that shaped the crowd's prophet-acclamation. Availability and coherence are strong; this clarifies how a first-century audience read raising-the-dead as the signature of an Elijah figure.

echoes.text: The people believed, and when they heard that Yahweh had visited the children of Israel, and that he had seen their affliction, then they bowed their heads and worshiped.
echoes.note: The acclamation 'God has visited his people' echoes the language of divine visitation by which Israel recognized God's saving action in the Exodus and was moved to worship. The 'visitation' motif recurs in Luke (1:68, 78; 19:44), giving it thematic recurrence even though no single passage is cited verbatim.

echoes.text: Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.”
echoes.note: Joseph's promise that 'God will surely visit you' supplies the Septuagintal vocabulary of episkeptomai underlying 'God has visited his people.' The link is one strand in a broader biblical visitation theme rather than a targeted allusion, so confidence is low and contested.

pericopes.text: The disciples of John told him about all these things. John, calling to himself two of his disciples, sent them to Jesus, saying, “Are you the one who is coming, or should we look for another?” When the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptizer has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?’” In that hour he cured many of diseases and plagues and evil spirits; and to many who were blind he gave sight. Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you have seen and heard: that the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me.”

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: Jesus' answer to John catalogs the eyes of the blind opened, the lame leaping, and the deaf hearing in the precise pattern of Isaiah's vision of God's coming to save. The cluster of signs is verbally and thematically anchored in Isaiah, and Luke arranges them as a deliberate composite of Isaianic salvation oracles. High volume and coherence with Luke's programmatic Isaiah citations.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: The climactic 'the poor have good news preached to them' cites Isaiah 61:1, the same text Jesus reads as his manifesto in Luke 4:18. Its placement as the answer's capstone and its recurrence across Luke make this the interpretive key: Jesus identifies himself as the anointed herald of Isaiah's jubilee.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'The dead are raised up' draws on Isaiah's promise that the dead shall live and the dwellers in the dust awake, the only item in Jesus' list not covered by Isaiah 35 or 61. Coherence with the surrounding Isaianic catalog and the immediately preceding Nain resurrection gives strong volume.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness. The humble also will increase their joy in Yahweh, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
echoes.note: Isaiah 29 pairs the deaf hearing and the blind seeing with the poor and meek rejoicing, supplying a second Isaianic source for the same sign-cluster and reinforcing the composite character of Jesus' reply. Recurrence within Isaiah strengthens the case even if Luke's wording leans more on chs. 35 and 61.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant's task of opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners overlaps the healing-of-the-blind motif and supports reading Jesus' deeds through Isaiah's Servant. Faint relative to chs. 35/61 but coherent with Luke's Servant Christology.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: The beatitude 'Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me' may invert Isaiah's stone of stumbling on which many fall, casting Jesus as the rock that tests Israel. The connection is conceptual and contested, hanging on the skandalon imagery rather than direct citation.

pericopes.text: When John’s messengers had departed, he began to tell the multitudes about John, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are gorgeously dressed, and live delicately, are in kings’ courts. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and much more than a prophet. This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ “For I tell you, among those who are born of women there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptizer, yet he who is least in the Kingdom of God is greater than he.”

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Luke 7:27 cites 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way' as written of John, fusing Malachi 3:1 with Exodus 23:20. The explicit 'it is written' formula and verbatim wording make this a high-volume quotation that identifies John as the eschatological forerunner.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you by the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.
echoes.note: The opening 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face' draws its first clause from Exodus 23:20 LXX, blended with Malachi to form the composite citation. The wilderness-guide angel of the Exodus is read typologically as John preparing the way, giving the conflation strong scriptural depth.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: Malachi's promise to send Elijah before the great Day undergirds Jesus' claim that John is 'more than a prophet,' since the same prophetic book that supplies the messenger oracle also identifies him with the returning Elijah. Coherence with the chapter's pervasive Elijah typology raises this above incidental.

echoes.text: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.
echoes.note: The 'wilderness' setting where the crowds went out to John, and the language of preparing the way, evoke Isaiah's voice crying in the desert, which Luke applied to John explicitly at 3:4. Its recurrence makes this a coherent background echo for the 'what did you go out into the wilderness to see' question.

pericopes.text: When all the people and the tax collectors heard this, they declared God to be just, having been baptized with John’s baptism. But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God, not being baptized by him themselves. “To what then will I liken the people of this generation? What are they like? They are like children who sit in the marketplace, and call one to another, saying, ‘We piped to you, and you didn’t dance. We mourned, and you didn’t weep.’ For John the Baptizer came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man, and a drunkard; a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Wisdom is justified by all her children.”

echoes.text: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction, and be wise. Don’t refuse it. Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts. For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh. But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul. All those who hate me love death.”
echoes.note: 'Wisdom is justified by all her children' personifies divine Wisdom as a mother vindicated by her offspring, drawing on Proverbs' figure of Lady Wisdom who calls and blesses those who heed her. The coherence with Jewish Wisdom-Christology, where Jesus and John are Wisdom's emissaries, supports the allusion, though it is a conceptual rather than verbal link.

echoes.text: And she, being one, has power to do all things; And remaining in herself, reneweth all things: And from generation to generation passing into holy souls She makes men friends of God and prophets.
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical portrait of Wisdom who in every generation passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets illuminates 'Wisdom is justified by her children.' This Second-Temple development of personified Wisdom is the most available background for Luke's aphorism, supplying its sense of Wisdom's children as those she sends and saves.

echoes.text: Wisdom will praise herself, And will glory in the midst of her people. In the congregation of the Most High will she open her mouth, And glory in the presence of his power. I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, And covered the earth as a mist. I lived in high places, And my throne is in the pillar of the cloud. Alone I compassed the circuit of heaven, And walked in the depth of the abyss. In the waves of the sea, and in all the earth, And in every […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's hymn of Wisdom inviting her children to eat and drink of her and be filled provides a deuterocanonical model for Wisdom's vindication through those who receive her, set against this generation that refuses both John's fasting and Jesus' feasting. Faint and one of several Wisdom intertexts.

echoes.text: Again will I build you, and you shall be built, O virgin of Israel: again you shall be adorned with your tambourines, and shall go out in the dances of those who make merry.
echoes.note: The marketplace children's complaint 'we piped to you and you did not dance, we mourned and you did not weep' loosely recalls the prophetic imagery of dancing and mourning as the proper responses to God's acts, here refused by an unresponsive generation. The link is thematic and weak.

pericopes.text: One of the Pharisees invited him to eat with him. He entered into the Pharisee’s house, and sat at the table. Behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she knew that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, she brought an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing behind at his feet weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment. Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw it, he said to himself, “This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.” Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” He said, “Teacher, say on.” “A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they couldn’t pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?” Simon answered, “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.” He said to him, “You have judged correctly.” Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head. You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But to whom little is forgiven, the same loves little.” He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” Those who sat at the table with him began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you.
