Go in peace.”

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me. Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge. Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin […]
echoes.note: The sinful woman's tears and the pronouncement 'her sins, which are many, are forgiven' enact the penitential dynamic of David's great psalm of contrition, where the sinner pleads for mercy and cleansing. Coherence with the forgiveness-and-love theme of the two-debtors parable supports the echo, though it is figural rather than cited.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The anointing of feet faintly recalls the beauty of the feet of the herald of good news, but the connection is tenuous and likely coincidental given the scene's focus on hospitality and forgiveness. Marked low and contested.

echoes.text: Then washed I you with water; yes, I thoroughly washed away your blood from you, and I anointed you with oil. I clothed you also with embroidered work, and shod you with sealskin, and I dressed you about with fine linen, and covered you with silk. I decked you with ornaments, and I put bracelets on your hands, and a chain on your neck. I put a ring on your nose, and earrings in your ears, and a beautiful crown on your head. Thus you were decked with gold […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's allegory of God washing, anointing with oil, and adorning the unfaithful Jerusalem provides a backdrop of cleansing love extended to the sinner that resonates with the anointing and forgiveness of the sinful woman. The link is thematic and contested.

echoes.text: Your oils have a pleasing fragrance. Your name is oil poured out, therefore the virgins love you.
echoes.note: The fragrant ointment poured out and the love-language of the anointing scene faintly evoke the perfumed devotion of the Song, a possible figural overtone in early Christian reading of the woman's love. Faint and contested, offered for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
echoes.note: Jesus' rebuke that Simon gave no water for his feet invokes the ancient Near Eastern duty of hospitality typified by Abraham washing the feet of his guests at Mamre. The omitted courtesies (water, kiss, oil) are measured against this hospitality norm, making the echo coherent though not a targeted allusion.

echoes.text: Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness. He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
echoes.note: The astonished question 'Who is this who even forgives sins?' presupposes the prophetic confession that God alone pardons iniquity and casts sins into the sea, so the scene quietly trades on Israel's conviction that forgiveness is a divine prerogative. The link is conceptual and supports the christological force of the pericope.

pericopes.text: Soon afterwards, he went about through cities and villages, preaching and bringing the good news of the Kingdom of God. With him were the twelve, and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others; who served them from their possessions.

echoes.text: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]
echoes.note: The women who 'served them from their possessions' faintly recall the wealthy Shunammite woman who provisions and hosts Elisha and his entourage. Coherence is moderate (female patron supporting a prophetic band) but Volume is low and there is no verbal contact, so the echo is contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: The pattern of women materially sustaining a prophet (the widow of Zarephath feeding Elijah) is a broad scriptural type Luke may activate, but the link is thematic rather than verbal. Marked contested for low Volume.

pericopes.text: When a great multitude came together, and people from every city were coming to him, he spoke by a parable. “The farmer went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the road, and it was trampled under foot, and the birds of the sky devoured it. Other seed fell on the rock, and as soon as it grew, it withered away, because it had no moisture. Other fell amid the thorns, and the thorns grew with it, and choked it. Other fell into the good ground, and grew, and produced one hundred times as much fruit.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!”

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The sower's seed that yields fruit aligns with Isaiah's rain/word that does not return empty but accomplishes God's purpose; Luke's own interpretation (8:11, 'the seed is the word of God') makes the identification of seed with the efficacious divine word, satisfying Coherence and Availability. Volume rests on conceptual rather than verbal correspondence.

echoes.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: Isaac sowing and reaping a hundredfold in one year ('a hundred times', meah shearim) supplies the exact extraordinary yield figure of 8:8. The shared numeric idiom of blessed harvest gives some Volume, but the allusion is faint and contested.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's 'sow not among thorns' provides the agrarian image of seed choked by thorns (8:7), an established prophetic metaphor for a heart unready for the word. Low Volume but real Coherence with Luke's interpretation.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: Hosea's call to 'sow righteousness, reap steadfast love' and break up fallow ground belongs to the same prophetic sowing topos that frames the parable. Contested; thematic only.

pericopes.text: Then his disciples asked him, “What does this parable mean?” He said, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables; that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: Jesus directly cites Isaiah's commission, 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand,' to explain why he teaches in parables. The verbal dependence is explicit and abbreviated from the LXX, giving maximal Volume, Recurrence (a key NT text), and Availability.

echoes.text: ‘Hear now this, foolish people, and without understanding; who have eyes, and don’t see; who have ears, and don’t hear:
echoes.note: Jeremiah's 'who have eyes but see not, who have ears but hear not' is a cognate prophetic oracle of judicial obduracy that stands behind the Isaiah 6 citation and reinforces it. Volume is real but secondary to the explicit Isaiah quotation.

echoes.text: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's 'they have eyes to see but see not, ears to hear but hear not, for they are a rebellious house' is the third member of the prophetic obduracy cluster Luke draws on. Coherence with the seeing/hearing motif is strong; contested only as to whether Luke intends it specifically alongside Isaiah.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's 'the LORD has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, ears to hear' is the wilderness root of the seeing/hearing-but-not idiom. Faint and contested behind the nearer prophetic texts.

pericopes.text: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. Those along the road are those who hear, then the devil comes, and takes away the word from their heart, that they may not believe and be saved. Those on the rock are they who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but these have no root, who believe for a while, then fall away in time of temptation. That which fell among the thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring no fruit to maturity. That in the good ground, these are such as in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produces fruit with patience.

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: Luke's interpretive key, 'the seed is the word of God' that bears fruit with patience, draws on Isaiah's image of the word that goes forth and accomplishes its purpose like rain on the soil. The explicit identification of seed and word grounds the Coherence.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: The thorns that choke the word (8:14) reapply Jeremiah's agrarian warning against sowing among thorns. Low Volume, supporting echo.

echoes.text: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's maxim that the fruit discloses the cultivation of the heart parallels Luke's 'honest and good heart' that holds the word and bears fruit, a Second-Temple wisdom resonance. Contested; thematic.

pericopes.text: “No one, when he has lit a lamp, covers it with a container, or puts it under a bed; but puts it on a stand, that those who enter in may see the light. For nothing is hidden, that will not be revealed; nor anything secret, that will not be known and come to light. Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.”

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: 'Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed' echoes Qoheleth's conclusion that God will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing. The disclosure-of-the-concealed motif gives genuine Coherence, though Luke's eschatological revelation is broader.

echoes.text: he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
echoes.note: Daniel's praise that God 'reveals the deep and hidden things, knowing what is in the darkness, and light dwells with him' supplies the light/revelation-of-the-hidden pairing of 8:16-17. Faint verbal contact; contested.

echoes.text: For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light. Reproofs of instruction are the way of life,
echoes.note: 'The commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light' offers the lamp-as-word imagery for the lit lamp set on a stand, coherent with the surrounding word-of-God context. Low Volume, contested.

pericopes.text: His mother and brothers came to him, and they could not come near him for the crowd. It was told him by some saying, “Your mother and your brothers stand outside, desiring to see you.” But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are these who hear the word of God, and do it.”

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: Levi's prizing of God's word and covenant above kin ('he disregarded his brothers') parallels Jesus' redefinition of family as those who hear and do the word of God. Coherence is real but Volume is faint and contested.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might. These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart;
echoes.note: Jesus' criterion, 'those who hear the word of God and do it,' resonates with the Shema's command to hear (shema) and keep God's words in the heart. The hear-and-do pairing is Deuteronomic; contested as a specific allusion.

echoes.text: They come to you as the people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear your words, but don’t do them; for with their mouth they show much love, but their heart goes after their gain. Behold, you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument; for they hear your words, but they don’t do them.
echoes.note: Ezekiel rebukes those who hear the word but do not do it; Jesus' true family are precisely those who both hear and do. The hearing-versus-doing contrast supplies Coherence; Volume low.

pericopes.text: Now on one of those days, he entered into a boat, himself and his disciples, and he said to them, “Let’s go over to the other side of the lake.” So they launched out. But as they sailed, he fell asleep. A wind storm came down on the lake, and they were taking on dangerous amounts of water. They came to him, and awoke him, saying, “Master, master, we are dying!” He awoke, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water, and they ceased, and it was calm. He said to them, “Where is your faith?” Being afraid they marveled, saying one to another, “Who is this, then, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?”

echoes.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]
echoes.note: The stilling of the storm closely follows the psalm's mariners who cry to the LORD in the tempest, whereupon 'he made the storm a calm and the waves were stilled' and brought them to harbor. The shared sequence (sea-peril, cry, divine stilling, calm) gives strong Volume and the clearest scriptural template for the pericope.

echoes.text: who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the turmoil of the nations.
echoes.note: God 'who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves' supplies the precise divine prerogative the disciples wonder at ('who is this that even the winds and water obey him?'). The identification of Jesus with YHWH's sea-mastery is the theological point, giving high Coherence.

echoes.text: You rule the pride of the sea. When its waves rise up, you calm them.
echoes.note: 'You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them' is a near-verbal parallel to Jesus rebuking the raging water (8:24). Reinforces the YHWH-as-sea-ruler matrix; Coherence strong, Volume moderate.

echoes.text: He rebuked the Red Sea also, and it was dried up; so he led them through the depths, as through a desert.
echoes.note: God 'rebuked the Red Sea and it dried up' supplies the verb of rebuking the sea applied to Jesus' rebuke of wind and water. Exodus-sea overtone; lower Volume, contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: “Or who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke out of the womb, when I made clouds its garment, and wrapped it in thick darkness, marked out for it my bound, set bars and doors, and said, ‘Here you may come, but no further. Here your proud waves shall be stayed?’
echoes.note: The Creator who set bounds for the sea, saying 'thus far shall you come and no farther,' grounds the disciples' awe that the winds and water obey Jesus. The creational mastery-of-chaos motif gives strong theological Coherence.

echoes.text: But Yahweh sent out a great wind on the sea, and there was a mighty storm on the sea, so that the ship was likely to break up. Then the mariners were afraid, and every man cried to his god. They threw the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten the ship. But Jonah had gone down into the innermost parts of the ship, and he was laying down, and was fast asleep. So the ship master came to him, and said to him, “What do you mean, sleeper? Arise, […]
echoes.note: The closest narrative analogue: a great storm at sea while the protagonist sleeps in the boat, terrified mariners, and a rousing to address the crisis. Volume from the shared scene (asleep in storm, awakened) is substantial, though Jesus' role inverts Jonah's.

echoes.text: Yahweh is slow to anger, and great in power, and will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. Yahweh has his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. He rebukes the sea, and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers. Bashan languishes, and Carmel; and the flower of Lebanon languishes.
echoes.note: 'His way is in the whirlwind and storm... he rebukes the sea and makes it dry' attributes storm-rebuking theophany to YHWH, coherent with Jesus' act. Faint verbal contact; contested.

echoes.text: You covered it with the deep as with a cloak. The waters stood above the mountains. At your rebuke they fled. At the voice of your thunder they hurried away. The mountains rose, the valleys sank down, to the place which you had assigned to them. You have set a boundary that they may not pass over; that they don’t turn again to cover the earth.
echoes.note: The Creator's rebuke that sets the waters' bounds belongs to the same chaos-control hymnody behind the scene. Low Volume, supporting echo.

pericopes.text: They arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus stepped ashore, a certain man out of the city who had demons for a long time met him. He wore no clothes, and didn’t live in a house, but in the tombs. When he saw Jesus, he cried out, and fell down before him, and with a loud voice said, “What do I have to do with you, Jesus, you Son of the Most High God? I beg you, don’t torment me!” For Jesus was commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man. For the unclean spirit had often seized the man. He was kept under guard, and bound with chains and fetters. Breaking the bands apart, he was driven by the demon into the desert. Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered into him. They begged him that he would not command them to go into the abyss. Now there was there a herd of many pigs feeding on the mountain, and they begged him that he would allow them to enter into those. He allowed them. The demons came out of the man, and entered into the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake, and were drowned. When those who fed them saw what had happened, they fled, and told it in the city and in the country. People went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus, and found the man from whom the demons had gone out, sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid. Those who saw it told them how he who had been possessed by demons was healed. All the people of the surrounding country of the Gadarenes asked him to depart from them, for they were very much afraid. He entered into the boat, and returned. But the man from whom the demons had gone out begged him that he might go with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, “Return to your house, and declare what great things God has done for you.” He went his way, proclaiming throughout the whole city what great things Jesus had done for him.

echoes.text: “I am inquired of by those who didn’t ask; I am found by those who didn’t seek me: I said, See me, see me, to a nation that was not called by my name. I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts; a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens, and burning incense on bricks; who sit among the graves, and lodge in the secret places; who eat pig’s flesh, […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's rebellious people 'who sit in tombs and lodge in secret places, who eat swine's flesh' and say 'keep to yourself, do not come near me' map strikingly onto the demoniac among the tombs, the herd of swine, and the man's cry 'what have I to do with you?' The cluster of tombs + swine + repulsion gives notable Volume.

echoes.text: who sit among the graves, and lodge in the secret places; who eat pig’s flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
echoes.note: The specific verse pairing dwelling among the tombs with eating swine's flesh concentrates the two defining impurities of the scene. Coherence with Luke's Gentile-territory unclean-spirit setting is strong.

echoes.text: The pig, because he has a split hoof, and is cloven-footed, but doesn’t chew the cud, he is unclean to you. Of their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch; they are unclean to you.
echoes.note: The classification of the pig as unclean (do not eat, do not touch its carcass) gives the swine their symbolic charge as fit vessels for unclean spirits in this Gentile region. Coherence is strong even though Luke does not cite the law.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The demons' dread of the 'abyss' (8:31) evokes the primordial deep (LXX abyssos in Gen 1:2) as the place of chaos/restraint; the swine drowning in the lake returns the chaotic powers to the watery abyss. Conceptual, contested.

echoes.text: Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, from the horns of the wild oxen, you have answered me.
echoes.note: The cry of one tormented, naked, and bound, delivered by God, faintly resonates with the psalmist's plea for rescue from beastly powers; the 'Most High God' title also recurs in the psalms. Low Volume; contested.

echoes.text: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace: he spoke and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here. Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the midst of the fire.
echoes.note: The Gentile address of God as 'the Most High God' (8:28) matches the Aramaic court-tale title used by Nebuchadnezzar, a Septuagintal idiom for the God of Israel on pagan lips. Real but minor lexical contact.

pericopes.text: When Jesus returned, the multitude welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. Behold, there came a man named Jairus, and he was a ruler of the synagogue. He fell down at Jesus’ feet, and begged him to come into his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. But as he went, the multitudes pressed against him. A woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years, who had spent all her living on physicians, and could not be healed by any, came behind him, and touched the fringe of his cloak, and immediately the flow of her blood stopped. Jesus said, “Who touched me?” When all denied it, Peter and those with him said, “Master, the multitudes press and jostle you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” But Jesus said, “Someone did touch me, for I perceived that power has gone out of me.” When the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared to him in the presence of all the people the reason why she had touched him, and how she was healed immediately. He said to her, “Daughter, cheer up. Your faith has made you well. Go in peace.”

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period; all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period: she is unclean. Every bed whereon she lies all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period: and everything whereon she sits shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period. Whoever touches these things […]
echoes.note: The woman's twelve-year 'flow of blood' is precisely the chronic discharge (zavah) of Leviticus that renders a woman and all she touches unclean. Luke's scene presupposes this purity legislation: her secret touch and trembling fear of exposure make sense only against the impurity she would transmit. Strong Volume and Availability.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: The 'fringe' (kraspedon, tzitzit) she touches is the tassel commanded in Numbers as a reminder of the LORD's commandments. Luke's specific detail of the garment's fringe activates this legal-symbolic object as the locus of healing power.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: Malachi's promise that 'the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (kanaph)' uses the same word as the garment's 'fringe/corner,' a wordplay long read here: healing flows from the hem of the messianic figure. Coherence is strong though the link rests on the kanaph double sense.

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood, she shall be in her impurity seven days: and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening. “‘Everything that she lies on in her impurity shall be unclean. Everything also that she sits on shall be unclean. Whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the evening. Whoever touches anything that she sits on shall wash his […]
echoes.note: The broader menstrual-impurity statutes reinforce why anyone touched by the woman, and she by the crowd, incurs uncleanness, sharpening the scandal of her contact with Jesus. Supporting Coherence; lower independent Volume.

pericopes.text: While he still spoke, one from the ruler of the synagogue’s house came, saying to him, “Your daughter is dead. Don’t trouble the Teacher.” But Jesus hearing it, answered him, “Don’t be afraid. Only believe, and she will be healed.” When he came to the house, he didn’t allow anyone to enter in, except Peter, John, James, the father of the child, and her mother. All were weeping and mourning her, but he said, “Don’t weep. She isn’t dead, but sleeping.” They were ridiculing him, knowing that she was dead. But he put them all outside, and taking her by the hand, he called, saying, “Child, arise!” Her spirit returned, and she rose up immediately. He commanded that something be given to her to eat. Her parents were amazed, but he commanded them to tell no one what had been done.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah's raising of the widow of Zarephath's son is the prototype Luke evokes: a prophet restores a dead child, here a 'spirit returned' (8:55) echoing the LXX's restoration of the boy's breath. The Elijah/Elisha raising type is programmatic for Luke's Christology.

echoes.text: When the child was grown, one day he went out to his father to the reapers. He said to his father, “My head! My head!” He said to his servant, “Carry him to his mother.” When he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees until noon, and then died. She went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God, and shut the door on him, and went out. She called to her husband, and said, “Please send me one of the servants, and one of the […]
echoes.note: Elisha's raising of the Shunammite's only child supplies the closest structural parallel: an only/beloved child dies, mourners are excluded, the prophet acts privately and the child revives. Strong narrative Volume and Recurrence in Luke's prophet-typology.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Jesus' 'she is not dead but sleeping' draws on the established sleep-as-death metaphor that Daniel crystallizes for resurrection ('those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake'). Coherence with Luke's awakening of the girl is good; Volume conceptual.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: The specific motif of giving the revived child sustenance and the privacy of the act recalls Elisha shutting the door; reinforces the Elisha parallel above. Listed for the closing detail (8:55, give her to eat). Contested as independent.

pericopes.text: He called the twelve together, and gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases. He sent them out to preach the Kingdom of God, and to heal the sick. He said to them, “Take nothing for your journey—neither staffs, nor wallet, nor bread, nor money; neither have two coats apiece. Into whatever house you enter, stay there, and depart from there. As many as don’t receive you, when you depart from that city, shake off even the dust from your feet for a testimony against them.” They departed, and went throughout the villages, preaching the Good News, and healing everywhere.

echoes.text: Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the face of the child.”
echoes.note: The terse travel-light, single-minded urgency of the mission ('take nothing... salute no one') resonates with Elisha dispatching Gehazi with his staff and the command to greet no one on the road. Coherence with Luke's Elijah/Elisha typology for the prophetic mission is moderate, but the verbal contact is faint and the prop (staff) is inverted, so contested.

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Shaking off the dust 'for a testimony against them' enacts a prophetic curse-gesture; Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his garment as a symbolic execration on covenant-breakers. The shared shaking-as-witness logic gives moderate volume; the gesture is a recognizable Second-Temple idiom of repudiation.

echoes.text: Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
echoes.note: Washing the dust of a place from the feet recalls the ancient hospitality of footwashing (Abraham to the three visitors); refusal of hospitality is symmetrically answered by dust-shaking. The connection is thematic and faint, hence contested.

pericopes.text: Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him; and he was very perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead, and by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the old prophets had risen again. Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this, about whom I hear such things?” He sought to see him.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The popular guess that 'Elijah had appeared' presupposes Malachi's promise that Elijah returns before the day of the LORD, a live Second-Temple expectation (cf. Sirach 48:10). High coherence with Luke's whole Elijah-return motif and high availability.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The alternative guess, 'one of the old prophets has risen,' draws on the Mosaic promise of a raised-up prophet like Moses and broader expectation of an eschatological prophet. Moderate volume; coherent with Luke's prophet Christology, climaxing in the Transfiguration 'listen to him.'

echoes.text: Who was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, To pacify anger, before it brake forth into wrath; To turn the heart of the father to the son, And to restore the tribes of Jacob.
echoes.note: Sirach explicitly canonizes the returning-Elijah hope ('ready... to turn the hearts'), the very expectation Herod's informants voice. Deuterocanonical availability strengthens the case that this is the operative cultural script behind v.8.

pericopes.text: The apostles, when they had returned, told him what things they had done. He took them, and withdrew apart to a deserted place of a city called Bethsaida. But the multitudes, perceiving it, followed him. He welcomed them, and spoke to them of the Kingdom of God, and he cured those who needed healing. The day began to wear away; and the twelve came, and said to him, “Send the multitude away, that they may go into the surrounding villages and farms, and lodge, and get food, for we are here in a deserted place.” But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we should go and buy food for all these people.” For they were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples, “Make them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” They did so, and made them all sit down. He took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to the sky, he blessed them, and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the multitude. They ate, and were all filled. They gathered up twelve baskets of broken pieces that were left over.

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with the protest 'how can I set this before a hundred?', the command to give, eating, and food left over. The structural parallel (insufficient loaves, servant objection, feeding, surplus) is the closest single antecedent and high in volume and coherence with Luke's Elijah/Elisha matrix.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: Bread provided to a vast crowd in a 'deserted place' (wilderness), gathered and fully satisfied with leftovers measured, evokes the manna narrative. High coherence with the new-Moses wilderness-feeding typology that the very next pericopes (Transfiguration, 'exodus') develop.

echoes.text: Where could I get meat to give to all this people? For they weep to me, saying, ‘Give us meat, that we may eat.’ I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If you treat me this way, please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight; and don’t let me see my wretchedness.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over […]
echoes.note: Moses' despairing 'Where am I to get meat for all this people?' and God's provision in the wilderness underlie the disciples' 'send the multitude away... we are in a deserted place.' The seating in companies recalls Israel's ordered camp; volume and coherence both strong.

echoes.text: Yes, they spoke against God. They said, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, so that waters gushed out, and streams overflowed. Can he give bread also? Will he provide flesh for his people?” Therefore Yahweh heard, and was angry. A fire was kindled against Jacob, anger also went up against Israel, because they didn’t believe in God, and didn’t trust in his salvation. Yet he commanded the skies above, and opened the doors […]
echoes.note: 'Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?'—the psalm's retrospect on manna and quail, where the people 'ate and were well filled,' matches Luke's 'they ate and were all filled.' Strong verbal echo ('filled') and thematic coherence with wilderness provision.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me. You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil. My cup runs over.
echoes.note: The shepherd seating the flock on grass and spreading a table in the presence of need colors the orderly groups and abundant provision; Mark makes the 'green grass' explicit. Moderate in Luke, where the pastoral detail is muted, so lower volume here.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: The crowd as sheep without a shepherd needing a leader to go before them (Moses' prayer for a successor) frames Jesus' compassion and shepherd-feeding; explicit in Mark's parallel and coherent with Luke's new-Moses theme.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.
echoes.note: The promise of one Davidic shepherd who feeds the scattered flock undergirds the feeding as messianic shepherding. Faint in Luke's spare account; figural and contested.

pericopes.text: As he was praying alone, the disciples were with him, and he asked them, “Who do the multitudes say that I am?” They answered, “‘John the Baptizer,’ but others say, ‘Elijah,’ and others, that one of the old prophets is risen again.” He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “The Christ of God.”

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: Peter's confession 'the Christ of God' names the Anointed One of Psalm 2, the royal son set by God against the nations' rulers. Coherent with the immediately surrounding Herod material and the Transfiguration's 'my Son'; moderate volume by title alone.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The crowd's repeated options—John, Elijah, a risen old prophet—again invoke the Malachi/Sirach returning-Elijah and eschatological-prophet hopes, here set against the true confession. Recurrence within the chapter strengthens it.

pericopes.text: But he warned them, and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up.” He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross,and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake, the same will save it. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self? For whoever will be ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed, when he comes in his glory, and the glory of the Father, and of the holy angels. But I tell you the truth: There are some of those who stand here, who will in no way taste of death, until they see the Kingdom of God.”

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected' echoes the Servant who is 'despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows.' High coherence with Luke's passion theology (cf. Luke 22:37 citing Isa 53), strong volume on rejection/suffering.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of Man,' here joined to suffering and to coming 'in his glory' (v.26), draws on Daniel's heavenly figure who receives dominion and glory. Strong availability and coherence; Luke fuses Danielic glory with Isaianic suffering.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: Being 'rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes' evokes the stone the builders rejected, which Luke cites explicitly at 20:17. Moderate volume here (no quotation yet) but high coherence with Luke's rejection-vindication pattern.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'The third day be raised up' may echo Hosea's 'on the third day he will raise us up,' read messianically in later Jewish tradition. Verbal contact is suggestive but the third-day formula is multiply sourced, so contested and low volume.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Raised up on the third day' and the promise that some will not 'taste death' draw on resurrection/awakening hope crystallized in Daniel. Faint and diffuse; figural support for the resurrection language.

echoes.text: But if the wicked turn from all his sins that he has committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die.
echoes.note: 'Whoever desires to save his life will lose it' has a distant gravitational pull toward prophetic life/death covenant choices, but the saying is proverbial and not verbally anchored. Low volume, contested.

pericopes.text: About eight days after these sayings, he took with him Peter, John, and James, and went up onto the mountain to pray. As he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became white and dazzling. Behold, two men were talking with him, who were Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory, and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they were fully awake, they saw his glory, and the two men who stood with him. As they were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let’s make three tents: one for you, and one for Moses, and one for Elijah,” not knowing what he said. While he said these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered into the cloud. A voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!” When the voice came, Jesus was found alone. They were silent, and told no one in those days any of the things which they had seen.

echoes.text: Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud. The appearance of Yahweh’s glory was like devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the eyes of the children of Israel. Moses entered into the midst of the cloud, and went up on the mountain; and Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
echoes.note: Going up the mountain, the cloud overshadowing, the glory, the entering into the cloud, and the divine voice replay Moses' Sinai ascent. 'About eight days' may even mirror Exodus 24:16's 'six days... the seventh day.' Very high volume and coherence in Luke's new-Sinai staging.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him. Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses spoke to them. […]
echoes.note: The altered, shining appearance of Jesus' face directly parallels Moses' face shining after speaking with God on the mountain. Strong verbal/visual volume; Luke uniquely heightens the facial transformation, tightening the Moses typology.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: 'Listen to him' from the cloud quotes the Mosaic 'a prophet like me... him you shall heed,' identifying Jesus as the eschatological prophet-like-Moses. High volume (near-verbatim imperative) and total coherence with Moses' presence on the mount.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: 'This is my beloved Son' draws on the royal decree 'You are my Son,' fusing enthronement sonship with the Transfiguration glory. High coherence with the chapter's Christ-confession and the baptismal voice Luke echoes.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: The heavenly designation of the Son in whom God delights blends the Servant 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights' with the royal Son. Moderate volume in Luke's wording; coherent with the Isaianic-Servant note already sounded in v.22.

echoes.text: “Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded to him in Horeb for all Israel, even statutes and ordinances. Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Moses and Elijah standing together is precisely the Malachi pairing—'remember the law of Moses... I will send Elijah'—epitomizing the Law and the Prophets that witness to Jesus. Strong coherence; their joint appearance is unlikely to be accidental.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.
echoes.note: The dazzling white clothing ('white as snow,' raiment 'glistering') colors the transfigured glory with the apocalyptic radiance of the Ancient of Days and heavenly beings. Moderate volume via the whiteness motif; coherent with the Danielic Son of Man already in v.26.

echoes.text: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle. Moses wasn’t able to enter into the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud stayed on it, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle.
echoes.note: The overshadowing cloud from which the voice speaks recalls the glory-cloud filling the tabernacle, especially as Peter proposes building 'tents/booths' for the three. The tent/tabernacle-glory linkage gives moderate volume and good coherence.

echoes.text: It will happen that everyone who is left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up from year to year to worship the King, Yahweh of Armies, and to keep the feast of tents.
echoes.note: Peter's wish to make three 'booths' may glance at the eschatological Feast of Tabernacles when the nations keep the festival before the King. Faint and dependent on the skene wordplay; contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night:
echoes.note: Moses and Elijah speak of Jesus' 'exodus' he was to accomplish at Jerusalem; the very word frames the passion as a new exodus, with the guiding cloud as a faint backdrop. The 'exodus' lexeme is load-bearing but the pillar-of-cloud link is diffuse.

echoes.text: He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the Mount of God. He came there to a cave, and lodged there; and behold, Yahweh’s word came to him, and he said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I […]
echoes.note: Elijah's own theophany on the mountain (Horeb), reached after a fast and meeting God in stillness, undergirds his presence at this mountain revelation. Moderate coherence given Elijah is literally present; volume carried by the mountain-theophany pattern.

pericopes.text: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great multitude met him. Behold, a man from the crowd called out, saying, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. Behold, a spirit takes him, he suddenly cries out, and it convulses him so that he foams, and it hardly departs from him, bruising him severely. I begged your disciples to cast it out, and they couldn’t.” Jesus answered, “Faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” While he was still coming, the demon threw him down and convulsed him violently. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. They were all astonished at the majesty of God. But while all were marveling at all the things which Jesus did, he said to his disciples,

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: 'O faithless and perverse generation' quotes the Song of Moses' indictment of a 'perverse and crooked generation,' placing Jesus in Moses' prophetic-judge role just after descending the mountain. High verbal volume and pointed coherence with the new-Moses framing.

echoes.text: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.
echoes.note: The same Song continues, 'they are a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness,' reinforcing the 'faithless and perverse' double charge. Recurrence within Deuteronomy 32 strengthens the allusion's volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will this people despise me? and how long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have worked among them?
echoes.note: 'How long shall I be with you and bear with you?' resonates with God's 'How long will this people despise me... how long will they not believe?' in the wilderness. Faint verbal contact but coherent with the wilderness-generation motif; contested.

echoes.text: He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
echoes.note: Jesus restoring the convulsed only son and 'giving him back to his father' faintly recalls Elisha raising the Shunammite's son and giving him back. The 'gave him back' gesture (cf. also 1 Kings 17:23) is the load-bearing link; low volume, contested.

echoes.text: Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
echoes.note: Elijah 'delivered him to his mother'—'see, your son lives'—parallels Jesus giving the healed only child back to his father. Coherent with Luke's Elijah typology (cf. the 'only son' at Nain, 7:12-15) but verbally faint here.

pericopes.text: “Let these words sink into your ears, for the Son of Man will be delivered up into the hands of men.” But they didn’t understand this saying. It was concealed from them, that they should not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man will be delivered up into the hands of men' echoes the Servant whom 'the LORD delivered up' for iniquity (LXX paradidomi). Moderate volume via the handing-over verb; coherent with the Isaianic passion reading begun in v.22.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The recurring 'Son of Man' title keeps the Danielic figure in view even as Luke subverts expectation toward suffering. Recurrence across vv.22, 26, 44 builds cumulative volume.

pericopes.text: There arose an argument among them about which of them was the greatest. Jesus, perceiving the reasoning of their hearts, took a little child, and set him by his side, and said to them, “Whoever receives this little child in my name receives me. Whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For whoever is least among you all, this one will be great.”

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is least among you all, this one will be great' inverts status as in Hannah's song, where God raises the poor and lowly and seats them with princes—a Lukan reversal motif (cf. Magnificat). Thematic coherence is high but verbal contact faint; contested.

echoes.text: Now the man Moses was very humble, above all the men who were on the surface of the earth.
echoes.note: The valorizing of the least/humblest in a dispute over greatness faintly recalls Moses, 'very meek, above all men,' set over against the leaders' rivalry. Diffuse and figural, hence contested.

pericopes.text: John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he doesn’t follow with us.” Jesus said to him, “Don’t forbid him, for he who is not against us is for us.”

echoes.text: But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told Moses, and said, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!” Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen men, answered, “My lord Moses, forbid them!” Moses said to him, “Are you […]
echoes.note: John's 'we forbade him, because he doesn't follow with us' replays Joshua's 'My lord Moses, forbid them!' when Eldad and Medad prophesy outside the camp, and Jesus' 'Do not forbid' answers with Moses' 'Would that all the LORD's people were prophets.' Strong structural and verbal parallel (forbid/the Spirit working beyond the inner circle); high coherence with Luke's broader-Spirit theme.

pericopes.text: It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem, and sent messengers before his face. They went, and entered into a village of the Samaritans, so as to prepare for him. They didn’t receive him, because he was traveling with his face set towards Jerusalem. When his disciples, James and John, saw this, they said, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky, and destroy them, just as Elijah did?” But he turned and rebuked them, “You don’t know of what kind of spirit you are. For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them.” They went to another village.

echoes.text: Elijah answered to the captain of fifty, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky, and consume you and your fifty!” Fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty. Again he sent to him another captain of fifty and his fifty. He answered him, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down quickly!’” Elijah answered them, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky, and consume you and your fifty!” The fire of God came down […]
echoes.note: 'Command fire to come down from the sky... just as Elijah did' explicitly cites Elijah calling down fire on the messengers from Samaria; the Samaritan setting makes the reference exact. High volume (named comparison) and coherence; Jesus' rebuke signals a deliberate contrast with the Elijah model.

echoes.text: When Yahweh was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
echoes.note: 'The days were near that he should be taken up' and Jesus 'set his face' draw on Elijah's assumption ('when the LORD was about to take up Elijah') and prophetic resolve. The analepsis/analambano language tightly binds the journey's start to Elijah's ascent; high coherence.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.
echoes.note: Jesus 'set his face' resolutely toward Jerusalem echoes the Servant's 'I have set my face like a flint' in obedient suffering. Moderate volume via the face-setting idiom; coherent with the Isaianic Servant strand running through the chapter.

echoes.text: Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, and preach toward the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the land of Israel;
echoes.note: 'Set your face toward Jerusalem and prophesy' is a recurring prophetic commission idiom that colors Jesus' face-setting as prophetic confrontation. The phrase is multiply attested in Ezekiel, so diffuse and contested.

pericopes.text: As they went on the way, a certain man said to him, “I want to follow you wherever you go, Lord.” Jesus said to him, “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head.” He said to another, “Follow me!” But he said, “Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father.” But Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead, but you go and announce the Kingdom of God.” Another also said, “I want to follow you, Lord, but first allow me to say good-bye to those who are at my house.” But Jesus said to him, “No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the Kingdom of God.”

echoes.text: So he departed there, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing, with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed over to him, and cast his mantle on him. He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?” He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, […]
echoes.note: 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back' directly engages Elisha's call: found plowing, he asks to kiss his parents farewell before following, and Elijah lets him. Jesus radicalizes the precedent—no looking back, no delayed farewell—making the plowing image and the farewell request unmistakable. Very high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?”
echoes.note: 'Allow me first to say good-bye to those at my house' nearly quotes Elisha's 'let me kiss my father and mother, and then I will follow you.' The verbal correspondence in the third would-be follower is the strongest single anchor for the Elisha typology here.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
echoes.note: 'Looking back' as fatal hesitation may glance at Lot's wife, the proverbial backward look that forfeits deliverance. Faint and figural relative to the dominant Elisha frame; contested.

echoes.text: And he called him, and said, “My child, if I die, bury me. Don’t despise your mother. Honor her all the days of your life, and do that which is pleasing to her, and don’t grieve her.
echoes.note: 'Let me first bury my father' reflects the supreme filial duty of burial dramatized in Tobit, against which Jesus' 'leave the dead to bury their dead' is shockingly subversive. Deuterocanonical availability illuminates the cultural weight Jesus overturns, though it is background rather than a textual echo.

echoes.text: but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him into the ship, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship.
echoes.note: 'The birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head' may faintly invert creation's provision of resting places (the dove finding no rest, then nesting). Very low volume; offered only as a faint figural counterpoint.

pericopes.text: Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place, where he was about to come. Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest. Go your ways. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves. Carry no purse, nor wallet, nor sandals. Greet no one on the way. Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house.’ If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you. Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Don’t go from house to house. Into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat the things that are set before you. Heal the sick who are therein, and tell them, ‘The Kingdom of God has come near to you.’ But into whatever city you enter, and they don’t receive you, go out into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust from your city that clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the Kingdom of God has come near to you.’ I tell you, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.
echoes.note: Jesus appoints seventy and sends them out as bearers of his commissioned authority, evoking the seventy elders on whom God places the spirit that was on Moses. Volume is strong in the precise number seventy and the theme of delegated, Spirit-empowered authority; coherence with Luke's Moses typology (the prophet like Moses, Acts 3) reinforces it.

echoes.text: Moses went out, and told the people Yahweh’s words; and he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people, and set them around the Tent. Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more.
echoes.note: The gathering and dispersal of the seventy who then prophesy parallels the sending two by two and the later joyful report of empowered ministry. Recurrence of the seventy-elders motif within the same Numbers pericope strengthens the linkage to Luke's mission.

echoes.text: He said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance.
echoes.note: The seventy who ascend with Moses to ratify the covenant supply an alternate or supplementary base for the number seventy as a body of authorized representatives of Israel. Availability and the fixed numeral make it a plausible secondary source alongside Numbers 11.

echoes.text: Now this is the history of the generations of the sons of Noah and of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth were: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer were: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan were: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. Of these were the islands of the nations divided in their lands, everyone after his language, after their families, in […]
echoes.note: The Table of Nations was reckoned in Jewish tradition as seventy (LXX seventy-two) nations, so a seventy(-two)-fold mission figurally anticipates the Gentile harvest, fitting Luke-Acts' universal scope. The textual variant seventy/seventy-two mirrors the MT/LXX count of the nations, a coherence rarely coincidental.

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: The plentiful harvest needing laborers draws on the prophetic harvest as eschatological ingathering and judgment, where the sickle is put in because the harvest is ripe. The agrarian-eschatological coherence with the kingdom drawing near and the Sodom verdict supports the echo.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that Yahweh will thresh from the flowing stream of the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt; and you will be gathered one by one, children of Israel.
echoes.note: Isaiah's image of Israel gathered one by one in a threshing harvest offers a salvific (not only judicial) backdrop for the abundant harvest and few laborers. The link is faint, resting on shared harvest-of-the-people imagery rather than verbal contact.

echoes.text: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.
echoes.note: Sending disciples as lambs among wolves inverts Ezekiel's indictment of Israel's leaders as wolves tearing prey, casting the unreceptive towns in the role of predators against God's defenseless agents. The predator-prey coherence and prophetic-judgment context align with Luke's woes that follow.

echoes.text: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day.
echoes.note: Zephaniah likewise depicts the city's officials as evening wolves leaving nothing till morning, a stock prophetic figure for rapacious leadership menacing the righteous. The recurrence of the wolf-against-flock trope makes it a plausible faint background to lambs among wolves.

echoes.text: The two angels came to Sodom at evening. Lot sat in the gate of Sodom. Lot saw them, and rose up to meet them. He bowed himself with his face to the earth, and he said, “See now, my lords, please turn aside into your servant’s house, stay all night, wash your feet, and you can rise up early, and go on your way.” They said, “No, but we will stay in the street all night.” He urged them greatly, and they came in with him, and entered into his house. He made […]
echoes.note: The verdict that it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for the rejecting city invokes the paradigmatic destruction of Sodom as the measure of judgment for inhospitality. Volume and availability are high, and the inhospitality theme coheres exactly with rejecting the sent messengers.

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Shaking the dust off as a sign-act against the city recalls prophetic gestures of curse and separation, of which Nehemiah's shaking out his lap is a near analogue. The connection is by gesture-type rather than wording, so it remains faint.

pericopes.text: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you. You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades. Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me. Whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me.”

echoes.text: The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of Tarshish! For it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in. From the land of Kittim it is revealed to them. Be still, you inhabitants of the coast, you whom the merchants of Sidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished. On great waters, the seed of the Shihor, the harvest of the Nile, was her revenue. She was the market of nations. Be ashamed, Sidon; for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the […]
echoes.note: The naming of Tyre and Sidon as objects of judgment draws on the classic prophetic oracle against Tyre, here flipped so the Phoenician cities would have repented sooner than the Galilean towns. Availability and the precise city pairing support the allusion to the burden-of-Tyre tradition.

echoes.text: In the eleventh year, in the first of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, because Tyre has said against Jerusalem, Aha, she is broken: the gate of the peoples; she is turned to me; I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste: therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea causes its waves to come up. They shall destroy the walls of Tyre, and […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's extended oracles against Tyre (and Sidon) form the deepest reservoir for Tyre and Sidon as archetypes of proud, doomed Gentile power. The pairing and the judgment frame recur strongly enough to count as a deliberate evocation.

echoes.text: “Yes, and what are you to me, Tyre, and Sidon, and all the regions of Philistia? Will you repay me? And if you repay me, I will swiftly and speedily return your repayment on your own head. Because you have taken my silver and my gold, and have carried my finest treasures into your temples, and have sold the children of Judah and the children of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, that you may remove them far from their border. Behold, I will stir them up […]
echoes.note: Joel arraigns Tyre and Sidon together for their treatment of God's people, a near-verbal precedent for Luke's paired cities under judgment. The link is secondary to Isaiah/Ezekiel but adds recurrence to the Tyre-Sidon judgment motif.

echoes.text: and Hamath, also, which borders on it; Tyre and Sidon, because they are very wise. Tyre built herself a stronghold, and heaped up silver like the dust, and fine gold like the mire of the streets. Behold, the Lord will dispossess her, and he will strike her power in the sea; and she will be devoured with fire.
echoes.note: Zechariah foretells Tyre and Sidon's downfall despite their wisdom and wealth, reinforcing the proverbial doom of the pair. It is a faint contributory echo rather than the primary source.

echoes.text: The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
echoes.note: Repenting in sackcloth and ashes echoes the Ninevites' (and their king's) repentance, the Bible's signal case of a Gentile city repenting at a prophet's word. The coherence is pointed: pagan cities would have repented, shaming unrepentant Israel.

echoes.text: I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.
echoes.note: Sackcloth and ashes as the posture of contrition appears in Daniel's penitential prayer, part of a recurring biblical idiom for mourning and repentance. It is a stock-phrase echo supplying availability rather than a specific allusion.

echoes.text: You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.
echoes.note: Capernaum exalted to heaven yet brought down to Hades closely tracks the taunt over the king of Babylon who said he would ascend to heaven but is brought down to Sheol. Volume is high (near-verbal antithesis of heaven/Hades) and coherence with proud-city judgment is exact.

echoes.text: Son of man, tell the prince of Tyre, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Because your heart is lifted up, and you have said, I am a god, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet you are man, and not God, though you set your heart as the heart of God— behold, you are wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that is hidden from you; by your wisdom and by your understanding you have gotten yourself riches, and have gotten gold and silver into your […]
echoes.note: The prince of Tyre's self-exaltation to divine heights and his being cast down to the pit parallels Capernaum's reversal and sits beside the Tyre material just invoked. It is a coherent secondary backdrop to the heaven-to-Hades descent.

pericopes.text: The seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” He said to them, “I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven. Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you. Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

echoes.text: How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low!
echoes.note: Seeing Satan fall like lightning from heaven echoes the Day Star (LXX heosphoros) fallen from heaven in the Babylon taunt, a text read in Second Temple Judaism as the fall of a heavenly rebel. The immediate reuse of Isaiah 14 from the preceding woes strengthens recurrence and coherence.

echoes.text: You will tread on the lion and cobra. You will trample the young lion and the serpent underfoot.
echoes.note: Authority to tread on serpents and scorpions draws directly on the promise that the faithful will tread on the lion and the serpent, a psalm of protection from all harm. Volume (treading on serpents) and the explicit you-will-not-be-hurt assurance make this the primary base.

echoes.text: who led you through the great and terrible wilderness, with fiery serpents and scorpions, and thirsty ground where there was no water; who poured water for you out of the rock of flint;
echoes.note: The pairing serpents and scorpions matches Deuteronomy's description of the wilderness of fiery serpents and scorpions through which God led Israel safely. The exact lexical pair (serpents + scorpions) is rare enough to mark this as a deliberate combination with Psalm 91.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: Trampling the serpent and overcoming the power of the enemy figurally fulfills the protoevangelium's enmity between the woman's seed and the serpent whose head is crushed.
