The serpent-conquest coherence with Satan's fall makes the figural reading apt though it is not verbally explicit.

echoes.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Whoever has sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book.
echoes.note: Rejoicing that your names are written in heaven invokes the divine book from which the unfaithful may be blotted out, first named in Moses' intercession. Volume and the heavenly-register concept are strong, anchoring the saying in the book-of-life tradition.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: The eschatological deliverance of everyone found written in the book gives the names-in-heaven motif its end-time, salvific force matching Luke's contrast with mere demonic subjection. Coherence with the resurrection-life horizon supports the allusion.

echoes.text: Let them be blotted out of the book of life, and not be written with the righteous.
echoes.note: The book of the living, from which the wicked are blotted out and not enrolled among the righteous, supplies the negative counterpart to having one's name written in heaven. It adds recurrence to the heavenly-register tradition.

echoes.text: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.
echoes.note: The book of remembrance written before God for those who fear him is another instance of the heavenly registry of the faithful. It is a faint contributory echo within the same motif cluster.

pericopes.text: In that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, and said, “I thank you, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight.” Turning to the disciples, he said, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows who the Son is, except the Father, and who the Father is, except the Son, and he to whomever the Son desires to reveal him.” Turning to the disciples, he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes which see the things that you see, for I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them, and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.”

echoes.text: He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth:
echoes.note: Addressing the Father as Lord of heaven and earth echoes Melchizedek's blessing of God Most High, maker of heaven and earth, a creation-sovereignty title. The set phrase heaven and earth and the maker-of-all sense give moderate verbal contact.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”
echoes.note: Hiding these things from the wise and understanding but revealing them to little children reverses human wisdom in line with Isaiah's threat that the wisdom of the wise shall perish. The pointed wise-and-understanding wording matches Isaiah closely, supporting a deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we desired of you; for you have made known to us the king’s matter.
echoes.note: Daniel praises God who gives wisdom to the wise and reveals deep and hidden things, a revelation-of-mysteries pattern resonant with the Father revealing hidden things to the simple. The link is thematic (divine disclosure of mysteries) rather than verbal, so it stays faint.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: All things have been delivered to me by my Father figurally aligns with the Son of Man to whom dominion and authority are given. The handing-over-of-all coherence is real but the saying lacks distinctive Danielic vocabulary, so it is a low-confidence figural reading.

echoes.text: then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him, Rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.
echoes.note: The mutual delight of Father and Son and the Father's good pleasure faintly recall Wisdom rejoicing before God and delighting in humanity. The connection rests on the joy-before-God motif and is contested.

pericopes.text: Behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?” He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.” He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The lawyer's answer cites the Shema's command to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and strength, the heart of Israel's covenant confession. This is a near-verbatim quotation (Luke adds mind), unmistakable in volume and availability.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: And your neighbor as yourself quotes verbatim the Holiness Code's neighbor-love command, which then drives the Who is my neighbor question. The exact wording and its programmatic role make this a clear quotation.

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Do this, and you will live echoes the Levitical promise that the one who keeps God's statutes shall live by them, framing eternal life as covenant obedience. The do-them-and-live formula is distinctive enough to register as an allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: The promise that God will circumcise the heart so Israel may love the LORD with all heart and soul stands behind the wholehearted love demanded here. It is a faint reinforcing echo of the Deuteronomic love-command cluster.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Inherit eternal life draws on the only clear OT promise of everlasting life, where some awake to everlasting life. The phrase supplies the eschatological referent though the contact is conceptual rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?” Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead. By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side. In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place, and saw him, passed by on the other side. But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, and gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’ Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

echoes.text: The men who have been mentioned by name rose up, and took the captives, and with the plunder clothed all who were naked among them, dressed them, gave them sandals, and gave them something to eat and to drink, anointed them, carried all the feeble of them on donkeys, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.
echoes.note: The compassionate Samaritan who binds wounds, anoints with oil, sets the man on his own animal, and brings him to care closely mirrors the men of Samaria who clothed, anointed, carried on donkeys, and brought the Judean captives to Jericho. The cluster of shared details (Samaritans, oil/anointing, animal, conveying the helpless toward Jericho) is too dense to be coincidental.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, ‘A priest shall not defile himself for the dead among his people; except for his relatives that are near to him: for his mother, for his father, for his son, for his daughter, for his brother, and for his virgin sister who is near to him, who has had no husband; for her he may defile himself.
echoes.note: The priest passing by on the other side gains its edge from the priestly prohibition against defilement by a corpse, since the victim appeared half dead. The corpse-purity background coheres with the priest's and Levite's avoidance, sharpening the parable's irony.

echoes.text: “He who touches the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. He shall purify himself with water on the third day, and on the seventh day he shall be clean; but if he doesn’t purify himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean. Whoever touches a dead person, the body of a man who has died, and doesn’t purify himself, defiles Yahweh’s tabernacle; and that soul shall be cut off from Israel; because the water for impurity was not […]
echoes.note: The general corpse-impurity law (seven-day uncleanness from touching a dead body) reinforces the ritual motive a priest and Levite might invoke for keeping their distance. It supplies recurrence to the purity rationale behind the passing by.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: The verdict that the neighbor is the one who showed mercy embodies Hosea's I desire mercy and not sacrifice, prioritizing compassion over the cultic scruples of priest and Levite. The mercy-over-cult coherence with the parable's structure supports the allusion.

echoes.text: From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it: wounds, welts, and open sores. They haven’t been closed, neither bandaged, neither soothed with oil.
echoes.note: Pouring oil and wine on wounds faintly recalls Isaiah's image of wounds not pressed out or softened with oil, the standard idiom for medicinal care. The contact is on the treatment imagery only and remains low-confidence.

pericopes.text: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house. She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word. But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.” Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

echoes.text: One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after, that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.
echoes.note: Mary's choice of the one thing needful, to sit and hear the Lord's word, resonates with the psalmist's one thing I have asked, to dwell in the LORD's house and gaze on his beauty. The shared one-thing focus on devoted presence before God gives a genuine if non-verbal echo.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my portion, says my soul; therefore will I hope in him.
echoes.note: Mary has chosen the good part faintly evokes the confession the LORD is my portion, the language of choosing God himself as one's allotted share. The portion/part motif is suggestive but the lexical bridge is thin.

echoes.text: Yahweh assigned my portion and my cup. You made my lot secure.
echoes.note: The LORD as my chosen portion and cup supplies the same theology of God as one's lasting allotment that the good part which will not be taken away expresses. It is a contributory echo within the portion-of-the-LORD tradition.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: Martha's busy hospitality toward the Lord visiting her house figurally recalls Abraham hastening to serve the three visitors at Mamre, the model scene of hospitality to a divine guest. The link is thematic (welcoming and serving the Lord) and faint, hence figural and contested.

pericopes.text: When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.” He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. Give us day by day our daily bread. Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’”

echoes.text: I will sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you have profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am Yahweh, says the Lord Yahweh, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes.
echoes.note: "May your name be kept holy" (hallowed be your name) echoes God's promise to sanctify his great name profaned among the nations. The eschatological hallowing of the Name is exactly the petition's force, supplying coherence with the kingdom-come request that follows.

echoes.text: But when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in the midst of him, they will sanctify my name. Yes, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and will stand in awe of the God of Israel.
echoes.note: "They will sanctify my name... and stand in awe of the God of Israel" supplies the human-side counterpart of the hallowing petition. Combined with Ezekiel 36:23 this gives recurrence of the sanctify-the-Name motif in the prophets, the petition's most available source.

echoes.text: You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be made holy among the children of Israel. I am Yahweh who makes you holy,
echoes.note: "You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel" is the legal seed of the later prophetic hope and may stand behind the liturgical formula. Faint and diffuse; flagged as low volume.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: "You, LORD, are our Father" grounds the direct address "Our Father." Isaiah's fatherhood-of-God language is a primary Second-Temple availability for the prayer's opening invocation.

echoes.text: But now, Yahweh, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you our potter; and we all are the work of your hand.
echoes.note: "You are our Father; we are the clay" reinforces the address to God as Father. Coherent with 63:16 but adds little independent volume, so marked low.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: "Your kingdom come" draws on the apocalyptic expectation that the God of heaven will set up an everlasting kingdom that shall never be destroyed. Daniel is the chief Second-Temple source for the coming-kingdom hope the petition voices.

echoes.text: Saviors will go up on Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau, and the kingdom will be Yahweh’s.
echoes.note: "The kingdom shall be the LORD's" anticipates the kingdom petition. A diffuse prophetic background rather than a verbal source; low volume.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: "Give us day by day our daily bread" evokes the manna gathered "a day's portion every day," testing daily dependence on God. The day-by-day rationing of Exodus 16 supplies the petition's coherence; Luke's distinctive "day by day" strengthens the link.

echoes.text: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me;
echoes.note: Agur's plea "feed me with the food that is needful for me" matches the bread petition's modest sufficiency and may inform the rare word epiousios. A strong thematic and lexical candidate for the source of "daily bread."

echoes.text: Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray.
echoes.note: "Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray" is the closest Second-Temple parallel to the reciprocal forgiveness clause. The conditional structure (forgive others / be forgiven) coheres tightly with Luke 11:4.

echoes.text: Help us, God of our salvation, for the glory of your name. Deliver us, and forgive our sins, for your name’s sake.
echoes.note: "Deliver us, and forgive our sins, for your name's sake" combines forgiveness, deliverance, and the Name in one verse, paralleling the prayer's later petitions. Diffuse and contested, but coherent with the whole prayer.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “Which of you, if you go to a friend at midnight, and tell him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread, for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,’ and he from within will answer and say, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you’? I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs.

echoes.text: Don’t say to your neighbor, “Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,” when you have it by you.
echoes.note: "Don't say to your neighbor, 'Go, and come again... when you have it by you'" rebukes the very deferral the sleeping friend voices. A wisdom backdrop to the parable's neighbor-obligation rather than a quotation; low volume.

echoes.text: Abraham drew near, and said, “Will you consume the righteous with the wicked? What if there are fifty righteous within the city? Will you consume and not spare the place for the fifty righteous who are in it? Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?” Yahweh said, “If I find in Sodom fifty […]
echoes.note: Abraham's persistent intercession with God, importunately pressing request upon request, prefigures the friend's shameless persistence rewarded. Figural rather than verbal; flagged contested.

pericopes.text: “I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened. “Which of you fathers, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, he won’t give him a snake instead of a fish, will he? Or if he asks for an egg, he won’t give him a scorpion, will he? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”

echoes.text: I love those who love me. Those who seek me diligently will find me.
echoes.note: "Those who seek me diligently will find me" supplies the seek-and-find logic of "keep seeking and you will find." Wisdom's promise of reward to the seeker is the most available source for the ask-seek-knock triad.

echoes.text: You shall seek me, and find me, when you shall search for me with all your heart.
echoes.note: "You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart" is the classic seek-and-find promise undergirding 11:9-10. Its recurrence with Proverbs 8:17 strengthens the case.

echoes.text: But from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: "You shall seek the LORD your God, and you shall find him, if you search after him" is another seek-find promise feeding the same matrix. Adds recurrence but little independent volume; low.

echoes.text: Seek Yahweh while he may be found; call you on him while he is near:
echoes.note: "Seek the LORD while he may be found; call on him while he is near" parallels the imperative to seek and the promise of access. Diffuse prophetic backdrop, contested.

echoes.text: The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger, but those who seek Yahweh shall not lack any good thing.
echoes.note: "Those who seek the LORD shall not lack any good thing" coheres with the assurance that the Father gives good gifts to those who ask. A faint sapiential-psalmic echo behind 11:13.

pericopes.text: He was casting out a demon, and it was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke; and the multitudes marveled. But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons.” Others, testing him, sought from him a sign from heaven. But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation. A house divided against itself falls. If Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. But if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore will they be your judges. But if I by the finger of God cast out demons, then the Kingdom of God has come to you. “When the strong man, fully armed, guards his own dwelling, his goods are safe. But when someone stronger attacks him and overcomes him, he takes from him his whole armor in which he trusted, and divides his plunder. “He that is not with me is against me. He who doesn’t gather with me scatters.

echoes.text: Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God:” and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.
echoes.note: "If I by the finger of God cast out demons" directly invokes the Egyptian magicians' confession, "This is the finger of God," before Pharaoh. The phrase ties Jesus' exorcisms to the Exodus power that defeats hostile powers and inaugurates God's reign; high volume and exact verbal correspondence.

echoes.text: Yahweh delivered to me the two stone tablets written with the finger of God On them were all the words which Yahweh spoke with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire in the day of the assembly.
echoes.note: The tablets "written with the finger of God" supply the other major OT use of the idiom, framing the finger as God's direct, unmediated agency. Recurrence of the phrase reinforces the Exodus 8:19 allusion behind 11:20.

echoes.text: Shall the plunder be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captives be delivered? But thus says Yahweh, “Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the plunder of the terrible shall be delivered; for I will contend with him who contends with you, and I will save your children.
echoes.note: "Shall the prey be taken from the mighty... yet the captives of the mighty shall be taken away" underlies the stronger-one despoiling the armed strong man (11:21-22). The image of plunder reclaimed from a mighty captor is the source of the binding-the-strong-man logic.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: "He shall divide the spoil with the strong" lends the dividing-of-plunder language in 11:22. A faint Servant-song coloring of the strong-man saying; contested and low.

echoes.text: If a man doesn’t relent, he will sharpen his sword; he has bent and strung his bow.
echoes.note: The enemy who "whets his sword... and makes ready his weapons" is a faint backdrop to the strong man "fully armed" guarding his goods. Diffuse imagery rather than source; low.

pericopes.text: The unclean spirit, when he has gone out of the man, passes through dry places, seeking rest, and finding none, he says, ‘I will turn back to my house from which I came out.’ When he returns, he finds it swept and put in order. Then he goes, and takes seven other spirits more evil than himself, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first.”

echoes.text: But wild animals of the desert will lie there, and their houses will be full of jackals. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will frolic there.
echoes.note: Desolate places haunted by desert demons ("wild beasts... satyrs shall dance there") inform the unclean spirit wandering through "dry places" seeking rest. The waterless-wilderness as demonic habitat is the OT backdrop; faint.

echoes.text: But the goat, on which the lot fell for the scapegoat, shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement for him, to send him away for the scapegoat into the wilderness.
echoes.note: Azazel's goat sent "into the wilderness" associates the desert with the locus of impurity/demonic banishment, paralleling the spirit's exile to dry places. Diffuse and contested.

echoes.text: When the demon smelled that smell, it fled into the uppermost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.
echoes.note: The demon Asmodeus fleeing to "the remotest parts of Egypt" (the desert) where he is bound parallels the unclean spirit traversing waterless regions. A Second-Temple availability for desert-as-demonic-haunt; low.

pericopes.text: It came to pass, as he said these things, a certain woman out of the multitude lifted up her voice, and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which nursed you!” But he said, “On the contrary, blessed are those who hear the word of God, and keep it.”

echoes.text: Leah said, “Happy am I, for the daughters will call me happy.” She named him Asher.
echoes.note: Leah's "the daughters will call me happy" is the OT type of the blessing-cry pronounced over a woman, here transferred to Jesus' mother. A faint formal parallel to the beatitude on the womb; contested.

echoes.text: You shall be blessed in the fruit of your body, the fruit of your ground, the fruit of your animals, the increase of your livestock, and the young of your flock.
echoes.note: "Blessed shall be the fruit of your body" supplies covenant blessing-language on the womb that the woman's exclamation reworks. Diffuse and low volume.

pericopes.text: When the multitudes were gathering together to him, he began to say, “This is an evil generation. It seeks after a sign. No sign will be given to it but the sign of Jonah, the prophet. For even as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, so will also the Son of Man be to this generation. The Queen of the South will rise up in the judgment with the men of this generation, and will condemn them: for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, one greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will stand up in the judgment with this generation, and will condemn it: for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, one greater than Jonah is here.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: "The sign of Jonah" explicitly names the prophet swallowed by the great fish, the type for the Son of Man's vindication. The Jonah narrative is the controlling intertext of 11:29-30, named directly.

echoes.text: The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least.
echoes.note: "They repented at the preaching of Jonah" recounts the Ninevites' belief and repentance in sackcloth. The Ninevites' repentance is cited as the standard that condemns the unrepentant generation (11:32).

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning Yahweh’s name, she came to prove him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bore spices, and very much gold, and precious stones; and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart. Solomon told her all her questions: there was not anything hidden from the king which he didn’t tell her. When the queen of Sheba had […]
echoes.note: "The Queen of the South... came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon" cites the Queen of Sheba's visit to test Solomon with hard questions. The narrative is summoned directly as a witness against the generation (11:31).

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to prove Solomon with hard questions at Jerusalem, with a very great train, and camels that bore spices, and gold in abundance, and precious stones: and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart. Solomon told her all her questions; and there was not anything hidden from Solomon which he didn’t tell her. When the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of […]
echoes.note: The Chronicler's parallel account of the queen who came to hear Solomon's wisdom is the doublet source for 11:31. Its recurrence with 1 Kings 10 secures the allusion.

echoes.text: There came of all peoples to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.
echoes.note: "There came of all peoples to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all the kings of the earth" generalizes the nations' coming to Solomon's wisdom that the Queen of the South exemplifies. Supporting background; low.

pericopes.text: “No one, when he has lit a lamp, puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, that those who come in may see the light. The lamp of the body is the eye. Therefore when your eye is good, your whole body is also full of light; but when it is evil, your body also is full of darkness. Therefore see whether the light that is in you isn’t darkness. If therefore your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly full of light, as when the lamp with its bright shining gives you light.”

echoes.text: The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.
echoes.note: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inward parts" supplies the inner-lamp imagery for "the lamp of the body is the eye." The wisdom equation of lamp and inner illumination grounds 11:34.

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: "He who has a generous (good) eye will be blessed" lies behind the idiom of the "good eye" (single/generous) vs. the evil eye (stingy). A Semitic idiom backdrop to 11:34; low but coherent.

echoes.text: Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing; and he cry to Yahweh against you, and it be sin to you.
echoes.note: The warning against an "evil eye" toward the needy poor supplies the negative pole of the sound/evil eye antithesis. Contested idiomatic background to the dark-body saying.

echoes.text: For you will light my lamp, Yahweh. My God will light up my darkness.
echoes.note: "You will light my lamp; the LORD my God will lighten my darkness" pairs lamp and the dispelling of darkness as in 11:35-36. Faint psalmic coloring; low.

pericopes.text: Now as he spoke, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him. He went in, and sat at the table. When the Pharisee saw it, he marveled that he had not first washed himself before dinner. The Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the platter, but your inward part is full of extortion and wickedness. You foolish ones, didn’t he who made the outside make the inside also? But give for gifts to the needy those things which are within, and behold, all things will be clean to you. But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, but you bypass justice and the love of God. You ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone. Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seats in the synagogues, and the greetings in the marketplaces. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like hidden graves, and the men who walk over them don’t know it.”

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: "You bypass justice and the love of God" against punctilious tithing echoes "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God." Micah's prophetic priority of justice over ritual is the controlling intertext of the first woe (11:42).

echoes.text: “‘All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh’s. It is holy to Yahweh.
echoes.note: "The tithe... of the fruit of the tree, is the LORD's" supplies the legal basis the Pharisees scrupulously extend to mint and rue. The tithing command is the practice being weighed against neglected justice in 11:42.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice" reinforces the prophetic preference for justice/mercy over cultic precision behind 11:42. Recurs with Micah 6:8 but is not verbally present in Luke; low.

echoes.text: “Whoever in the open field touches one who is slain with a sword, or a dead body, or a bone of a man, or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.
echoes.note: "Whoever touches a grave shall be unclean seven days" underlies "you are like hidden graves" whose walkers contract defilement unknowingly. The purity law about corpse-contact through graves is the precise basis of the woe in 11:44.

echoes.text: “He who touches the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days.
echoes.note: "He who touches the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days" supplies the corpse-impurity principle the hidden-grave image exploits. Supports Numbers 19:16; low independent volume.

pericopes.text: One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying this you insult us also.” He said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load men with burdens that are difficult to carry, and you yourselves won’t even lift one finger to help carry those burdens. Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets, and your fathers killed them. So you testify and consent to the works of your fathers. For they killed them, and you build their tombs. Therefore also the wisdom of God said, ‘I will send to them prophets and apostles; and some of them they will kill and persecute, that the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation; from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zachariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary.’ Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. Woe to you lawyers! For you took away the key of knowledge. You didn’t enter in yourselves, and those who were entering in, you hindered.”

echoes.text: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: "You build the tombs of the prophets, and your fathers killed them" rests on the Chronicler's indictment that they "mocked the messengers of God... and scoffed at his prophets" until wrath rose. The murdered-prophets theme of 11:47-50 is summarized exactly here.

echoes.text: Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him. Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
echoes.note: "From the blood of Abel" cites Cain's murder of Abel whose blood "cries to me from the ground." Abel is named as the first martyr, the opening term of the canon-spanning blood-of-the-prophets formula in 11:51.

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house. Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his […]
echoes.note: "Zachariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary" cites Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned "in the court of the house of the LORD," the last martyr in the Hebrew canon's order. Abel-to-Zechariah spans Genesis to Chronicles, naming the whole canon's witness against the generation.

echoes.text: Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but killed his son. When he died, he said, “May Yahweh look at it, and repay it.”
echoes.note: Zechariah's dying cry "The LORD see it, and require it" supplies the requital language "may be required of this generation" in 11:50-51. The verbal echo of blood being "required" strengthens the Zechariah identification.

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: God's persistent sending of "all my servants the prophets... yet they did not listen" prefigures Wisdom's "I will send to them prophets" who are killed (11:49). A diffuse Deuteronomistic prophet-rejection pattern; low.

echoes.text: Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again to Yahweh; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear.
echoes.note: "He sent prophets to them to bring them again to the LORD... but they would not listen" parallels Wisdom's sending of prophets who are rejected and slain. Coheres with the Zechariah context of 11:49-51; low.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars. She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table. She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him, “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed! Leave your simple ways, and live. Walk in the way of […]
echoes.note: Personified Wisdom who sends out her maids and issues invitation stands behind "the wisdom of God said, 'I will send to them prophets'" (11:49). A faint Wisdom-figure availability for the sending-and-rejection oracle; contested.

echoes.text: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you, that you may be no priest to me. Because you have forgotten your God’s law, I will also forget your children.
echoes.note: "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge... you have rejected knowledge" colors the woe over lawyers who "took away the key of knowledge" (11:52). A prophetic backdrop to withheld knowledge; low.

pericopes.text: Meanwhile, when a multitude of many thousands had gathered together, so much so that they trampled on each other, he began to tell his disciples first of all, “Beware of the yeast of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. But there is nothing covered up, that will not be revealed, nor hidden, that will not be known. Therefore whatever you have said in the darkness will be heard in the light. What you have spoken in the ear in the inner rooms will be proclaimed on the housetops.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's closing maxim that God will bring every hidden work into judgment coheres with Jesus' apocalyptic disclosure that 'nothing is covered up that will not be revealed.' The wisdom-tradition theme of concealment overturned by divine exposure gives moderate Volume and strong Coherence with the warning against Pharisaic hypocrisy.

echoes.text: He uncovers deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shadow of death.
echoes.note: Job's praise that God 'uncovers deep things out of darkness and brings deep shadow to light' supplies the same imagery of hidden things brought into the light. The verbal overlap (darkness/light, revealing) is suggestive but the motif is widespread, so confidence is low.

echoes.text: Exalt not yourself, lest you fall, And bring dishonor upon your soul; And so the Lord will reveal your secrets, And will cast you down in the midst of the congregation; Because you came not to the fear of the Lord, And your heart was full of deceit.
echoes.note: Ben Sira warns the hypocrite that the Lord will reveal his secrets and cast him down in the assembly for not coming in fear of the Lord — a close conceptual parallel to leaven/hypocrisy that will be made manifest. Second-Temple Availability and shared hypocrisy theme support a faint echo.

pericopes.text: “I tell you, my friends, don’t be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. But I will warn you whom you should fear. Fear him, who after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna.Yes, I tell you, fear him. “Aren’t five sparrows sold for two assaria coins? Not one of them is forgotten by God. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Therefore don’t be afraid. You are of more value than many sparrows.

echoes.text: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized. Yahweh of Armies is who you must respect as holy. He is the one you must fear. He is the one you must dread.
echoes.note: Isaiah's oracle—'do not fear what they fear... the LORD of hosts, him you shall regard as holy, let him be your fear'—is the structural template for Jesus' contrast between fearing human killers and fearing the One who can cast into Gehenna. The transfer of fear from men to God is verbally and thematically precise, giving high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: Let us not fear him who thinks he kills; for great is the trial of soul and danger of eternal torment laid up for those who transgress the commandment of God.
echoes.note: The martyr brothers say 'let us not fear him who thinks he kills' but rather dread the danger of eternal torment for transgressing God's law. This Second-Temple martyrology supplies the exact body-vs-soul, kill-but-fear-God logic and a post-mortem judgment, making it strong Availability for Luke's saying.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: The prophetic reassurance 'do not be afraid of them, for I am with you' coheres with Jesus encouraging fearless witness before hostile authorities. The 'fear not' formula is widespread, so this is a faint coherence echo rather than a targeted allusion.

echoes.text: In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?
echoes.note: 'In God I trust; I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?' parallels Jesus' 'don't be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have no more they can do.' The flesh-can-do-no-more logic is a plausible echo of psalmic confidence.

echoes.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
echoes.note: The oath that not one hair of Jonathan's head shall fall to the ground is the idiomatic source for divine protection imagery behind 'the very hairs of your head are all numbered.' The hair idiom is the link, though Luke intensifies it from preservation to enumeration, so confidence is low.

echoes.text: He provides food for the livestock, and for the young ravens when they call.
echoes.note: God 'gives to the animals their food, and to the young ravens that cry' grounds the providence logic that not one sparrow is forgotten before God. The creature-care theme recurs more fully in 12:24, making this a coherent but light echo here.

pericopes.text: “I tell you, everyone who confesses me before men, him will the Son of Man also confess before the angels of God; but he who denies me in the presence of men will be denied in the presence of the angels of God. Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. When they bring you before the synagogues, the rulers, and the authorities, don’t be anxious how or what you will answer, or what you will say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that same hour what you must say.”

echoes.text: A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
echoes.note: The Son of Man confessing or denying before 'the angels of God' draws on Daniel's heavenly court where thousands of angels attend and the Son of Man is presented before the Ancient of Days. The Son-of-Man title plus an angelic tribunal gives strong Coherence and apt Availability.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Jesus' self-designation 'Son of Man' acting as eschatological acknowledger before God depends on Daniel's exalted Son of Man who receives dominion. This recurs across Luke's Son-of-Man sayings, satisfying Recurrence even where the verbal contact here is the title and heavenly setting.

echoes.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
echoes.note: God's promise to Moses, 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak,' is the prototype for 'the Holy Spirit will teach you in that same hour what you must say.' The divine teaching-of-speech-under-trial motif gives good Coherence and clear Availability.

echoes.text: “‘But the soul who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native-born or a foreigner, the same blasphemes Yahweh. That soul shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised Yahweh’s word, and has broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off. His iniquity shall be on him.’”
echoes.note: The Torah's distinction between forgivable inadvertent sin and the high-handed sin that 'reviles the LORD' and is cut off without forgiveness loosely underlies the unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit. The defiant-sin-without-pardon concept is the link, so a faint echo.

pericopes.text: One of the multitude said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?” He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?'—the Hebrew's rebuke of Moses—is verbally echoed in Jesus' 'Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?' The near-quotation of the question gives notable Volume, though the speaker roles are inverted, marking it a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.
echoes.note: 'Whoever loves money will not be satisfied with money'—Qoheleth's verdict on the futility of abundance—coheres directly with 'a man's life doesn't consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.' The wisdom critique of accumulation supports the warning against covetousness.

echoes.text: If a man has two wives, the one beloved, and the other hated, and they have borne him children, both the beloved and the hated; and if the firstborn son is hers who was hated; then it shall be, in the day that he causes his sons to inherit that which he has, that he may not give the son of the beloved the rights of the firstborn before the son of the hated, who is the firstborn; but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the hated, by giving him a […]
echoes.note: The Torah law of inheritance division among heirs supplies the legal backdrop for the brother's request to divide the inheritance. It is the unstated Availability rather than an allusion Luke develops, hence low confidence.

pericopes.text: He spoke a parable to them, saying, “The ground of a certain rich man produced abundantly. He reasoned within himself, saying, ‘What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?’ He said, ‘This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, and build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. I will tell my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, be merry.”’ “But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’ So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”

echoes.text: There is that waxes rich by his wariness and pinching, And this is the portion of his reward: When he says, I have found rest, And now will I eat of my goods; Yet he knows not what time will pass, And he will leave them to others, and die.
echoes.note: Ben Sira describes one who grows rich, says 'I have found rest, now I will enjoy my goods,' yet does not know his death is near and must leave them to others. This is the closest Second-Temple template for the rich fool: the inner monologue of ease, the unexpected death, and the unanswered 'whose will they be,' giving very high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's refrain that there is nothing better than to eat, drink, and find enjoyment underlies the rich fool's 'take your ease, eat, drink, be merry.' Luke ironizes the wisdom counsel by exposing its folly when death intervenes, giving strong thematic Coherence.

echoes.text: Then I commended mirth, because a man has no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that will accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun.
echoes.note: 'I commend enjoyment, for man has nothing better under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry' is virtually quoted in the fool's resolve. The verbal triad eat/drink/be merry makes this a direct verbal source, though Luke subverts it.

echoes.text: “Surely every man walks like a shadow. Surely they busy themselves in vain. He heaps up, and doesn’t know who shall gather.
echoes.note: 'He heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather it' is closely echoed by God's 'the things you have prepared—whose will they be?' The psalm's lament over the futility of hoarding against death gives strong Coherence and good Volume.

echoes.text: As the partridge that sits on eggs which she has not laid, so is he who gets riches, and not by right; in the midst of his days they shall leave him, and at his end he shall be a fool.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's proverb that one who gets riches unjustly will leave them in the midst of his days and prove a fool at his end supplies both the 'fool' verdict and the premature loss of wealth. The shared fool-and-forfeited-riches motif gives notable Coherence.

echoes.text: For what is the hope of the godless, when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?
echoes.note: 'What is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life?' parallels the question posed to the rich man whose soul is required. The taking of the life of the prosperous-but-godless undergirds the parable's verdict.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid when a man is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased. For when he dies he shall carry nothing away. His glory shall not descend after him. Though while he lived he blessed his soul— and men praise you when you do well for yourself— he shall go to the generation of his fathers. They shall never see the light. A man who has riches without understanding, is like the animals that perish.
echoes.note: The psalm warns not to fear the rich who lay up wealth, for they carry nothing away at death and perish like the beasts. The 'man in his pomp who does not understand' is a near-portrait of the rich fool, giving good Coherence to 'not rich toward God.'

echoes.text: “If I have made gold my hope, and have said to the fine gold, ‘You are my confidence;’ If I have rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because my hand had gotten much; if I have seen the sun when it shined, or the moon moving in splendor, and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my hand threw a kiss from my mouth, this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges; for I should have denied the God who is above.
echoes.note: Job's disavowal of making gold his hope reflects the parable's contrast between trusting accumulated wealth and being 'rich toward God.' The trust-in-riches-as-folly theme is a coherent but lighter echo.

echoes.text: Wakefulness that comes of riches consumes the flesh, And the anxiety thereof puts away sleep. Wakeful anxiety will crave slumber; And in a sore disease sleep will be broken. A rich man toileth in gathering money together; And when he rests, he is filled with his good things. A poor man toileth in lack of substance; And when he rests, he becomes needy. He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's reflections on wealth, sleepless anxiety over riches, and the rare rich man who is blameless complement the parable's critique of storing goods. A faint Second-Temple coherence echo behind the barn-building scheme.

pericopes.text: He said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life, what you will eat, nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Life is more than food, and the body is more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they don’t sow, they don’t reap, they have no warehouse or barn, and God feeds them. How much more valuable are you than birds! Which of you by being anxious can add a cubit to his height? If then you aren’t able to do even the least things, why are you anxious about the rest? Consider the lilies, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin; yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if this is how God clothes the grass in the field, which today exists, and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith? Don’t seek what you will eat or what you will drink; neither be anxious. For the nations of the world seek after all of these things, but your Father knows that you need these things. But seek God’s Kingdom, and all these things will be added to you.

echoes.text: Who provides for the raven his prey, when his young ones cry to God, and wander for lack of food?
echoes.note: 'Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry to God?' is the direct source of 'Consider the ravens... God feeds them.' The named bird (raven, not a generic fowl) and the divine feeding make this a high-Volume allusion to God's wilderness providence.

echoes.text: He provides food for the livestock, and for the young ravens when they call.
echoes.note: God 'gives to the animals their food, and to the young ravens that cry' reinforces the raven providence saying with a second Scripture. The recurrence of the ravens-fed-by-God motif across Job and Psalms strengthens the case (Recurrence).

echoes.text: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: 'All flesh is grass... the grass withers, the flower fades' is the template for the grass which today exists and tomorrow is cast into the oven. The transience-of-grass imagery is verbally close and thematically apt to the 'little faith' contrast, giving high Volume.

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, and the house that he had built, and the food of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their clothing, and his cup bearers, and his ascent by which he went up to Yahweh’s house; there was no more spirit in her. She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts, and of your wisdom. However I didn’t believe the words, […]
echoes.note: The queen of Sheba's astonishment at Solomon's wealth and splendor stands behind 'even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.' The named figure (Solomon) and his proverbial glory give high Volume; the lilies surpass the richest king of Israel's memory.

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, and the house that he had built, and the food of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their clothing, his cup bearers also, and their clothing, and his ascent by which he went up to Yahweh’s house; there was no more spirit in her. She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts, and of your wisdom. However I didn’t […]
echoes.note: The Chronicler's parallel account of Solomon's overwhelming glory before the queen of Sheba supports the 'Solomon in all his glory' reference. Recurrence of the Solomon-splendor tradition across Kings and Chronicles strengthens Availability.

echoes.text: As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.
echoes.note: 'As for man, his days are like grass... the wind passes over it and it is gone' echoes the perishable grass clothed by God yet cast into the oven. The grass-as-human-frailty motif coheres with the call not to be anxious.

echoes.text: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.
echoes.note: God who causes grass to grow and brings forth food, wine, and bread supplies the providential clothing-and-feeding logic. A general creation-providence echo behind 'God clothes the grass.'

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: 'Man does not live by bread alone' coheres with 'life is more than food.' The principle that life exceeds material sustenance is a plausible Torah echo underlying the anti-anxiety teaching.

pericopes.text: Don’t be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom. Sell that which you have, and give gifts to the needy. Make for yourselves purses which don’t grow old, a treasure in the heavens that doesn’t fail, where no thief approaches, neither moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

echoes.text: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold.
echoes.note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold' is the closest source for 'make for yourselves... a treasure in the heavens that doesn't fail.' The almsgiving-as-imperishable-treasure logic gives high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity;
echoes.note: 'You will be laying up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity' directly follows Tobit's exhortation to give alms. The treasure-stored-by-almsgiving theme is a precise Second-Temple parallel to selling possessions and giving to the needy.

echoes.text: Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:
echoes.note: Ben Sira's fuller counsel to spend silver on a brother and store up almsgiving in the chambers of the Most High undergirds the whole purse-that-does-not-grow-old image. Recurrence within Sirach's treasure theology strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: The kingdom given to the people of the saints of the Most High coheres faintly with 'it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the Kingdom' for the 'little flock.' The granting of the kingdom to a faithful remnant is a coherent but light echo.

pericopes.text: “Let your waist be dressed and your lamps burning. Be like men watching for their lord, when he returns from the marriage feast; that, when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him. Blessed are those servants, whom the lord will find watching when he comes. Most certainly I tell you, that he will dress himself, and make them recline, and will come and serve them. They will be blessed if he comes in the second or third watch, and finds them so. But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what hour the thief was coming, he would have watched, and not allowed his house to be broken into. Therefore be ready also, for the Son of Man is coming in an hour that you don’t expect him.”

echoes.text: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.
echoes.note: The Passover command to eat 'with your waist girded, your sandals on your feet... in haste' supplies 'let your waist be dressed,' the posture of readiness for the Lord's deliverance/coming. The girded-loins idiom for eschatological vigilance is a strong, apt allusion.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' grounds the sudden, unexpected return of the master for whom the servants watch. The Lord-coming-suddenly motif coheres with both the watchful-servants and the thief-in-the-night sayings.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on Elijah; and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
echoes.note: Elijah 'girded up his loins and ran' is a representative instance of the girded-loins idiom for urgent service. It supports the readiness imagery though Exodus 12 is the primary cultic source.

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: The bridegroom-rejoicing imagery of God's eschatological marriage faintly underlies the lord 'returning from the marriage feast.' The wedding-banquet eschatology is a coherent but light echo.

pericopes.text: Peter said to him, “Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or to everybody?” The Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise steward, whom his lord will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the right times? Blessed is that servant whom his lord will find doing so when he comes. Truly I tell you, that he will set him over all that he has. But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My lord delays his coming,’ and begins to beat the menservants and the maidservants, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken, then the lord of that servant will come in a day when he isn’t expecting him, and in an hour that he doesn’t know, and will cut him in two, and place his portion with the unfaithful. That servant, who knew his lord’s will, and didn’t prepare, nor do what he wanted, will be beaten with many stripes, but he who didn’t know, and did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten with few stripes. To whomever much is given, of him will much be required; and to whom much was entrusted, of him more will be asked.

echoes.text: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand. From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Yahweh’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field. He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he […]
echoes.note: Joseph set over Potiphar's whole household, entrusted with everything, is the wisdom prototype of the faithful steward whom the lord sets over his household and, proving faithful, over all he has. The trusted-slave-over-the-house motif gives good Coherence.

echoes.text: Fodder, a stick, and burdens, for an ass; Bread, and discipline, and work, for a servant. Set your servant to work, and you shall find rest: Leave his hands idle, and he will seek liberty. Yoke and thong will bow the neck: And for an evil servant there are racks and tortures. Send him to labor, that he be not idle; For idleness teaches much mischief. Set him to work, as is fit for him; And if he obey not, make his fetters heavy. And be not excessive […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's instructions about treatment of slaves—the prudent versus the abusive—loosely cohere with the steward who either feeds the household or beats the menservants. A Second-Temple wisdom backdrop to the parable's master/servant ethics.

echoes.text: “‘If one person sins unwittingly, then he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering. The priest shall make atonement for the soul who errs, when he sins unwittingly before Yahweh, to make atonement for him; and he shall be forgiven. You shall have one law for him who does anything unwittingly, for him who is native-born among the children of Israel, and for the stranger who lives as a foreigner among them. “‘But the soul who does anything […]
echoes.note: The Torah's graded culpability—lighter for inadvertent sin, heavier for high-handed sin—undergirds 'beaten with many stripes' versus 'few stripes' according to knowledge of the lord's will. The proportional-punishment-by-knowledge principle gives clear Coherence.

echoes.text: It shall be, if the wicked man is worthy to be beaten, that the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face, according to his wickedness, by number. He may sentence him to no more than forty stripes. He shall not give more; lest, if he should give more, and beat him more than that many stripes, then your brother will be degraded in your sight.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic law limiting and proportioning the number of stripes to the offense supplies the legal idiom behind 'many stripes... few stripes.' Availability for the beating imagery, though not developed verbally.

pericopes.text: “I came to throw fire on the earth. I wish it were already kindled. But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished! Do you think that I have come to give peace in the earth? I tell you, no, but rather division. For from now on, there will be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. They will be divided, father against son, and son against father; mother against daughter, and daughter against her mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: 'The son treats the father with contempt, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law'—Micah's portrait of social collapse—is virtually quoted in the household divisions of 12:53. The matching kinship triads (father/son, mother/daughter, mother-in-law/daughter-in-law) make this a high-Volume allusion.

echoes.text: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and refine them as gold and silver; and they shall offer to Yahweh offerings in righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Who can endure the day of his coming? For he is like a refiner's fire' grounds 'I came to throw fire on the earth.' The eschatological refining-and-purging fire of the coming Lord gives strong Coherence to Jesus' fire-bringing mission.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: 'The day comes, burning like an oven... it will set them ablaze' reinforces the kindled fire Jesus casts on the earth. Recurrence of Malachi's fire-of-judgment imagery across chapters 3-4 strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”
echoes.note: God will 'put this third into the fire, and refine them as one refines silver' divides a remnant by fire and trial. The refining-fire-that-divides motif coheres with both the fire and the division Jesus brings rather than peace.

echoes.text: Now will I show you the truth. Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all: and when he has grown strong through his riches, he shall stir up all against the realm of Greece. A mighty king shall stand up, who shall rule with great dominion, and do according to his will. When he shall stand up, his kingdom shall be broken, and shall be divided toward the four winds of the sky, but not to his […]
echoes.note: Apocalyptic expectation that the end-times bring conflict rather than tranquility loosely supports Jesus' 'not peace but division.' Faint coherence with the tribulation-before-the-end pattern.

pericopes.text: He said to the multitudes also, “When you see a cloud rising from the west, immediately you say, ‘A shower is coming,’ and so it happens. When a south wind blows, you say, ‘There will be a scorching heat,’ and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and the sky, but how is it that you don’t interpret this time?

echoes.text: On the seventh time, he said, “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, is rising out of the sea.” He said, “Go up, tell Ahab, ‘Get ready and go down, so that the rain doesn’t stop you.’” In a little while, the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. Ahab rode, and went to Jezreel.
echoes.note: The little cloud rising from the sea heralding heavy rain in Elijah's drought account parallels 'a cloud rising from the west... a shower is coming.' The reading-of-cloud-as-rain-sign offers a faint scriptural precedent for weather discernment.

echoes.text: If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth; and if a tree falls toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there shall it be. He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's observation that 'if the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth' and that the wind-watcher fails to act coheres with reading clouds and wind yet failing to read 'this time.' A wisdom echo on weather-signs and discernment.

pericopes.text: Why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right? For when you are going with your adversary before the magistrate, try diligently on the way to be released from him, lest perhaps he drag you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison. I tell you, you will by no means get out of there, until you have paid the very last penny.”

echoes.text: Don’t be hasty in bringing charges to court. What will you do in the end when your neighbor shames you?
echoes.note: 'Do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame?' is the wisdom counsel behind settling with your adversary on the way before the magistrate. The avoid-the-courtroom-by-prior-settlement logic gives clear Coherence and apt Availability.

echoes.text: My son, if you have become collateral for your neighbor, if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger; You are trapped by the words of your mouth. You are ensnared with the words of your mouth. Do this now, my son, and deliver yourself, since you have come into the hand of your neighbor. Go, humble yourself. Press your plea with your neighbor. Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids. Free yourself, like a gazelle from the hand of […]
echoes.note: The urgent counsel to free yourself at once from a debt-snare, 'like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter,' coheres with hastening to be released from one's accuser before imprisonment. A wisdom echo on urgent self-extraction from legal/financial peril.

echoes.text: For jealousy arouses the fury of the husband. He won’t spare in the day of vengeance. He won’t regard any ransom, neither will he rest content, though you give many gifts.
echoes.note: The implacable creditor/accuser who will accept no ransom parallels the warning that one will not get out 'until you have paid the very last penny.' A faint coherence echo on inescapable debt-satisfaction.

pericopes.text: Now there were some present at the same time who told him about the Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. Jesus answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, no, but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way. Or those eighteen, on whom the tower in Siloam fell, and killed them; do you think that they were worse offenders than all the men who dwell in Jerusalem? I tell you, no, but, unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way.”

echoes.text: Therefore I will judge you, house of Israel, everyone according to his ways, says the Lord Yahweh. Return, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away from you all your transgressions, in which you have transgressed; and make yourself a new heart and a new spirit: for why will you die, house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies, says the Lord Yahweh: therefore turn yourselves, […]
echoes.note: Jesus' refrain 'unless you repent, you will all perish' restates Ezekiel's prophetic logic that each person bears responsibility and must 'turn and live' lest he die. High Volume in the shared death/repentance vocabulary; strong Coherence with Luke's repentance theme; the prophet is widely available.

echoes.text: Tell them, As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, house of Israel?
echoes.note: 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that he turn from his way and live' supplies the same individualized call to repentance against assumed corporate judgment. Recurrence of Ezekiel's repent-or-perish motif strengthens the echo alongside 18:30-32.

echoes.text: “Remember, now, whoever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?
echoes.note: Eliphaz's 'who ever perished, being innocent?' frames the retributive assumption ('worse sinners... because they suffered') that Jesus overturns. Faint and contested, but coherent with the OT debate over suffering as proof of guilt.
