echoes.text: “Because this people have refused the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah’s son;
echoes.note: The 'waters of Shiloah' (Siloam) carry, in Isaiah, judgment imagery for those who reject the gentle stream; the tower 'in Siloam' may faintly evoke the site's prophetic charge. Low Volume and contested; geography may be incidental.

pericopes.text: He spoke this parable. “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it, and found none. He said to the vine dresser, ‘Behold, these three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and found none. Cut it down. Why does it waste the soil?’ He answered, ‘Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it, and fertilize it. If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down.’”

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The owner of a vineyard who comes seeking fruit and finds none, threatening destruction, directly mirrors Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard, the canonical type for Israel's failure to yield justice. High Volume (vineyard + seeking fruit + judgment), strong Coherence, and prime Availability as the standard prophetic indictment.

echoes.text: I will utterly consume them, says Yahweh: no grapes shall be on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade; and the things that I have given them shall pass away from them.
echoes.note: 'There are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree' is Jeremiah's judgment oracle on fruitlessness, pairing the fig tree with the vineyard exactly as Luke does. Strong Volume in the fig-tree/no-fruit collocation and high Coherence with the threat to 'cut it down.'

echoes.text: Misery is mine! Indeed, I am like one who gathers the summer fruits, as gleanings of the vineyard: There is no cluster of grapes to eat. My soul desires to eat the early fig.
echoes.note: 'There is no cluster to eat; my soul desires the first-ripe fig' voices the same disappointed search for fruit on the fig tree as an image of a faithless people. Medium Volume; recurrence of the fruitless-fig motif across the prophets supports the echo.

echoes.text: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree at its first season; but they came to Baal Peor, and consecrated themselves to the shameful thing, and became abominable like that which they loved.
echoes.note: Israel was found 'like the first fruit on the fig tree,' a hope reversed in 9:16 ('they shall bear no fruit'). The fig tree as figure for Israel's fruitfulness-turned-barren coheres tightly with the parable's verdict.

echoes.text: Ephraim is struck. Their root has dried up. They will bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, yet I will kill the beloved ones of their womb.”
echoes.note: 'Ephraim is struck down... they shall bear no fruit' supplies the barrenness-and-judgment outcome that the parable holds in suspense. Coherent with the prophetic fig-tree complex; medium Volume.

echoes.text: For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls:
echoes.note: 'Though the fig tree does not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines' shares the fig-and-vine pairing for a season of barrenness. Faint here because Habakkuk's tone is trust amid loss rather than indictment; offered honestly as a low-confidence resonance.

echoes.text: He has laid my vine waste, and stripped my fig tree. He has stripped its bark, and thrown it away. Its branches are made white.
echoes.note: 'It has laid waste my vine and splintered my fig tree' joins vine and fig under devastation, the same agrarian pair behind Luke's parable. Low Volume and contested, but recurrence of the vine-fig motif gives it some weight.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine brought out of Egypt, now burned and cut down for lack of protection, parallels the threatened destruction of the unfruitful planting. Contested because no fig tree appears, but the vineyard-judgment frame is coherent.

pericopes.text: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath day. Behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and she was bent over, and could in no way straighten herself up. When Jesus saw her, he called her, and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your infirmity.” He laid his hands on her, and immediately she stood up straight, and glorified God. The ruler of the synagogue, being indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the multitude, “There are six days in which men ought to work. Therefore come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day!” Therefore the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Doesn’t each one of you free his ox or his donkey from the stall on the Sabbath, and lead him away to water? Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?” As he said these things, all his adversaries were disappointed, and all the multitude rejoiced for all the glorious things that were done by him.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The Sabbath controversy turns on the Decalogue command to keep the Sabbath holy, which the synagogue ruler invokes ('six days... ought to work'). High Volume and unmistakable Availability; the dispute is intelligible only against this commandment.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's Sabbath form explicitly rests the ox and donkey and frames the day as liberation from bondage, the very logic Jesus deploys ('free his ox or donkey... ought not this woman... be freed'). Strong Coherence: Jesus reads the Sabbath as release, matching Deuteronomy's exodus rationale.

echoes.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD raises up those who are bowed down' supplies the precise theological image of the bent woman 'made straight,' identifying Jesus' act with the LORD's characteristic work. Medium Volume; the verbal match (bowed down / raised) is striking.

echoes.text: Yahweh upholds all who fall, and raises up all those who are bowed down.
echoes.note: 'The LORD upholds all who fall, and raises up all who are bowed down' doubles the motif of God straightening the bent, reinforcing Psalm 146:8. Recurrence across the Psalter of God raising the bowed strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless. I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.” Abram fell on his face. God talked with him, saying, “As for me, behold, my covenant is with you. You will be the father of a multitude of nations. Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made […]
echoes.note: Calling the woman a 'daughter of Abraham' reads her into the Abrahamic covenant of blessing and offspring, asserting her full claim to Sabbath release. Figural rather than verbal, but coherent with Luke's covenant-inclusion theme.

echoes.text: Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.
echoes.note: 'Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you' invokes Abrahamic descent as ground of restoration, resonant with 'daughter of Abraham.' Low Volume and contested; offered as a possible source for the covenant-daughter language.

echoes.text: So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
echoes.note: Satan afflicting a body with infirmity ('whom Satan had bound eighteen years') recalls Job, where the Adversary inflicts physical disease by divine permission. Low Volume, but the attribution of bodily affliction to Satan has its clearest OT precedent in Job.

pericopes.text: He said, “What is the Kingdom of God like? To what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and put in his own garden. It grew, and became a large tree, and the birds of the sky lodged in its branches.”

echoes.text: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
echoes.note: 'The birds of the sky lodged in its branches' closely echoes Daniel's great tree in which 'the birds of heaven dwelt,' a kingdom-as-tree image. High Volume in the nesting-birds clause and strong Coherence with the Kingdom-of-God comparison.

echoes.text: whose leaves were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all; under which the animals of the field lived, and on whose branches the birds of the sky had their habitation:
echoes.note: Daniel's interpretation repeats the tree 'in whose branches the birds of heaven lived,' reinforcing the imperial-tree imagery now applied to God's kingdom. Recurrence within Daniel 4 itself strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.
echoes.note: The messianic cedar planted on the mountain, under which 'birds of every sort will nest,' is the prophetic prototype of a small planting that becomes a sheltering tree for the nations. High Coherence: Luke's tiny seed-to-tree growth tracks Ezekiel's promise.

echoes.text: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.
echoes.note: Assyria as a great cedar 'in whose boughs all the birds of the heavens made their nests' provides another canonical world-tree with nesting birds. Medium Volume; recurrence with Daniel and Ezekiel 17 makes the nesting-birds topos secure.

echoes.text: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.
echoes.note: 'By the streams the birds of the sky have their habitation; they sing among the branches' offers a creation-praise image of birds nesting in branches. Low Volume and likely incidental compared with the prophetic world-tree texts.

pericopes.text: Again he said, “To what shall I compare the Kingdom of God? It is like yeast, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.”

echoes.text: Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”
echoes.note: 'Three measures of flour' matches the three seahs of fine meal Sarah kneads for the three visitors, an unusually specific quantity. Medium Volume; the precise figure suggests deliberate evocation of hospitality/promise to Abraham, though it may simply denote a large baking.

echoes.text: Gideon went in, and prepared a young goat, and unleavened cakes of an ephah of meal. He put the meat in a basket and he put the broth in a pot, and brought it out to him under the oak, and presented it.
echoes.note: Gideon's ephah of flour for the angelic visitor is another large measure baked at a moment of divine encounter, paralleling the 'three measures.' Low Volume and contested; offered as an alternative quantity-of-flour resonance.

echoes.text: “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel. In the first day there shall be to you a holy convocation, and in the seventh day a holy convocation; no kind of work shall be done in them, except that which every man must eat, that only may be done by you. You shall observe the feast […]
echoes.note: Leaven's pervasive, hidden spread plays against the Passover law that purges all leaven as corruption, making the Kingdom's leaven a pointed reversal of the usual negative valence. Contested and figural; the parable's positive use of leaven only registers against this background.

pericopes.text: He went on his way through cities and villages, teaching, and traveling on to Jerusalem. One said to him, “Lord, are they few who are saved?” He said to them, “Strive to enter in by the narrow door, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter in, and will not be able. When once the master of the house has risen up, and has shut the door, and you begin to stand outside, and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us!’ then he will answer and tell you, ‘I don’t know you or where you come from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ He will say, ‘I tell you, I don’t know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.’ There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets, in the Kingdom of God, and yourselves being thrown outside. They will come from the east, west, north, and south, and will sit down in the Kingdom of God. Behold, there are some who are last who will be first, and there are some who are first who will be last.”

echoes.text: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for Yahweh has heard the voice of my weeping.
echoes.note: 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' reproduces the psalmist's dismissal of evildoers almost verbatim as the householder's rejection. High Volume (near-exact wording) and strong Availability make this a direct quotation, here on the lips of the eschatological judge.

echoes.text: And gathered out of the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south.
echoes.note: The redeemed 'gathered from the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south' supplies Luke's exact four-direction ingathering ('east, west, north, and south'). High Volume in the matching compass formula and strong Coherence with eschatological gathering.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid; for I am with you. I will bring your seed from the east, and gather you from the west. I will tell the north, ‘Give them up!’ and tell the south, ‘Don’t hold them back! Bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth—
echoes.note: 'I will bring your offspring from the east... from the west... to the north... and to the south' is the classic restoration oracle of God gathering his people from every direction. High Coherence with the kingdom-feast ingathering of outsiders.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: Reclining at table 'in the Kingdom of God' with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob evokes Isaiah's eschatological feast 'for all peoples' on the mountain. Medium Volume; the banquet image grounds the seating/dining language and the Gentile inclusion.

echoes.text: Behold, these shall come from far; and behold, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim.”
echoes.note: 'These shall come from afar... from the north and from the west' adds to the prophetic ingathering-from-all-directions tradition behind Luke's east-west-north-south. Recurrence across Isaiah strengthens the directional motif.

echoes.text: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'From the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations' anticipates worship gathered from all peoples east to west, coherent with outsiders streaming into the kingdom. Medium Volume; reinforces the Gentile-inclusion theme.

echoes.text: The wicked will see it, and be grieved. He shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away. The desire of the wicked will perish.
echoes.note: 'The wicked... gnashes his teeth and melts away' supplies the OT idiom of teeth-gnashing in frustrated exclusion that Luke fuses with weeping. Medium Volume for the distinctive gnashing-of-teeth phrase applied to the excluded wicked.

echoes.text: Those who went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God commanded him; then Yahweh shut him in.
echoes.note: 'The LORD shut him in' after Noah entered the ark prefigures the master who 'has shut the door,' sealing insiders from outsiders before judgment. Low Volume and contested, but the door-shut-before-judgment pattern is coherent with Luke's warning.

pericopes.text: On that same day, some Pharisees came, saying to him, “Get out of here, and go away, for Herod wants to kill you.” He said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I complete my mission. Nevertheless I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the next day, for it can’t be that a prophet perish outside of Jerusalem.’

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house. Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his […]
echoes.note: 'A prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem' draws on the tradition of prophets killed in the holy city, exemplified by Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned in the temple court. Medium Volume; this murdered-prophet text undergirds the saying and the lament that follows.

echoes.text: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]
echoes.note: Uriah son of Shemaiah, a prophet hunted down and killed for his message, illustrates the deadly fate of prophets in Jerusalem behind Jesus' words. Coherent with the prophet-perishing motif; recurrence with 2 Chronicles 24 secures it.

echoes.text: Israel, your prophets have been like foxes in the waste places.
echoes.note: 'Your prophets are like foxes among ruins' offers an OT precedent for 'fox' as a label of destructive cunning, here aimed at Herod. Low Volume and contested; the fox insult may be proverbial rather than a specific citation.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'On the third day he will raise us up' may stand faintly behind 'the third day I complete my mission,' tying Jesus' goal to a resurrection-shaped 'third day.' Contested and low Volume; the numerical phrasing here is more idiomatic than citational.

pericopes.text: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that kills the prophets, and stones those who are sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children together, like a hen gathers her own brood under her wings, and you refused! Behold, your house is left to you desolate. I tell you, you will not see me, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

echoes.text: Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD' is quoted verbatim as the cry that will precede Jerusalem's seeing Jesus again. High Volume (direct citation) and strong Availability from the Hallel make this an unambiguous quotation.

echoes.text: They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'Jerusalem... that kills the prophets and stones those sent to her' alludes to Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court at the king's command, the paradigm of the city's murder of God's messengers. High Coherence; stoning-of-the-sent matches the verb precisely.

echoes.text: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]
echoes.note: The killing of the prophet Uriah reinforces the indictment of Jerusalem as a city that slays those sent to it. Recurrence with 2 Chronicles 24 establishes the prophet-killing tradition behind the lament.

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: 'They killed your prophets who had warned them to turn back to you' summarizes the very pattern Jesus laments. Medium Volume; this confessional retrospect is a strong conceptual source for 'kills the prophets.'

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's complaint that Israel 'has killed your prophets with the sword' voices the same charge of prophet-slaying. Low Volume relative to the Jerusalem-specific texts, but coherent with the tradition.

echoes.text: He will cover you with his feathers. Under his wings you will take refuge. His faithfulness is your shield and rampart.
echoes.note: 'He will cover you with his feathers, and under his wings you will take refuge' is the closest OT image to gathering children 'under her wings,' associating Jesus' maternal longing with God's sheltering protection. High Volume in the under-the-wings refuge motif.

echoes.text: As an eagle that stirs up her nest, that flutters over her young, he spread abroad his wings, he took them, he bore them on his feathers.
echoes.note: The eagle that 'hovers over its young, spreading out its wings' to bear them models God's parental gathering, paralleling the hen and brood. Medium Volume; the Song of Moses' wing-protection image is a likely source.

echoes.text: May Yahweh repay your work, and a full reward be given you from Yahweh, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”
echoes.note: Coming to take refuge 'under the wings' of the LORD supplies the same shelter-under-wings idiom for those gathered to God. Recurrence of the wings-refuge motif across the canon supports the allusion.

echoes.text: Keep me as the apple of your eye. Hide me under the shadow of your wings,
echoes.note: 'Hide me in the shadow of your wings' extends the wing-protection imagery in the Psalter behind the hen-and-brood figure. Low Volume on its own but part of a coherent recurring motif (Pss 36:7; 57:1; 63:7).

echoes.text: As birds hovering, so Yahweh of Armies will protect Jerusalem. He will protect and deliver it. He will pass over and preserve it.”
echoes.note: 'Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem' joins bird-protection imagery specifically to Jerusalem, the very city Jesus longs to shelter. Medium Volume; the Jerusalem-specific bird-shielding tightens the Coherence.

echoes.text: But if you will not hear these words, I swear by myself, says Yahweh, that this house shall become a desolation.
echoes.note: 'This house shall become a desolation' supplies the judgment formula behind 'your house is left to you desolate,' spoken against the royal house/temple. High Coherence; the desolation-of-the-house oracle is the prophetic backdrop of the saying.

echoes.text: I have forsaken my house, I have cast off my heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.
echoes.note: 'I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my heritage' gives the divine-abandonment sense of 'your house is left to you,' God withdrawing from the temple. High Volume in the forsaken-house motif and strong Coherence with impending desolation.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The warning that the temple will become 'a heap of ruins' and Israel cast off if they forsake the LORD underlies the threat that the house is left desolate. Medium Volume; the conditional house-desolation oracle resonates with Luke's pronouncement.

echoes.text: Let their habitation be desolate. Let no one dwell in their tents.
echoes.note: 'May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents' offers an imprecatory desolation formula faintly behind 'left desolate.' Low Volume and contested; the connection is thematic rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: When he went into the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees on a Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him. Behold, a certain man who had dropsy was in front of him. Jesus, answering, spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” But they were silent. He took him, and healed him, and let him go. He answered them, “Which of you, if your sonor an ox fell into a well, wouldn’t immediately pull him out on a Sabbath day?” They couldn’t answer him regarding these things.

echoes.text: You shall not see your brother’s donkey or his ox fallen down by the way, and hide yourself from them. You shall surely help him to lift them up again.
echoes.note: Jesus' rescue argument — 'which of you, if your son or an ox fell into a well, wouldn't immediately pull him out on a Sabbath?' — draws on the Torah's humane-rescue command not to leave a brother's ox or donkey fallen by the way without lifting it up. The qal-wahomer (how much more a person) presupposes this animal-rescue obligation as available scriptural premise; high coherence with Jesus' wider Sabbath-mercy disputes (Luke 13:15).

echoes.text: If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him, you shall surely help him with it.
echoes.note: The parallel Torah duty to help even an enemy's donkey lying under its burden reinforces the same fallen-animal-rescue logic Jesus invokes for the well-fallen ox. Recurrence of the rescue motif across Deut 22:4 and Exod 23:5 strengthens availability, though Deut 22:4 is the closer verbal match.

echoes.text: “‘Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation; you shall do no kind of work. It is a Sabbath to Yahweh in all your dwellings.
echoes.note: The Sabbath-rest command framing the whole conflict ('Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?') stands behind the scene; the dropsy healing is staged precisely against the holy-convocation rest prescription. Faint and diffuse — the Sabbath law is assumed background rather than cited.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The Decalogue Sabbath command is the legal ground the lawyers and Pharisees presuppose in watching whether Jesus will heal. Coherent with Luke's recurring Sabbath-controversy pattern but only ambiently present here.

pericopes.text: He spoke a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the best seats, and said to them, “When you are invited by anyone to a marriage feast, don’t sit in the best seat, since perhaps someone more honorable than you might be invited by him, and he who invited both of you would come and tell you, ‘Make room for this person.’ Then you would begin, with shame, to take the lowest place. But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may tell you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at the table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

echoes.text: Don’t exalt yourself in the presence of the king, or claim a place among great men; for it is better that it be said to you, “Come up here,” than that you should be put lower in the presence of the prince, whom your eyes have seen.
echoes.note: The counsel 'do not sit in the best seat... go and sit in the lowest place, so that he may tell you, Friend, move up higher' closely reworks Proverbs 25:6-7: 'do not put yourself forward in the king's presence... for it is better to be told Come up here than to be put lower.' High volume (verbal and structural correspondence), high coherence with Luke's reversal theme; among the strongest sapiential echoes in the chapter.

echoes.text: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor, than to divide the plunder with the proud.
echoes.note: The concluding maxim 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted' resonates with the proverb that pride goes before destruction and that it is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor. Coherent wisdom-of-humility background reinforcing the Prov 25 banquet scene.

echoes.text: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.
echoes.note: 'A man's pride will bring him low, but the humble in spirit will obtain honor' supplies the exact exalt/humble inversion of v.11. Recurrence of this antithesis across Proverbs strengthens its availability as the wisdom matrix for Jesus' aphorism.

echoes.text: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.
echoes.note: The prophetic reversal formula 'exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high' parallels the abasement/exaltation of v.11. Faint and contested — the verbal medium is closer to Proverbs, but the prophetic reversal topos adds availability for Luke's broader Magnificat-style theme.

echoes.text: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's 'the greater you are, the more you must humble yourself, and you will find favor in the sight of the Lord' is the nearest Second-Temple analogue to Jesus' self-humbling counsel, set likewise in a context of social honor. Deuterocanonical availability and thematic coherence make this a plausible direct echo.

echoes.text: The wisdom of the lowly will lift up his head, And make him to sit in the midst of great men.
echoes.note: 'The wisdom of the humble lifts up his head and seats him among the great' offers a banquet-seating image of humble exaltation strikingly like 'move up higher.' Low confidence and contested given proximity to Prov 25, but the seating-among-the-great motif raises recurrence within the wisdom tradition.

pericopes.text: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back. But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”

echoes.text: The Levite, because he has no portion nor inheritance with you, and the foreigner living among you, and the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates, shall come, and shall eat and be satisfied; that Yahweh your God may bless you in all the work of your hand which you do.
echoes.note: Jesus' command to invite those who cannot repay — instead of friends and rich neighbors — recalls the third-year tithe given to the Levite, sojourner, fatherless, and widow 'that the Lord may bless you in all the work of your hands.' The blessing-for-giving-to-the-needy logic ('you will be blessed, because they don't have the resources to repay you') maps onto the Deuteronomic almsgiving promise.

echoes.text: For whatever man he is that has a defect, he shall not draw near: a blind man, or a lame, or he who has a flat nose, or any deformity,
echoes.note: The guest list 'the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind' inverts the priestly disqualifications of Lev 21:18 (no blind, lame, or mutilated man may approach the altar) — precisely those bodies barred from priestly table-service are summoned to the eschatological banquet. Figural reversal with strong coherence to Luke's inclusion theme.

echoes.text: David said on that day, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites, let him get up to the watercourse, and strike the lame and the blind, who are hated by David’s soul.” Therefore they say, “The blind and the lame can’t come into the house.”
echoes.note: 'The blind and the lame shall not come into the house' (the Jebusite proverb attached to David's capture of Jerusalem) is the exclusionary saying Jesus' open invitation of the lame and blind overturns. Faint and contested, but coheres with the Lev 21 disqualification reversal as a second exclusion-text being inverted.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'You will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous' presupposes the doctrine of bodily resurrection and reward first articulated in Daniel 12:2, where many who sleep awake, some to everlasting life. Availability of the resurrection-of-the-just hope grounds Jesus' eschatological recompense.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, and he will repay him for his deed' is the wisdom axiom behind being repaid not by guests but at the resurrection. Strong thematic coherence with the repay-by-God logic of vv.13-14.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you.
echoes.note: Tobit's almsgiving instruction — give to the poor and do not turn your face away, laying up a good treasure against the day of necessity — parallels Jesus' counsel to give where no repayment is possible. Deuterocanonical availability and coherence with Luke's almsgiving theology (cf. Luke 12:33).

pericopes.text: When one of those who sat at the table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is he who will feast in the Kingdom of God!” But he said to him, “A certain man made a great supper, and he invited many people. He sent out his servant at supper time to tell those who were invited, ‘Come, for everything is ready now.’ They all as one began to make excuses. “The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go and see it. Please have me excused.’ “Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I must go try them out. Please have me excused.’ “Another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I can’t come.’ “That servant came, and told his lord these things. Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame.’ “The servant said, ‘Lord, it is done as you commanded, and there is still room.’ “The lord said to the servant, ‘Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste of my supper.’”

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: The exclamation 'Blessed is he who will feast in the Kingdom of God!' and the parable of the great supper draw directly on Isaiah's eschatological banquet on Mount Zion — 'a feast of fat things, a feast of wine on the lees' for all peoples. High volume and coherence: the messianic banquet is the controlling image, and the eventual inclusion of outsiders mirrors Isaiah's 'all peoples.'

echoes.text: The officers shall speak to the people, saying, “What man is there who has built a new house, and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man dedicate it. What man is there who has planted a vineyard, and has not used its fruit? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man use its fruit. What man is there who has pledged to be married a wife, and has not taken her? […]
echoes.note: The three excuses parody the Deuteronomic war-exemptions: the man who built a new house (cf. 'I have bought a field'), the man who planted a vineyard, and the man newly betrothed who need not go to battle. The banquet-summons is cast as a holy-war muster the invitees decline, inverting the exemptions into culpable refusals.

echoes.text: When a man takes a new wife, he shall not go out in the army, neither shall he be assigned any business. He shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer his wife whom he has taken.
echoes.note: 'I have married a wife, and therefore I can't come' echoes the exemption granting a newly married man a year free from military service and public duty. The legitimate Torah exemption is repurposed as a self-condemning excuse, sharpening the parody of the war-muster reading.

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.
echoes.note: 'Be silent before the Lord God, for the day of the Lord is at hand; the Lord has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests' supplies the motif of a prepared feast/sacrifice with summoned guests on the day of the Lord — matching 'everything is ready now' and the judgment on those who refuse ('none of those men... will taste of my supper').

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn’t satisfy? listen diligently to me, and eat you that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
echoes.note: The free invitation 'Come, for everything is ready now' resonates with Isaiah's 'Come, buy and eat... without money and without price.' Faint but coherent with the gratuitous-banquet and the bringing-in of those who would not otherwise come.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars. She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table. She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him, “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!
echoes.note: Wisdom 'has slaughtered her beasts, mixed her wine, set her table, and sent out her maidens' to call guests — 'Come, eat of my bread.' The sent-servant-summoning-the-invited pattern and the call to the simple closely parallel the great supper's structure and the gathering of the lowly.

echoes.text: Neither let the foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people”; neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says Yahweh, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast my covenant: to them I will give in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, […]
echoes.note: The gathering of outsiders — foreigners and eunuchs brought to God's house, 'others besides those already gathered' — anticipates the master sending into highways and hedges to fill the house. Coheres with Luke's Gentile-inclusion trajectory but verbally diffuse.

echoes.text: As soon as you have come into the city, you shall immediately find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat; for the people will not eat until he come, because he blesses the sacrifice. Afterwards those who are invited eat. Now therefore go up; for at this time you shall find him.”
echoes.note: Samuel's sacrificial feast where 'the people will not eat until he comes... afterward those eat who are invited' supplies the formal vocabulary of invited guests waiting on the host's bidding. A faint background to the supper's summons protocol.

pericopes.text: Now great multitudes were going with him. He turned and said to them, “If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregardhis own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple. Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross, and come after me, can’t be my disciple.

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: 'If anyone... doesn't disregard his own father, mother, wife, children' echoes the blessing of Levi, who said of father and mother 'I have not seen him,' disowned his brothers and ignored his children — keeping covenant fidelity above kin. The radical preference of covenant loyalty over family ties is the closest scriptural precedent for Jesus' hyperbolic 'hate.'

echoes.text: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]
echoes.note: The Levites' ordination by slaying brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command — 'each one at the cost of his son and his brother' — is the narrative behind Deut 33:9's praise of Levi. It models the disciple's willingness to set covenant allegiance above family, coherent with Jesus' demand and the cross-bearing that follows.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: Micah's portrait of eschatological family division — son dishonoring father, daughter against mother, 'a man's enemies are the men of his own household' — undergirds Jesus' setting discipleship against the closest kin (and is explicitly cited at Luke 12:53). Recurrence in Luke strengthens its availability here.

echoes.text: If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend, who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods,” which you have not known, you, nor your fathers; of the gods of the peoples who are around you, near to you, or far off from you, from the one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth; you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; neither […]
echoes.note: The command to show no pity even to a brother, son, daughter, or wife who entices to false worship — placing exclusive devotion to the Lord above the dearest relations — offers a Torah analogue to subordinating family to higher allegiance. Faint and contested, but coheres with the covenant-over-kin theme of Deut 33:9.

pericopes.text: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it? Or perhaps, when he has laid a foundation, and is not able to finish, everyone who sees begins to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build, and wasn’t able to finish.’ Or what king, as he goes to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends an envoy, and asks for conditions of peace. So therefore whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple.

echoes.text: for by wise guidance you wage your war; and victory is in many advisors.
echoes.note: The king who 'will not sit down first and consider' before going to war reflects the proverb 'by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in an abundance of counselors there is victory.' The counsel to deliberate before battle is the sapiential ground of Jesus' second illustration about counting the cost.

echoes.text: Plans are established by advice; by wise guidance you wage war!
echoes.note: 'Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war' doubles the counting-the-cost-before-war motif of vv.31-32. Recurrence of this maxim across Proverbs 20:18 and 24:6 strengthens the wisdom-deliberation background of the tower-and-war pair.

echoes.text: Prepare your work outside, and get your fields ready. Afterwards, build your house.
echoes.note: 'Prepare your work outside... and after that build your house' supplies the prudence-before-building logic behind the tower illustration ('count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it'). Faint but coherent with the sapiential planning theme.

echoes.text: Let reason be the beginning of every work, And let counsel go before every action.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's 'before every action let counsel go, and before every undertaking deliberation' captures the count-the-cost-first principle of both illustrations. Deuterocanonical availability adds Second-Temple recurrence to the wisdom-deliberation reading.

pericopes.text: Salt is good, but if the salt becomes flat and tasteless, with what do you season it? It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile. It is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

echoes.text: Every offering of your meal offering you shall season with salt; neither shall you allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meal offering. With all your offerings you shall offer salt.
echoes.note: 'Salt is good, but if the salt becomes flat and tasteless...' draws on the covenant-of-salt requirement that every grain offering be seasoned with salt — salt as the indispensable mark of acceptable offering. Saltless disciples 'fit neither for soil nor manure pile' invert the covenant-of-salt's enduring fidelity.

echoes.text: All the wave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer to Yahweh, have I given you, and your sons and your daughters with you, as a portion forever. It is a covenant of salt forever before Yahweh to you and to your seed with you.”
echoes.note: The 'covenant of salt forever before the Lord' given to the priests defines salt as a symbol of permanent, unbreakable covenant — the very quality lost when salt goes flat. Coherent with the disqualification-from-covenant-service theme and reinforces Lev 2:13's availability.

echoes.text: Ought you not to know that Yahweh, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?
echoes.note: The Davidic kingship granted 'by a covenant of salt' extends the salt-as-perpetual-covenant idiom that gives Jesus' saltlessness saying its bite. Faint and contested, but adds recurrence to the covenant-of-salt motif across the canon.

echoes.text: For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good comes, but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, a salt land and not inhabited.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's curse on the one who trusts in man — dwelling in 'a salt land not inhabited,' barren and uninhabitable — resonates with salt-spoiled ground 'fit neither for the soil nor the manure pile.' Faint figural overlap between barren salt-land and the worthless flat salt thrown out.

pericopes.text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were coming close to him to hear him. The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.”

echoes.text: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?” Moses said, “Now Yahweh shall give you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to satisfy you; because Yahweh hears your murmurings which you murmur against him. And who are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against Yahweh.”
echoes.note: The Pharisees and scribes 'murmured' (diegongyzon) that Jesus eats with sinners; LXX uses gongyzo precisely for Israel's murmuring against God's provision in the wilderness. Luke evokes the recurrent grumbling motif to cast the objectors as faithless Israel resisting God's gracious feeding. Coherence is strong because the parables that follow defend a divine table.

echoes.text: who say, Stand by yourself, don’t come near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burns all the day.
echoes.note: The separatist who says 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am holier than you' supplies the exact posture Luke's Pharisees adopt against table fellowship with sinners. Isaiah condemns this self-segregating holiness as a stench before God, which coheres with Jesus' vindication of welcoming sinners. Availability and thematic coherence are high; verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: The wisdom ideal that the righteous do not sit with sinners frames the Pharisees' assumption that eating with sinners defiles. Luke inverts the maxim: Jesus' table redefines blessedness as seeking rather than separating. Faint and contested, resting on shared sinner/righteous vocabulary.

pericopes.text: He told them this parable. “Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep, and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one that was lost, until he found it? When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing. When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’ I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: God declares 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost,' the precise plot of the one shepherd who leaves the flock to find the strayed (vv. 4,6,16). Volume is high (sustained seeking-shepherd oracle), recurrence strong (Ezekiel 34 is a touchstone for Luke's shepherd Christology), and coherence exact: God's own searching contrasts the failed shepherds, just as Jesus seeks sinners the Pharisees abandon.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The shepherd who gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom illuminates the man carrying the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing. The tender carrying gesture is distinctive and shared, strengthening the divine-shepherd reading. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the comfort-of-God shepherd image.

echoes.text: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.
echoes.note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the penitent's voice answered by the seeking shepherd. The verbal pairing of straying sheep and divine seeking is close, and coherence with the repentance emphasis (v.7) is strong. Slightly lower volume than Ezekiel 34.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical image of straying that the parable assumes for 'one sinner who repents.' Recurrence in Luke's passion theology supports availability; the echo is thematic rather than cited here. Contested as to whether Luke intends the Servant song specifically.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: The woe on shepherds who scatter and the promise that God will gather the remnant and set true shepherds over them stands behind the lost-sheep rescue. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the prophetic indictment of leaders who fail the flock, paralleling the Pharisees. Lower volume, so an echo.

echoes.text: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.
echoes.note: God's promise to gather the remnant of Israel 'like sheep in a fold' supplies the regathering motif. Faint and one of several gathering oracles; included for recurrence within the shepherd-restoration cluster. Contested because no distinctive verbal link to a single lost sheep.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: The flock doomed to slaughter and the shepherd's care/abandonment drama belongs to the same prophetic shepherd field Luke draws on. Faint here; included as availability for the seeking-shepherd theme. Contested.

pericopes.text: Or what woman, if she had ten drachmacoins, if she lost one drachma coin, wouldn’t light a lamp, sweep the house, and seek diligently until she found it? When she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I had lost.’ Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting.”

echoes.text: It will happen at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are settled on their dregs, who say in their heart, “Yahweh will not do good, neither will he do evil.”
echoes.note: God 'searches Jerusalem with lamps' to find the complacent, a near image to the woman lighting a lamp and sweeping to find the coin. The lamp-search vocabulary is suggestive, though Zephaniah's search is judicial, here gracious. Contested and faint.

echoes.text: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:
echoes.note: Seeking wisdom 'as silver, and searching for it as for hidden treasure' parallels the diligent search for the lost silver drachma until found. The seek-until-found wisdom pattern coheres with the parable's diligence, but the link is thematic. Contested.

echoes.text: By night on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. I will get up now, and go about the city; in the streets and in the squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. The watchmen who go about the city found me; “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” I had scarcely passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him […]
echoes.note: The beloved who seeks through the night 'until I found him' and then summons others to rejoice mirrors the woman's seek-find-celebrate structure. Faint, figural, contested; included as a seek-and-find availability rather than a deliberate citation.

pericopes.text: He said, “A certain man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ He divided his livelihood between them. Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living. When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need. He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs. He wanted to fill his belly with the husks that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any.

echoes.text: but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the hated, by giving him a double portion of all that he has; for he is the beginning of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.
echoes.note: The law of inheritance giving the firstborn a double portion frames 'give me my share of your property' and the father's division between the two sons. The legal background makes the younger son's premature demand pointed and the father's later 'all that is mine is yours' (v.31) the firstborn's lawful due. Coherence high; verbal link thematic.

echoes.text: There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land.
echoes.note: The patriarchal pattern of departing to a far country when 'a severe famine' strikes the land underlies the son's far-country famine. The famine-driven sojourn is a recurrent Genesis motif (also 26:1; 41-47), lending availability. Contested as a specific source; an ambient echo.

echoes.text: The pig, because he has a split hoof, and is cloven-footed, but doesn’t chew the cud, he is unclean to you.
echoes.note: The pig is declared unclean, so feeding swine and craving their husks marks the Jewish son's total degradation and ritual estrangement. For a Torah-formed audience the swine signal maximal defilement, intensifying the depth from which the father's mercy reaches. Volume modest but coherence and distinctiveness high.

echoes.text: Whoever loves wisdom brings joy to his father; but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.
echoes.note: 'Whoever loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth' compactly anticipates both the prodigal's wasteful living and the elder son's accusation of harlots (v.30). The proverb pairs squandering and harlotry with a father, exactly Luke's configuration. Coherence strong.

echoes.text: Give not your soul to harlots, That you lose not your inheritance.
echoes.note: 'Do not give yourself to prostitutes, lest you lose your inheritance' (deuterocanonical wisdom) joins squandering to harlotry and lost inheritance, the prodigal's exact fall. Availability within Second-Temple wisdom strengthens the moral frame. Contested and faint as a direct source.

pericopes.text: But when he came to himself he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.”’

echoes.text: Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron in haste, and he said, “I have sinned against Yahweh your God, and against you.
echoes.note: Pharaoh's 'I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you' is the closest verbal template for 'I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight,' the dual against-God-and-against-you formula. The parallel sharpens the son's confession as a recognized penitential script. Contested between this and the Davidic confessions.

echoes.text: Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge.
echoes.note: 'Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight' supplies the language of sinning before God's sight that the son rehearses. As the paradigmatic penitential psalm it carries high recurrence in Jewish repentance piety, cohering with Luke's repentance theme (vv.7,10). Distinctive 'in your sight' overlap.
echoes.lxxText: Against thee only have I sinned, and done evil before thee: that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged.

echoes.text: David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against Yahweh.” Nathan said to David, “Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.
echoes.note: David's terse 'I have sinned against the LORD' models confession answered immediately by restoration, the rhythm of the son's resolve answered by the father. Recurrence of the 'I have sinned' formula across Saul/David/Pharaoh makes any single attribution contested. Faint.

pericopes.text: “He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ “But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe, and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat, and celebrate; for this, my son, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ They began to celebrate.

echoes.text: Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
echoes.note: Esau 'ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, and kissed him, and they wept' is the precise gesture-cluster of the father who ran, fell on his neck, and kissed the returning son. Volume and verbal distinctiveness are very high (run + fall on neck + kiss in sequence), and coherence is strong: an estranged brother/son reunion of unexpected mercy.

echoes.text: He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck, and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck. He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.
echoes.note: Joseph falling on his brothers' necks, weeping and kissing them, reinforces the reconciliation embrace, and the broader Joseph reunion (46:29, falling on Jacob's neck) supplies the lost-then-found-alive frame. Recurrence of the Joseph story across this pericope (robe, ring, 'dead/alive') is strong. Slightly lower verbal match than Genesis 33:4.

echoes.text: Pharaoh took off his signet ring from his hand, and put it on Joseph’s hand, and arrayed him in robes of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck,
echoes.note: Pharaoh exalts Joseph by putting a ring on his hand and clothing him in fine robes, the exact pair of honors (best robe + ring) the father bestows. The Joseph parallel makes the restored son a reinstated heir, not merely a forgiven servant. Distinctive robe-and-ring combination yields high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and was standing before the angel. He answered and spoke to those who stood before him, saying, “Take the filthy garments off of him.” To him he said, “Behold, I have caused your iniquity to pass from you, and I will clothe you with rich clothing.” I said, “Let them set a clean turban on his head.” So they set a clean turban on his head, and clothed him; and Yahweh’s angel was standing by.
echoes.note: Joshua the high priest has his filthy garments removed and is clothed in rich robes as a sign of restored standing, illuminating the 'best robe' that re-clothes the defiled son. The figural logic of imputed honor replacing defilement coheres tightly with the swine-defiled returnee. Verbal link is the robe of restoration.

echoes.text: Abraham ran to the herd, and fetched a tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it.
echoes.note: Abraham's slaughter of a choice, tender calf for honored guests supplies the cultural background of the fattened calf killed for celebration. Faint and one of several calf-feast scenes (1 Samuel 28:24); included for the hospitality-feast availability. Contested.

echoes.text: He recognized it, and said, “It is my son’s coat. An evil animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn in pieces.” Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days. All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, “For I will go down to Sheol to my son mourning.” His father wept for him.
echoes.note: Jacob mourns Joseph as dead and refuses comfort, so that Joseph's later disclosure that he is alive (45:26-28) is the canonical 'was dead and is alive, was lost and is found' reversal the father proclaims. The figural fit of a father's lost-and-restored son is strong and recurs across this pericope's Joseph allusions. Lower verbal volume, hence figural.

pericopes.text: “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants to him, and asked what was going on. He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’ But he was angry, and would not go in. Therefore his father came out, and begged him. But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this, your son, came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’ “He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’”

echoes.text: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry. He prayed to Yahweh, and said, “Please, Yahweh, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and you relent of doing harm. Therefore now, Yahweh, take, I beg you, my life from me; for it is better for me to die than to live.” Yahweh said, “Is it […]
echoes.note: Jonah is angry at God's mercy to the undeserving, sulks outside, and God comes out reasoning with him to the parable's open end, exactly the elder son angry at mercy whom the father comes out and entreats, ending on an unanswered appeal. Coherence is very high (resentment at grace, divine entreaty, open conclusion) and the structural parallel is distinctive. A strong figural-allusive frame for Luke's audience of grumblers.

echoes.text: but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell. Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: Cain is angry and downcast over a brother's favored standing, and the LORD comes out to him with entreaty and warning, paralleling the elder brother's anger and the father's coming out to plead. The elder-resents-younger pattern is the primal sibling-rivalry script. Coherence good; verbal link thematic.

echoes.text: If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son, who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and though they chasten him, will not listen to them; then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city, and to the gate of his place. They shall tell the elders of his city, “This our son is stubborn and rebellious. He will not obey our voice. He is a glutton and a drunkard.” All the men of his […]
echoes.note: The law of the stubborn and rebellious son who is gluttonous and a drunkard, to be brought before the elders and stoned, is the dark legal backdrop the parable deliberately subverts: the father runs to embrace rather than condemn. Directly preceding the inheritance law (21:17) already echoed, strengthening recurrence. Coherence high as a subverted intertext.

echoes.text: When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with an exceeding great and bitter cry, and said to his father, “Bless me, even me also, my father.” He said, “Your brother came with deceit, and has taken away your blessing.” He said, “Isn’t he rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times. He took away my birthright. See, now he has taken away my blessing.” He said, “Haven’t you reserved a blessing for me?” Isaac answered Esau, “Behold, […]
echoes.note: Esau's bitter outcry and resentment over a blessing/inheritance given to the younger brother colors the elder son's grievance about service and unrewarded faithfulness. Recurrence of the older-brother-aggrieved motif (Cain, Esau) supports availability; verbal link is faint. Contested.

echoes.text: Whoever loves wisdom brings joy to his father; but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.
echoes.note: The elder son's charge that the younger 'devoured your living with prostitutes' restates Proverbs' 'companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth,' tying the two parts of the parable together with one wisdom maxim. Recurrence with 15:13 makes the proverb a coherent through-line. Verbal overlap of squandering plus harlotry.

pericopes.text: He also said to his disciples, “There was a certain rich man who had a manager. An accusation was made to him that this man was wasting his possessions. He called him, and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an accounting of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’ “The manager said within himself, ‘What will I do, seeing that my lord is taking away the management position from me? I don’t have strength to dig. I am ashamed to beg. I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from management, they may receive me into their houses.’ Calling each one of his lord’s debtors to him, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe to my lord?’ He said, ‘A hundred batosof oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘How much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred corsof wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’ “His lord commended the dishonest manager because he had done wisely, for the children of this world are, in their own generation, wiser than the children of the light.

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The manager's frantic foresight against future destitution ('I have no strength to dig, I am ashamed to beg') inverts the sluggard wisdom of Proverbs, where prudent provision against want is praised. The shared topos of provident foresight versus ruinous idleness gives modest coherence, though no verbal contact; faint and contested.

echoes.text: There was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine. Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the grain which they bought: and Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh’s house. When the money was all spent in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, and said, “Give […]
echoes.note: Joseph as the shrewd steward managing his lord's grain and debtors during scarcity offers a figural backdrop to a manager renegotiating debts of wheat and oil. Coherence is thematic (estate-steward over produce), but the moral valence is opposite and there is no diction overlap, so it is faint and contested.

pericopes.text: I tell you, make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Make friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive you into the eternal tents' coheres tightly with the proverb that lending to the poor lends to the LORD, who repays. The shared logic that present generosity with money secures future, divine reception gives strong coherence with a widely available sapiential maxim.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's counsel that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure against the day of necessity' and 'delivers from death' supplies the precise economy Jesus assumes: wealth converted into mercy yields eschatological security. High coherence and Second-Temple availability make this a strong deuterocanonical echo behind 'receive you into the eternal tents.'

echoes.text: Howbeit with a man in poor estate be longsuffering; And let him not wait for your alms. Help a poor man for the commandment’s sake; And according to his need send him not empty away. Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira urges laying up alms in one's treasury as a deposit that will rescue one from misfortune, framing charity to the poor as deferred self-interest. The volume and coherence with 'make friends... so they may receive you' is high, and Sirach was demonstrably available to Luke's milieu.

echoes.text: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.
echoes.note: Daniel's appeal to Nebuchadnezzar to 'redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercy to the poor' supplies the redemptive-almsgiving theology underlying using mammon to gain eternal welcome. Strong coherence with the verse's logic; the connection is conceptual rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches? If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own? No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to one, and despise the other. You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon.”

echoes.text: Incline your ear to a poor man, And answer him with peaceful words in meekness. Deliver him that is wronged from the hand of him that wrongeth him; And be not faint-hearted in giving judgement. Be as a father to the fatherless, And instead of a husband to their mother: So will you be as a son of the Most High, And he will love you more than your mother does.
