echoes.note: The maxim 'faithful in a very little is faithful in much' coheres with Ben Sira's wisdom that integrity in small dealings with the lowly proves character, but the gnomic form is broadly diffused and no single passage controls it. Faint and contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'No servant can serve two masters... you cannot serve God and Mammon' echoes the covenantal either/or of choosing whom to serve, the LORD versus rival gods. Coherence with the exclusive-service motif is real but the diction is independent, so it is a faint figural echo at best.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The demand for undivided love of God set against love of money draws on the Shema's totalizing claim ('with all your heart'), which forbids a divided heart. The opposition of single-hearted devotion versus a rival master gives modest coherence; verbal contact is absent, so it is contested.

pericopes.text: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, also heard all these things, and they scoffed at him. He said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of men, but God knows your hearts. For that which is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.

echoes.text: Everyone who is proud in heart is an abomination to Yahweh: they shall certainly not be unpunished.
echoes.note: 'That which is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God' closely matches the proverb that everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD. Strong verbal and conceptual coherence (the 'abomination'/divine-loathing of human self-exaltation) and high availability support an allusion.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: 'You justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts' rests on Samuel's principle that man looks on outward appearance while the LORD looks on the heart. The contrast of human-facing display versus divine heart-knowledge is a coherent and well-known scriptural axiom.

echoes.text: Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but Yahweh weighs the hearts.
echoes.note: 'Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the hearts' parallels self-justification before men exposed by God's knowledge of hearts. Coherence is high and the sapiential idiom was available, though Proverbs 16:5 and 1 Samuel 16:7 are the closer touchstones.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: The LORD who 'searches the heart' to repay each according to his ways undergirds 'God knows your hearts.' The heart-searching-God motif is recurrent in the prophets, giving thematic coherence but no controlling diction here.

pericopes.text: The law and the prophets were until John. From that time the Good News of the Kingdom of God is preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it. But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one tiny stroke of a pen in the law to fall.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John' presupposes the Elijah-figure who marks the close of the prophetic era and the turn to the day of the LORD. Malachi's promise of Elijah before the great day gives coherent, available background to John as the canon's hinge.

echoes.text: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: 'Easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to fall' coheres with 'the grass withers... but the word of our God stands forever,' affirming the imperishability of God's word against the transient cosmos. Strong conceptual coherence with a recurrent Isaianic theme.

echoes.text: Yahweh, your word is settled in heaven forever.
echoes.note: 'Forever, O LORD, your word is settled in heaven' parallels the indestructibility of the Law's least stroke. The endurance-of-Torah motif gives thematic coherence, though the saying's imagery of a 'stroke of a pen' is independent.

pericopes.text: Everyone who divorces his wife, and marries another, commits adultery. He who marries one who is divorced from a husband commits adultery.

echoes.text: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter […]
echoes.note: The divorce-and-remarriage saying directly engages the Mosaic certificate-of-divorce legislation, which Jesus reads against the grain by classing remarriage as adultery. Availability and coherence are decisive; this is the legal text the dictum addresses, framed by v.17's claim on the Law.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: The prohibition of divorce-and-remarriage as adultery rests on the creational one-flesh union that divorce cannot truly dissolve. The coherence with Genesis is high (Jesus' parallel teaching elsewhere makes the link explicit), supplying the theological ground here.

echoes.text: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]
echoes.note: Malachi's oracle against faithless divorce ('the LORD hates divorce... she is your companion by covenant') coheres with Jesus' hardening of the marriage bond. The prophetic critique of casual divorce gives recurrent, available support, though no verbal quotation.

pericopes.text: “Now there was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, living in luxury every day. A certain beggar, named Lazarus, was laid at his gate, full of sores, and desiring to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Yes, even the dogs came and licked his sores.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: Lazarus laid 'at the gate' desiring crumbs while the rich man feasts dramatizes the Deuteronomic command not to harden the heart against the poor brother at your gate, for the poor will never cease in the land. High coherence with the covenantal gate-and-poor topos.

echoes.text: So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head. He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.
echoes.note: Lazarus 'full of sores' with dogs licking him evokes Job afflicted with sores from sole to crown, scraping himself amid loss. The shared imagery of a body covered in sores as the type of the abject sufferer gives coherent, available background.

echoes.text: For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no struggles in their death, but their strength is firm. They are free from burdens of men, neither are they plagued like other men. Therefore pride is like a chain around their neck. Violence covers them like a garment. Their eyes bulge with fat. Their minds pass the limits of conceit. They scoff and speak with malice. In arrogance, they threaten oppression. They […]
echoes.note: The prospering, sumptuously clothed rich man set against the afflicted poor man echoes the psalmist's scandal at the wicked who are 'always at ease' and 'clothed with violence' while the godly suffer, resolved only at their end. Strong coherence with the reversal-of-fortunes frame that the parable will enact.

echoes.text: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come! Go to Calneh, and see; and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. are they better than these kingdoms? or is their border greater than your border? Those who put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; Who lie on beds of […]
echoes.note: The rich man 'clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting in luxury every day' matches Amos' woe on those who lie on ivory beds, eat lambs, and feast while not grieved over ruin, who go first into exile. The prophetic indictment of callous luxury gives recurrent, coherent background.

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: 'Whoever shuts his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard' anticipates the rich man's later unanswered cry from Hades after ignoring Lazarus at his gate. Coherence with the lex talionis of neglected mercy is real but the link is thematic, not verbal.

pericopes.text: The beggar died, and he was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died, and was buried. In Hades, he lifted up his eyes, being in torment, and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus at his bosom. He cried and said, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue! For I am in anguish in this flame.’ “But Abraham said, ‘Son, remember that you, in your lifetime, received your good things, and Lazarus, in the same way, bad things. But now here he is comforted and you are in anguish. Besides all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, that those who want to pass from here to you are not able, and that no one may cross over from there to us.’

echoes.text: but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried in a good old age.
echoes.note: Being 'carried to Abraham's bosom' and the rich man's address 'Father Abraham' draw on the patriarchal hope of being gathered to one's fathers, with Abraham as the paradigmatic destination of the righteous dead. Coherence with the gathered-to-Abraham motif is strong, though 'bosom' as the resting place is Second-Temple development.

echoes.text: If we suffer thus, Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob will receive us, and all the fathers will commend us.
echoes.note: 'Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will receive us' on the lips of the martyrs supplies the explicit Second-Temple picture of the righteous welcomed by the patriarchs after death, illuminating 'Abraham's bosom.' Availability and coherence with the post-mortem reception motif support the echo.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The rich man's torment, flame, and anguish in Hades draws on Isaiah's closing vision of the dead whose fire is not quenched, the canonical seedbed of post-mortem fiery punishment. Coherence with the unquenched-fire judgment is high and the text was widely available.

echoes.text: The congregation of wicked men is as tow wrapped together; And the end of them is a flame of fire. The way of sinners is made smooth with stones; And at the last end thereof is the pit of Hades.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's image of the assembly of the wicked as tow set to flame and the broad road of sinners ending in Hades coheres with the flame and fixed-gulf fate of the rich man. The link is thematic to the sapiential fate-of-the-wicked topos rather than verbal.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: Enoch's tour of the hollow places of the dead, where the righteous and wicked are separated by a great division awaiting judgment, parallels the great chasm fixed between Lazarus and the rich man. As pseudepigraphal background to Second-Temple afterlife topography it is warranted but faint and contested.

pericopes.text: “He said, ‘I ask you therefore, father, that you would send him to my father’s house; for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, so they won’t also come into this place of torment.’ “But Abraham said to him, ‘They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them.’ “He said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if one goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ “He said to him, ‘If they don’t listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead.’”

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]
echoes.note: 'They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them' presses the Deuteronomic demand to heed the words spoken in God's name, with refusal entailing accountability. Coherence with the obligation to 'hear' the authoritative Mosaic word is strong, framing the sufficiency-of-Scripture point.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]
echoes.note: Abraham's verdict that those who will not hear Moses will not be persuaded even by a resurrection coheres with Deuteronomy's insistence that the word is not far off in heaven or beyond reach but near, in mouth and heart, so no extraordinary sign is needed. The sufficiency and nearness of the revealed word grounds the saying.

echoes.text: Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.
echoes.note: Israel's stiff-necked refusal to listen to the LORD's testimony 'by every prophet' despite warnings prefigures brothers who 'will not be persuaded' though warned by Moses and the prophets. The recurrent prophetic-rejection motif gives coherence, but the connection is thematic rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: He said to the disciples, “It is impossible that no occasions of stumbling should come, but woe to him through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck, and he were thrown into the sea, rather than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble. Be careful. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him. If he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times returns, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him.”

echoes.text: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.
echoes.note: The Holiness Code commands 'you shall surely rebuke your neighbor' rather than bear sin against him, the foundational text for fraternal correction that Jesus reproduces almost as a paraphrase ('rebuke him'). High Coherence with the surrounding love-of-neighbor frame and strong recurrence of this verse in Second-Temple reproof ethics give it good standing.

echoes.text: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
echoes.note: Lamech's boast that he is avenged 'seventy-sevenfold' is the numerical foil that Jesus' sevenfold-forgiveness saying (and Matthew's seventy-seven) inverts: unlimited vengeance becomes unlimited pardon. The shared and distinctive sevenfold idiom gives moderate Volume; the figural reversal supplies Coherence.

echoes.text: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin will I remember no more.
echoes.note: The new-covenant promise that God will forgive iniquity and remember sin no more underwrites the disciples' obligation to forgive the repentant brother. The link is thematic rather than verbal, so confidence is low, but the forgiveness motif gives Coherence with the pericope.

echoes.text: Son of man, when a land sins against me by committing a trespass, and I stretch out my hand on it, and break the staff of its bread, and send famine on it, and cut off from it man and animal;
echoes.note: Ezekiel's oracle on a land that 'sins against me' and the prophet's responsibility for warning resonates faintly with the 'if your brother sins' correction logic, but the connection is diffuse and the vocabulary common, so this is a contested faint echo at best.

pericopes.text: It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck, and he were thrown into the sea, rather than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.

echoes.text: It shall be, when you have made an end of reading this book, that you shall bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates:
echoes.note: Jeremiah's sign-act binds a stone to the scroll and casts it into the Euphrates so Babylon will 'sink and not rise,' the closest OT image to a weight sunk in deep water as a figure of irreversible doom. The millstone-and-sea threat shares the distinctive stone-cast-into-water motif of total destruction, giving moderate Volume.

echoes.text: The deeps cover them. They went down into the depths like a stone.
echoes.note: The Song of the Sea says the enemy 'went down into the depths like a stone,' supplying the stone-sinking-in-the-sea imagery of judgment. The verbal overlap (stone, depths of the sea) is suggestive but the motif is widespread, so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: You divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on the dry land; and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into the mighty waters.
echoes.note: Nehemiah's prayer recalls the pursuers cast 'into the depths, like a stone into mighty waters,' reinforcing the same drowning-by-stone judgment topos. Low Volume and a commonplace image keep this contested.

pericopes.text: The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith.” The Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would tell this sycamore tree, ‘Be uprooted, and be planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.

echoes.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
echoes.note: Zechariah's word that the great 'mountain' shall become a plain before Zerubbabel by the Spirit, not by might, is the canonical pairing of faith with the moving/leveling of an immovable obstacle. The mountain-removed-by-faith logic gives Coherence with 'faith like a mustard seed,' though Luke uses a sycamore-into-sea rather than a mountain, lowering Volume.

echoes.text: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas;
echoes.note: The psalm's confidence even 'though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the very image of an immovable thing thrown into the sea, here recast as the work of faith. The verbal overlap (uprooted/carried into the sea) is real but the figure is proverbial, so it is faint.

echoes.text: He stood, and shook the earth. He looked, and made the nations tremble. The ancient mountains were crumbled. The age-old hills collapsed. His ways are eternal.
echoes.note: The theophany that scatters the everlasting mountains coheres with the faith-moves-mountains topos behind the uprooted-tree saying. The connection is conceptual and diffuse, so confidence is low.

echoes.text: For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed; but my loving kindness shall not depart from you, neither shall my covenant of peace be removed,” says Yahweh who has mercy on you.
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'the mountains may depart' as a figure of cosmic upheaval feeds the same stock of immovable-object-displaced imagery that the mustard-seed/sycamore saying exploits. Faint and contested.

pericopes.text: But who is there among you, having a servant plowing or keeping sheep, that will say, when he comes in from the field, ‘Come immediately and sit down at the table,’ and will not rather tell him, ‘Prepare my supper, clothe yourself properly, and serve me, while I eat and drink. Afterward you shall eat and drink’? Does he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded? I think not. Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’”

echoes.text: “Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him, that you make your ways perfect?
echoes.note: Eliphaz asks whether a man can be profitable to God or whether it is gain to the Almighty that one is righteous, the wisdom premise that human service places God under no obligation. This grounds the 'we are unworthy servants, we have only done our duty' logic; moderate Coherence with the servant parable.

echoes.text: If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand?
echoes.note: Elihu's 'if you are righteous, what do you give him?' states the same theology of non-meritorious obedience underlying the unprofitable-servant saying. Recurrence of the motif across Job strengthens the Availability and Coherence, though there is no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress; so our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us.
echoes.note: The image of servants' eyes fixed on the hand of their master, waiting on his command, supplies the master-servant deference picture the parable assumes. Conceptual rather than verbal, hence low confidence.

echoes.text: For to me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: God's claim that the Israelites are his servants whom he brought out of Egypt frames Israel's whole obedience as owed service, the covenantal backdrop to 'we have only done what was our duty.' Faint, diffuse, contested.

pericopes.text: As he was on his way to Jerusalem, he was passing along the borders of Samaria and Galilee. As he entered into a certain village, ten men who were lepers met him, who stood at a distance. They lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” When he saw them, he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” As they went, they were cleansed. One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice. He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan. Jesus answered, “Weren’t the ten cleansed? But where are the nine? Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this stranger?” Then he said to him, “Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you.”

echoes.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]
echoes.note: The Naaman narrative — a leprous Syrian foreigner cleansed who returns to the prophet to confess the God of Israel — is the structural template for the lone Samaritan leper who turns back to give thanks. The distinctive convergence of foreigner + leprosy + cleansing + grateful return gives strong Volume and Coherence, and Luke elsewhere cites Naaman explicitly (4:27), confirming Recurrence.

echoes.text: “The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes, and the hair of his head shall hang loose. He shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry, ‘Unclean! Unclean!’ All the days in which the plague is in him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall dwell alone. Outside of the camp shall be his dwelling.
echoes.note: The leprosy law requires the unclean to dwell apart and cry out, explaining why the ten 'stood at a distance' and lifted their voices. The pericope presupposes this purity legislation as its narrative grammar, giving high Coherence and Availability.

echoes.text: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper, then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop.
echoes.note: The cleansed leper must be presented to the priest for inspection and rites of restoration, exactly what Jesus commands: 'Go, show yourselves to the priests.' The direct dependence on the priestly examination law gives high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned. Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” Yahweh […]
echoes.note: Miriam's leprosy, exclusion 'outside the camp' for seven days, and restoration by intercession reinforce the segregation-and-cleansing pattern shaping the leper episode. Moderate Coherence; the motif overlaps with the Leviticus laws, so it adds recurrence rather than independent Volume.

echoes.text: Now there were four leprous men at the entrance of the gate. They said one to another, “Why do we sit here until we die?
echoes.note: The four lepers at the gate of Samaria who 'stood at the entrance' likewise embody the marginalized-leper-at-a-distance topos and the Samaria setting. Geographic and situational resonance, but no verbal dependence, so low.

echoes.text: Praise Yahweh, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name! Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits; who forgives all your sins; who heals all your diseases;
echoes.note: The psalm's call to 'bless the Lord, O my soul... who heals all your diseases' coheres with the Samaritan's loud-voiced glorifying of God for his healing. Thematic only; faint.

pericopes.text: Being asked by the Pharisees when the Kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The Kingdom of God doesn’t come with observation; neither will they say, ‘Look, here!’ or, ‘Look, there!’ for behold, the Kingdom of God is within you.”

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: Daniel's vision that the God of heaven will set up an everlasting kingdom underlies the Pharisees' question of when the Kingdom of God would come and Jesus' redefinition of its arrival. Moderate Volume from the shared 'kingdom of God' eschatology; Daniel is the key Second-Temple source for the expectation Jesus is correcting.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The everlasting dominion given to the one like a son of man frames the kingdom expectation in view; the link is conceptual, anticipating the Son-of-Man material that immediately follows, so it is low here.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]
echoes.note: Moses insists the commandment is 'not far off... but very near you, in your mouth and in your heart,' a nearness-not-distant idiom that resonates with 'the Kingdom of God is among/within you' rather than 'here' or 'there.' Suggestive but contested.

pericopes.text: He said to the disciples, “The days will come, when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. They will tell you, ‘Look, here!’ or ‘Look, there!’ Don’t go away, nor follow after them, for as the lightning, when it flashes out of the one part under the sky, shines to the other part under the sky; so will the Son of Man be in his day. But first, he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'the Son of Man' and his sudden, heaven-spanning revelation derive from Daniel's one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. This is the controlling OT source for the entire 'days of the Son of Man' discourse, giving high Volume, Recurrence, and Coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.
echoes.note: Zechariah's theophany where 'the Lord will appear... his arrow will go out like lightning' supplies the lightning-flash imagery for the Son of Man's day. The distinctive divine-lightning-of-judgment motif gives moderate Volume.

echoes.text: His lightning lights up the world. The earth sees, and trembles.
echoes.note: 'His lightnings light up the world' depicts the cosmic, world-illuminating theophany echoed in the lightning that shines from one part of the sky to the other. Common theophanic imagery, so low.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: The Suffering Servant 'despised and rejected by men' undergirds 'he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.' The must-suffer-and-be-rejected formula coheres strongly with Isaiah 53, giving moderate Volume to a figural reading.

pericopes.text: As it was in the days of Noah, even so will it be also in the days of the Son of Man. They ate, they drank, they married, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ship, and the flood came, and destroyed them all.

echoes.text: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came on the earth. Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives, because of the floodwaters. Clean animals, unclean animals, birds, and everything that creeps on the ground went by pairs to Noah into the ship, male and female, as God commanded Noah. After the seven days, the floodwaters came on the earth. In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the […]
echoes.note: The flood narrative — humanity eating and marrying in oblivious normalcy until Noah enters the ark and the deluge destroys them all — is explicitly invoked ('as in the days of Noah'). Direct named typology gives maximal Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: The verdict that human wickedness was great and every intention only evil supplies the moral indictment implicit in the days-of-Noah comparison: heedless wickedness met by sudden judgment. Strengthens the Coherence of the flood typology.

pericopes.text: Likewise, even as it was in the days of Lot: they ate, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they built; but in the day that Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from the sky, and destroyed them all. It will be the same way in the day that the Son of Man is revealed.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky. He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.
echoes.note: Sodom's destruction by fire and sulfur rained from heaven, with Lot going out on the day of doom, is named directly ('the days of Lot'). The explicit citation of fire-and-brimstone judgment gives maximal Volume and Coherence as the paired type to Noah.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous, I will go down now, and see whether their deeds are as bad as the reports which have come to me. If not, I will know.”
echoes.note: The outcry against Sodom's sin that prompts the divine visitation supplies the moral premise behind the eating-buying-building-as-usual-until-judgment picture. Coheres with the Lot typology and supports its Recurrence.

echoes.text: and that all of its land is sulfur, salt, and burning, that it is not sown, doesn’t produce, nor does any grass grow in it, like the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which Yahweh overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath;
echoes.note: The covenant curse describes the land as 'brimstone and salt... like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah,' showing Sodom's fire-and-sulfur as the standard type of sudden total ruin Luke is invoking. Adds Recurrence; faint as an independent source.

echoes.text: Behold, this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease was in her and in her daughters; neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy. They were haughty, and committed abomination before me: therefore I took them away when I saw it.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's reading of Sodom's sin as prosperous, complacent ease before judgment matches the buying/selling/planting/building complacency Luke emphasizes. Thematic reinforcement, low Volume.

pericopes.text: In that day, he who will be on the housetop, and his goods in the house, let him not go down to take them away. Let him who is in the field likewise not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife! Whoever seeks to save his life loses it, but whoever loses his life preserves it.

echoes.text: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
echoes.note: 'Remember Lot's wife' explicitly names the woman who looked back and became a pillar of salt, the warning against turning back when fleeing judgment. A direct citation by name gives maximal Volume and Coherence with 'let him not turn back.'

echoes.text: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
echoes.note: The angels' command 'do not look behind you... lest you be consumed' is the prohibition Lot's wife violated and the imperative behind 'let him not go down... not turn back.' The flee-without-looking-back instruction is closely reproduced, giving high Volume.

echoes.text: Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.
echoes.note: The proverb 'all that a man has he will give for his life' resonates faintly with the paradox of seeking to save one's life and losing it; the connection is thematic, not verbal, so low.

pericopes.text: I tell you, in that night there will be two people in one bed. The one will be taken, and the other will be left. There will be two grinding grain together. One will be taken, and the other will be left.”

echoes.text: and all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the female servant who is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of livestock.
echoes.note: The plague on the firstborn 'from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the maidservant who is behind the mill' pairs sleeping/grinding social opposites singled out for judgment, a structural analogue to the two in one bed and two grinding, one taken and one left. Suggestive selective-judgment motif, but no verbal dependence, so low.

echoes.text: Then you shall return and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him who serves God and him who doesn’t serve him.
echoes.note: Malachi's promise that you will again distinguish 'between the righteous and the wicked' on the day of judgment coheres with the sudden separation of the paired figures, one taken and one left. Thematic and faint.

pericopes.text: They, answering, asked him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the body is, there will the vultures also be gathered together.”

echoes.text: His young ones also suck up blood. Where the slain are, there he is.”
echoes.note: The Lord's speech on the eagle/vulture whose young suck up blood and that is wherever the slain are ('where the slain are, there is he') is the clearest source for 'where the body is, there the vultures gather.' The distinctive corpse-and-bird-of-prey proverb gives strong Volume and Coherence with the judgment scene.

echoes.text: Their horses also are swifter than leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves. Their horsemen press proudly on. Yes, their horsemen come from afar. They fly as an eagle that hurries to devour.
echoes.note: The Chaldean horsemen who fly 'like an eagle swift to devour' gathering to the prey supply the swooping-bird-of-prey-toward-the-doomed imagery. Moderate Volume; reinforces the judgment-by-gathering-raptors motif.

echoes.text: You, son of man, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Speak to the birds of every sort, and to every animal of the field, Assemble yourselves, and come; gather yourselves on every side to my sacrifice that I do sacrifice for you, even a great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel, that you may eat flesh and drink blood. You shall eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth, of rams, of lambs, and of goats, of bulls, all of them […]
echoes.note: The summons to the birds to gather to God's sacrificial slaughter and eat the flesh of the slain provides an eschatological carrion-gathering image very close to the saying's apocalyptic function. Good Coherence with the day-of-judgment context, lowered only by the eagles/vultures vs. generic-birds difference.

echoes.text: “Put the trumpet to your lips! Something like an eagle is over Yahweh’s house, because they have broken my covenant, and rebelled against my law.
echoes.note: 'Set the trumpet to your lips! One like an eagle is over the house of the Lord' offers an eagle-as-onrushing-judgment image. Faint and contested, but adds Recurrence to the bird-of-prey-judgment topos.

pericopes.text: He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray, and not give up, saying, “There was a judge in a certain city who didn’t fear God, and didn’t respect man. A widow was in that city, and she often came to him, saying, ‘Defend me from my adversary!’ He wouldn’t for a while, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God, nor respect man, yet because this widow bothers me, I will defend her, or else she will wear me out by her continual coming.’” The Lord said, “Listen to what the unrighteous judge says. Won’t God avenge his chosen ones, who are crying out to him day and night, and yet he exercises patience with them? I tell you that he will avenge them quickly. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”

echoes.text: He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall? He that serves God according to his good pleasure shall be accepted, And his supplication shall reach to the clouds. The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds; And till it come near, he will not be comforted; And he will not depart, till […]
echoes.note: Sirach declares the Lord will not ignore the widow's cry nor the supplication of the oppressed, the prayer that pierces the clouds, and that he will not delay nor be patient (slow) until he repays vengeance. Luke fuses the widow figure, the day-and-night crying, the question of God's delay, and the swift vindication, making this the densest Second-Temple background for the parable. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
echoes.note: The Torah forbids afflicting any widow or orphan, promising that if they cry out God will surely hear and his wrath will burn. This grounds the parable's premise that God vindicates the crying widow, drawing on the covenantal cry-and-hear pattern. Strong availability and coherence with the elect 'crying out day and night.'

echoes.text: You shall not deprive the foreigner or the fatherless of justice, nor take a widow’s clothing in pledge;
echoes.note: Deuteronomy commands not to pervert the justice due to the sojourner or fatherless and not to take a widow's garment in pledge. The unjust judge embodies the legal failure this law targets, while God is the true judge who defends the widow's case ('Defend me from my adversary'). Coherent with the legal-vindication theme though more diffuse than Sirach.

echoes.text: I will give thanks to Yahweh with my whole heart. I will tell of all your marvelous works. I will be glad and rejoice in you. I will sing praise to your name, O Most High. When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish in your presence. For you have maintained my just cause. You sit on the throne judging righteously. You have rebuked the nations. You have destroyed the wicked. You have blotted out their name forever and ever. The enemy is overtaken by […]
echoes.note: Psalm 9-10 (one psalm in LXX) praises God as the one who judges the oppressed, does not forget the cry of the afflicted, and vindicates the poor against the wicked who say God does not see. The widow's plea for vindication and God's avenging of his elect echo this petitionary justice psalm. Medium volume; thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
echoes.note: Habakkuk promises the vision awaits its appointed time, hastens to the end, will not lie, and 'though it delay, wait for it.' The parable's tension between God's apparent patience/delay and his coming swift vindication, capped by 'when the Son of Man comes,' resonates with this eschatological delay-yet-certain motif. Coherent with Luke's vindication eschatology.
echoes.lxxText: For the vision is yet for a time, and it shall shoot forth at the end, and not in vain: though he should tarry, wait for him; for he will surely come, and will not tarry.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before you. Let my prayer enter into your presence. Turn your ear to my cry. For my soul is full of troubles. My life draws near to Sheol. I am counted among those who go down into the pit. I am like a man who has no help, set apart among the dead, like the slain who lie in the grave, whom you remember no more. They are cut off from your hand. You have laid me in the lowest pit, in the darkest […]
echoes.note: The lament of crying to God day and night ('day and night I cry before you') supplies the unceasing-prayer language of the elect crying out day and night. The verbal pairing is common in the Psalter but Psalm 88 is its sharpest instance. Low confidence given the formula's diffusion.

echoes.text: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”
echoes.note: Abraham's appeal, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justice?' frames God as the just Judge contrasted here with the unjust human judge. The figural contrast between God-the-just-Judge and the city judge who fears neither God nor man may stand behind Luke's argument a fortiori. Faint and thematic.

pericopes.text: He spoke also this parable to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others. “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector. The Pharisee stood and prayed to himself like this: ‘God, I thank you, that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’ But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me. Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge. Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin […]
echoes.note: The tax collector's 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner' closely tracks the penitent's plea in Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, O God... blot out my transgressions,' the paradigmatic prayer of the contrite sinner. The shared vocabulary of mercy plus self-identification as sinner and the broken-and-contrite heart God accepts make this a strong verbal-thematic echo. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
echoes.note: The maxim 'God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble' underwrites the closing logion that the self-exalting are humbled and the self-humbling exalted. The Pharisee's proud self-display versus the tax collector's lowliness is precisely this proverb's contrast, and the LXX wording was a standard Second-Temple proof text. Strong coherence with Luke's reversal theme.
echoes.lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

echoes.text: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
echoes.note: Job 22:29 states that when one is brought low he says 'lift up,' for God saves the lowly of eyes, matching both the exaltation-of-the-humble logion and the detail that the tax collector would not lift up his eyes. The eyes-lowered humility detail strengthens the link beyond the common reversal topos. Medium volume.

echoes.text: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's oracle 'exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high' supplies a prophetic form of the humbled/exalted reversal that concludes the parable. The phrasing is a recognized OT antecedent for Luke's reversal sayings (cf. also 1:52). Thematic rather than verbal-specific here.

echoes.text: ‘Why have we fasted,’ say they, ‘and you don’t see? Why have we afflicted our soul, and you take no knowledge?’ “Behold, in the day of your fast you find pleasure, and exact all your labors. Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with the fist of wickedness: you don’t fast this day so as to make your voice to be heard on high. Is such the fast that I have chosen? the day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head as a […]
echoes.note: Isaiah 58 rebukes those who fast yet oppress, contrasting empty self-righteous fasting with the fast God chooses (justice and mercy to the poor). The Pharisee's boast of fasting twice a week and tithing, set against the justified penitent, draws on this prophetic critique of cultic display divorced from righteousness. Coherent with Luke's piety-critique.

echoes.text: For thus says the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.
echoes.note: God dwells 'with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the heart of the contrite,' which matches why the humbled tax collector goes home justified rather than the proud Pharisee. The contrite/humble spirit that God favors is the theological engine of the parable. Medium coherence.

echoes.text: He that keeps the law multiplies offerings; He that takes heed to the commandments sacrifices a peace offering. He that requites a good turn offers fine flour; And he that gives alms sacrifices a thank offering. To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; And to depart from unrighteousness is an atoning sacrifice.
echoes.note: Sirach insists that keeping the law and almsgiving outweigh mere sacrifice, a Second-Temple critique of confidence in cultic performance like the Pharisee's. Faint and contested, but coherent with the tithing/fasting boast being insufficient. Low volume.

echoes.text: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: The one who may ascend the temple hill is the clean of hands and pure of heart; the two men 'went up into the temple to pray' and only the contrite one is accepted. The temple-ascent and acceptability motif faintly underlies the scene. Low confidence.

pericopes.text: They were also bringing their babies to him, that he might touch them. But when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. Jesus summoned them, saying, “Allow the little children to come to me, and don’t hinder them, for the Kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Most certainly, I tell you, whoever doesn’t receive the Kingdom of God like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”

echoes.text: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham […]
echoes.note: The patriarch laying hands on and blessing children stands behind Jesus' touching and receiving the babies, a gesture of paternal blessing. The link is gestural and thematic rather than verbal. Low confidence given how common blessing-of-children scenes are.

echoes.text: Yahweh, my heart isn’t haughty, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me. Israel, hope in Yahweh, from this time forward and forever more.
echoes.note: The psalmist's posture of a weaned child, calm and humble, with eyes not raised too high, resonates with receiving the kingdom 'like a little child' as dependent lowliness. Coheres with the surrounding humility theme but verbally faint. Low confidence.

pericopes.text: A certain ruler asked him, saying, “Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus asked him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good, except one—God. You know the commandments: ‘Don’t commit adultery,’ ‘Don’t murder,’ ‘Don’t steal,’ ‘Don’t give false testimony,’ ‘Honor your father and your mother.’” He said, “I have observed all these things from my youth up.” When Jesus heard these things, he said to him, “You still lack one thing. Sell all that you have, and distribute it to the poor. You will have treasure in heaven. Come, follow me.” But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was very rich.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: Jesus recites the Decalogue's second table—do not commit adultery, murder, steal, bear false witness, honor father and mother—quoting the commandments nearly verbatim. This is an explicit citation of the Ten Commandments as the answer to inheriting eternal life. Highest volume; direct quotation.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic recension of the Decalogue is an equally valid source for the cited commandments; Luke's order (adultery, murder, steal, false witness, honor parents) reflects a known sequence in the LXX tradition shared by both Exodus and Deuteronomy. Direct quotation, high volume.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: Jesus' 'No one is good except God alone' echoes the Shema's confession of the one God as the sole locus of goodness and uniqueness. The monotheistic premise reframes the ruler's 'Good Teacher.' Medium volume; theological rather than verbal-exact.

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Leviticus' promise that the one who keeps the commandments 'shall live by them' undergirds the link between commandment-keeping and inheriting eternal life that frames the dialogue. This was the standard Second-Temple text connecting Torah obedience and life. Coherent though not quoted.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The 'sell all and give to the poor' command and the implicit demand of total neighbor-love stand near Leviticus' love-of-neighbor, often paired with the Decalogue in Jesus' teaching. Faint here since Luke does not cite the love command in this pericope. Low confidence.

echoes.text: Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: The question 'what shall I do to inherit eternal life' and the demand for clean conduct loosely recall the entrance-liturgy question 'Who shall ascend?' answered by moral purity. Thematic and faint. Low confidence.

pericopes.text: Jesus, seeing that he became very sad, said, “How hard it is for those who have riches to enter into the Kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to enter in through a needle’s eye, than for a rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God.” Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?” But he said, “The things which are impossible with men are possible with God.” Peter said, “Look, we have left everything, and followed you.” He said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, there is no one who has left house, or wife, or brothers, or parents, or children, for the Kingdom of God’s sake, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the world to come, eternal life.”

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: 'The things impossible with men are possible with God' closely echoes the LORD's word to Sarah, 'Is anything too hard for the LORD?', the foundational OT statement of divine possibility against human impossibility. The salvation of the rich, humanly impossible, is staked on this Abrahamic promise of God's power. High coherence and recurrence.

echoes.text: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.
echoes.note: Job's confession 'I know that you can do all things, and no purpose of yours can be thwarted' directly parallels 'what is impossible with men is possible with God.' This is a near-formulaic OT affirmation of divine omnipotence that Luke deploys at the climax of the rich-ruler episode. Strong volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my eyes?” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'If it is marvelous (impossible) in the eyes of the remnant... should it also be marvelous in my eyes? says the LORD' contrasts human impossibility with divine ease, mirroring Luke's antithesis. The eschatological restoration context fits Luke's kingdom-entry theme. Medium volume.

echoes.text: Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; there is nothing too hard for you,
echoes.note: Jeremiah prays 'Ah Lord GOD... nothing is too hard for you,' another standard OT declaration of divine possibility echoed by 'possible with God.' Reinforces the recurrence criterion alongside Genesis 18:14 and Job 42:2. Thematic, near-formulaic.

echoes.text: He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.
echoes.note: 'He who trusts in his riches will fall' coheres with the warning that the rich enter the kingdom only with difficulty. Wisdom's critique of riches stands generally behind the camel-and-needle saying. Low volume; no verbal contact.

pericopes.text: He took the twelve aside, and said to them, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all the things that are written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be completed. For he will be delivered up to the Gentiles, will be mocked, treated shamefully, and spit on. They will scourge and kill him. On the third day, he will rise again.” They understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they didn’t understand the things that were said.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we […]
echoes.note: 'Everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished'—his being delivered up, mocked, shamefully treated, spit on, scourged, and killed—draws directly on the Suffering Servant who was despised, gave his back to smiters, and was led to slaughter. Luke programmatically reads the passion as the prophesied Servant fate. High coherence; the chief scriptural script for the passion.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The Servant who gave his back to those who struck, his cheeks to those who pulled the beard, and hid not his face from shame and spitting matches Luke's specific list: mocked, shamefully treated, and spit upon. The spitting and shaming details are strikingly verbal. High volume.

echoes.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning? My God, I cry in the daytime, but you don’t answer; in the night season, and am not silent. But you are holy, you who inhabit the praises of Israel. Our fathers trusted in you. They trusted, and you delivered them. They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed. But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of […]
echoes.note: The mocking and shameful abuse of the righteous sufferer in Psalm 22 ('all who see me mock me') belongs to the prophetic passion script Luke invokes; Luke's passion narrative later cites this psalm directly. Here it stands among 'all that is written.' Medium volume in this verse, high recurrence in Luke.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of Man,' the figure whose fate the prophets foretell, derives from Daniel's heavenly one given dominion; Luke pairs the suffering with this exalted title pointing toward vindication and resurrection on the third day. The Son of Man designation carries Danielic resonance even in a passion context. Medium coherence.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'On the third day he will raise us up' is widely held to inform the 'on the third day he will rise again' formula of the passion predictions. The third-day vindication motif is a recognized Second-Temple resurrection backdrop. Medium volume; contested verbal link.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: The rejected stone made the cornerstone foreshadows the Son of Man rejected then vindicated/raised, part of the prophetic-fulfillment frame. Faint here since unquoted in this pericope. Low confidence.

pericopes.text: As he came near Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the road, begging. Hearing a multitude going by, he asked what this meant. They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. He cried out, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!” Those who led the way rebuked him, that he should be quiet; but he cried out all the more, “You son of David, have mercy on me!” Standing still, Jesus commanded him to be brought to him. When he had come near, he asked him, “What do you want me to do?” He said, “Lord, that I may see again.” Jesus said to him, “Receive your sight. Your faith has healed you.” Immediately he received his sight, and followed him, glorifying God. All the people, when they saw it, praised God.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: The blind man's confession 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me' invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting throne to David's offspring, identifying Jesus as the messianic Son of David. The title is the theological hinge of the healing, set en route to Jerusalem. High coherence with Luke's royal Christology.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened' is the signature prophecy of messianic restoration that Luke enacts in the Jericho healing, signaling the in-breaking kingdom. The opening of blind eyes is a programmatic Lukan fulfillment motif (cf. 4:18; 7:22). High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'The eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and darkness' adds to the Isaianic cluster promising sight to the blind in the day of restoration, reinforced by Luke's pattern of citing such oracles. Medium volume; part of a recurring Isaianic chain.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant is appointed 'to open the eyes that are blind,' tying the blind-man healing to the Servant's commission and complementing the passion's Servant Christology in the prior pericope. Coherent within Luke's Isaianic program. Medium confidence.

echoes.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind' attributes sight-giving to God, so that the crowd's praising God when the blind man sees enacts this psalm's confession of God who heals. Coheres with the closing 'glorifying God' and the Davidic-mercy frame. Medium volume.

echoes.text: I will sing of the loving kindness of Yahweh forever. With my mouth, I will make known your faithfulness to all generations. I indeed declare, “Love stands firm forever. You established the heavens. Your faithfulness is in them.” “I have made a covenant with my chosen one, I have sworn to David, my servant, ‘I will establish your seed forever, and build up your throne to all generations.’” Selah. The heavens will praise your wonders, Yahweh; your […]
echoes.note: Psalm 89's celebration of God's steadfast covenant mercy to David and his line reinforces the 'Son of David, have mercy' plea, linking Davidic sonship with covenant mercy (eleos). Thematic support for the title's mercy resonance. Low volume.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: The Servant anointed to proclaim 'recovery of sight to the blind' (so the LXX, taken up at Luke 4:18) faintly underlies the Jericho restoration as fulfillment of the Jubilee announcement. Faint here, strong in Luke overall. Low confidence.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

pericopes.text: He entered and was passing through Jericho. There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich. He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short. He ran on ahead, and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was to pass that way. When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully. When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.” Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.” Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

echoes.text: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it, or sells it; he shall pay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
echoes.note: Zacchaeus pledges to restore fourfold what he has wrongfully exacted, matching the Torah's penalty of four sheep for a stolen sheep. Luke's specific multiplier 'four times' aligns precisely with the lower of the Exodus restitution scales, signaling Zacchaeus's voluntary embrace of legal restitution beyond mere repayment. High volume and coherence with the conversion-as-restoration theme.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel: ‘When a man or woman commits any sin that men commit, so as to trespass against Yahweh, and that soul is guilty; then he shall confess his sin which he has done, and he shall make restitution for his guilt in full, and add to it the fifth part of it, and give it to him in respect of whom he has been guilty.
echoes.note: Numbers prescribes that one who wrongs another must confess, restore the principal in full, and add a fifth. Zacchaeus's confession plus voluntary restitution enacts this penitential statute, even exceeding it in the fourfold portion. The coherence of confession-and-restoration makes this a strong background for the verse's logic of repentance.

echoes.text: He shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!”
echoes.note: Nathan's parable has David decree the rich thief must restore the lamb fourfold, the same multiplier Zacchaeus invokes. The shared fourfold figure tied to a wealthy man's exploitation of the poor gives a narrative echo, though it derives the number from the Exodus statute David applies. Medium confidence as the link is mediated through the legal background.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: The Son of Man's mission to 'seek and to save that which was lost' echoes Ezekiel's promise that God himself will seek the lost sheep and bind up the strayed, in contrast to the false shepherds. Luke applies the divine shepherd-search directly to Jesus, with the rare verb pairing seek/lost matching the prophetic oracle. High volume and thematic coherence with Luke's lost-and-found motif.

echoes.text: therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.
echoes.note: Ezekiel adds that God will 'save' his flock so they shall no more be a prey, reinforcing the seek-and-save pairing of v. 10. The combination of seeking the lost and saving the flock in one oracle undergirds Luke's compressed mission statement. Medium because v. 16 carries the primary verbal weight.

echoes.text: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make nations of you. Kings will come out of you. I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: Jesus declares Zacchaeus 'a son of Abraham,' invoking the Abrahamic covenant and its promise of inclusion. The phrase asserts that the despised tax collector belongs to the covenant family, an echo of God's covenant with Abraham and his offspring. Medium volume; the title is idiomatic but covenantally loaded in Luke.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: The gathering of the scattered/lost of Israel as a restoration motif faintly underlies 'came to seek and to save that which was lost.' The remnant-gathering theme coheres with Luke's salvation-to-this-house, but the verbal contact is slight. Low confidence; Ezekiel 34 is the stronger source.

echoes.text: “In that day,” says Yahweh, “I will assemble that which is lame, and I will gather that which is driven away, and that which I have afflicted;
echoes.note: Micah's promise to gather 'her that is driven out' and 'the lost' (LXX) supplies another prophetic seeking-the-lost background for v. 10. The image of God assembling the strayed remnant coheres with Jesus's mission statement but is verbally faint beside Ezekiel. Low confidence, marked contested.

pericopes.text: As they heard these things, he went on and told a parable, because he was near Jerusalem, and they supposed that the Kingdom of God would be revealed immediately. He said therefore, “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return. He called ten servants of his, and gave them ten mina coins, and told them, ‘Conduct business until I come.’ But his citizens hated him, and sent an envoy after him, saying, ‘We don’t want this man to reign over us.’ “When he had come back again, having received the kingdom, he commanded these servants, to whom he had given the money, to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by conducting business. The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten more minas.’ “He said to him, ‘Well done, you good servant! Because you were found faithful with very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ “The second came, saying, ‘Your mina, Lord, has made five minas.’ “So he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’ Another came, saying, ‘Lord, behold, your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief, for I feared you, because you are an exacting man. You take up that which you didn’t lay down, and reap that which you didn’t sow.’ “He said to him, ‘Out of your own mouth will I judge you, you wicked servant! You knew that I am an exacting man, taking up that which I didn’t lay down, and reaping that which I didn’t sow. Then why didn’t you deposit my money in the bank, and at my coming, I might have earned interest on it?’ He said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina away from him, and give it to him who has the ten minas.’ “They said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ ‘For I tell you that to everyone who has, will more be given; but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away from him. But bring those enemies of mine who didn’t want me to reign over them here, and kill them before me.’”

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, tell a riddle, and speak a parable to the house of Israel; and say, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: A great eagle with great wings and long feathers, full of feathers, which had various colors, came to Lebanon, and took the top of the cedar: he cropped off the topmost of the young twigs of it, and carried it to a land of traffic; he set it in a city of merchants. He took also of the seed of the land, and planted it […]
echoes.note: The parable's transplanting and accountability imagery, where a vassal is set up and judged for fruitfulness, faintly resembles Ezekiel's eagle-and-vine allegory of kingship and rebellion. Both concern a ruler's delegated authority and reckoning, though the minas parable is closer to political memory than to this oracle. Low and contested.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The nobleman 'went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return' evokes the Son of Man approaching the Ancient of Days to receive dominion, kingship, and a returning reign. Luke frames the parable amid expectation that the Kingdom would appear, making the Danielic enthronement-and-return pattern a coherent backdrop. Medium volume given the political-historical surface.

echoes.text: Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian. His master saw that Yahweh was with him, and that Yahweh made all that he did prosper in his hand. Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand. From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for […]
echoes.note: The faithful servant entrusted with much and given authority over cities loosely recalls Joseph's stewardship rewarded with rule over Egypt. The steward-elevated-to-governance pattern coheres but is a common biblical type, so verbal contact is weak. Low confidence, contested.

echoes.text: You shall not lend on interest to your brother; interest of money, interest of food, interest of anything that is lent on interest. You may lend on interest to a foreigner; but to your brother you shall not lend on interest, that Yahweh your God may bless you in all that you put your hand to, in the land where you go in to possess it.
