echoes.note: The master's reproach about not depositing the money to earn interest plays against the Torah's regulation of usury, sharpening the third servant's failure. The interest/banking language gains bite against the Mosaic lending economy, though no quotation is intended. Low and contested.

echoes.text: Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles away, but he who gathers by hand makes it grow.
echoes.note: The contrast between increasing wealth by labor and the unproductive hoarded mina resonates with Proverbs' maxim that wealth gotten by vanity dwindles but he who gathers by labor increases it. The wisdom logic of fruitful versus idle stewardship coheres faintly. Low confidence.

echoes.text: He also rebelled against king Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God: but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart against turning to Yahweh, the God of Israel.
echoes.note: The citizens' embassy declaring 'We don't want this man to reign over us' echoes the recurrent rejection of the appointed king and rebellion against the suzerain, as when Zedekiah rebelled against the overlord. The rejected-ruler motif coheres with Israel's pattern of refusing God's anointed, but no single text is quoted. Low, contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not be king over them.
echoes.note: The subjects' refusal of the nobleman's reign recalls Israel's rejection of God as king ('they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them'). The verbal shape 'reign over us / over them' coheres with Luke's theme of rejecting the true king, though the parable's surface is Herodian politics. Low confidence, contested.

pericopes.text: Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples, saying, “Go your way into the village on the other side, in which, as you enter, you will find a colt tied, whereon no man ever yet sat. Untie it, and bring it. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say to him: ‘The Lord needs it.’” Those who were sent went away, and found things just as he had told them. As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” They said, “The Lord needs it.” They brought it to Jesus. They threw their cloaks on the colt, and set Jesus on them. As he went, they spread their cloaks on the road. As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen, saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!” Some of the Pharisees from the multitude said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples!” He answered them, “I tell you that if these were silent, the stones would cry out.”

echoes.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
echoes.note: The entry on a colt amid royal acclamation enacts Zechariah's oracle of the king coming to Zion humble and riding on a colt, the foal of a donkey. Though Luke does not cite the verse explicitly as Matthew does, the colt and the proclaimed king make this the controlling prophetic background. High volume and coherence with Luke's kingship theme.

echoes.text: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. To him will the obedience of the peoples be. Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Jacob's blessing on Judah foretells the ruler whose scepter does not depart, binding his colt to the vine, an early messianic colt image. The royal colt of the coming ruler coheres with Luke's enthronement entry and the kingly acclamation. Medium because the contact runs through the colt image rather than direct citation.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The crowd cries 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord,' quoting the pilgrim blessing of Psalm 118:26 with the added royal title 'the King.' This is a direct verbal citation embedded in the Hallel context of festal approach to the temple. High volume; the quotation is explicit and load-bearing.

echoes.text: The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.
echoes.note: Setting the king-to-be on a mount for a processional enthronement recalls Solomon riding David's mule to Gihon to be proclaimed king. The royal mounting and acclamation parallel the Davidic succession ritual, supporting Luke's kingship framing. Medium confidence; the mount differs (colt vs. mule) but the enthronement pattern is strong.

echoes.text: Then they hurried, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs, and blew the trumpet, saying, “Jehu is king.”
echoes.note: Spreading garments before the rider evokes the acclamation of Jehu, where the people put their cloaks under him on the steps and proclaimed 'Jehu is king.' The garment-strewing as royal enthronement gesture closely parallels the crowd's act here. Medium volume; the cloak ritual is a recognizable kingship sign.

echoes.text: Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh from the heavens! Praise him in the heights!
echoes.note: The acclamation 'Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest' echoes the heavenly-praise summons of the Psalms to praise the Lord 'in the heights.' The vertical glory-in-the-highest language coheres with the angelic Gloria pattern Luke reprises. Low because it is diffuse liturgical idiom.

echoes.text: For the stone will cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the woodwork will answer it.
echoes.note: Jesus's claim that 'the stones would cry out' if the disciples were silent draws on Habakkuk's woe, where the stone cries out from the wall and the beam answers against injustice. The personified crying stone witnessing truth coheres with the inevitability of acclaiming the coming king. High volume; the crying-stone image is rare and distinctive.

echoes.text: Sing, daughter of Zion! Shout, Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. Yahweh has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, Yahweh, is in your midst. You will not be afraid of evil any more.
echoes.note: The summons to Zion to rejoice because 'the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst' resonates with the rejoicing multitude hailing the coming king at the descent to Jerusalem. The Daughter-of-Zion joy at the king's arrival coheres with Luke's scene. Low confidence; Zechariah 9 is the dominant source.

pericopes.text: When he drew near, he saw the city and wept over it, saying, “If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace! But now, they are hidden from your eyes. For the days will come on you, when your enemies will throw up a barricade against you, surround you, hem you in on every side, and will dash you and your children within you to the ground. They will not leave in you one stone on another, because you didn’t know the time of your visitation.”

echoes.text: Woe to Ariel! Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts come around; then I will distress Ariel, and there will be mourning and lamentation. She shall be to me as an altar hearth. I will encamp against you all around you, and will lay siege against you with posted troops. I will raise siege works against you. You will be brought down, and will speak out of the ground. Your speech will mumble out of the dust. Your voice will be […]
echoes.note: The siege oracle against Ariel (Jerusalem), where the Lord encamps against her, raises siege-works, and brings her low so she speaks from the ground, supplies the language of barricade, encirclement, and being dashed to the ground. Luke's weeping prophecy closely tracks this Ariel oracle's imagery of the humbled city. High volume and coherence with the lament form.

echoes.text: For Yahweh of Armies said, “Cut down trees, and cast up a mound against Jerusalem: this is the city to be visited; she is wholly oppression in the midst of her. As a well produces its waters, so she produces her wickedness: violence and destruction is heard in her; before me continually is sickness and wounds. Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest my soul be alienated from you; lest I make you a desolation, a land not inhabited.” Thus says Yahweh of Armies, […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah commands to 'cast up a mound against Jerusalem' for the siege and indicts the people who 'did not know' and were not ashamed at the time of visitation. Luke's barricade, encirclement, and the charge 'you did not know the time of your visitation' draw directly on this oracle's siege-and-visitation structure. High volume; the visitation language is verbally close.

echoes.text: What will you do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation which will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'what will you do in the day of visitation' undergirds Jesus's reproach that Jerusalem 'did not know the time of your visitation.' The day-of-visitation as a moment of accountability and judgment coheres with Luke's siege lament. Medium; Jeremiah 6 carries the parallel verbal weight.

echoes.text: Happy shall he be, who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock.
echoes.note: The prophecy that enemies 'will dash you and your children within you to the ground' echoes the imprecatory Psalm's image of dashing children against the rock. The dash-children-to-the-ground violence of urban conquest supplies the horror Luke evokes for Jerusalem's fall. Medium; the verb dashing applied to children is distinctive.

echoes.text: You also, son of man, take a tile, and lay it before yourself, and portray on it a city, even Jerusalem: and lay siege against it, and build forts against it, and cast up a mound against it; set camps also against it, and plant battering rams against it all around. Take for yourself an iron pan, and set it for a wall of iron between you and the city: and set your face toward it, and it shall be besieged, and you shall lay siege against it. This shall be a […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's sign-act lays siege to a depicted Jerusalem, building siege-works and an iron wall against the city. Luke's 'your enemies will throw up a barricade against you' draws on this prophetic siege-enactment imagery. Medium volume; the barricade/siege-wall is the shared element.

echoes.text: Hazael said, “Why do you weep, my lord?” He answered, “Because I know the evil that you will do to the children of Israel. You will set their strongholds on fire, and you will kill their young men with the sword, and will dash in pieces their little ones, and rip up their women with child.”
echoes.note: Elisha's tearful prophecy of the coming atrocities, the slain young men and the dashed little ones, parallels Jesus's weeping over the city's foreseen destruction. The weeping prophet foreseeing the slaughter of children coheres with Luke's lament tone. Low; the contact is thematic.

echoes.text: Samaria will bear her guilt; for she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.”
echoes.note: Hosea's judgment that Samaria's infants will be dashed in pieces and her pregnant women ripped open supplies another prophetic image of children destroyed in conquest behind 'dash you and your children to the ground.' The atrocity-on-children topos coheres but Hosea concerns Samaria. Low and contested.

echoes.text: Yet was she carried away. She went into captivity. Her young children also were dashed in pieces at the head of all the streets, and they cast lots for her honorable men, and all her great men were bound in chains.
echoes.note: Nahum's depiction of conquered Thebes, whose little ones 'were dashed in pieces at the head of every street,' is another stock siege-atrocity image standing behind Luke's children-dashed-to-the-ground. The shared conquest-of-a-city horror coheres faintly. Low confidence.

echoes.text: Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I visit them, they shall be cast down,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Jeremiah declares that at 'the time of their visitation they shall be cast down,' the very phrase Luke turns into the reproach that Jerusalem failed to know its time of visitation. The visitation-as-judgment idiom is a direct conceptual borrowing. Medium, overlapping with the broader Jeremiah 6 siege oracle.

echoes.text: They will besiege you in all your gates, until your high and fortified walls come down, in which you trusted, throughout all your land. They will besiege you in all your gates throughout all your land, which Yahweh your God has given you. You will eat the fruit of your own body, the flesh of your sons and of your daughters, whom Yahweh your God has given you, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemies will distress you. The man who is tender […]
echoes.note: The covenant curse foretells the enemy besieging your towns until the high walls fall, with horrors befalling children during the siege. Luke's siege, encirclement, and destruction of the city read as the realization of the Deuteronomic covenant curse for disobedience. Medium; the curse-fulfillment frame coheres strongly with Luke's theology.

echoes.text: Your country is desolate. Your cities are burned with fire. Strangers devour your land in your presence, and it is desolate, as overthrown by strangers. The daughter of Zion is left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a field of melons, like a besieged city.
echoes.note: Isaiah's vision of the land laid waste, cities burned, and Daughter Zion left desolate provides a background for Jerusalem's coming devastation. The desolation-of-Zion motif coheres with Luke's lament but is diffuse. Low confidence.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: God's warning that he will cast out Israel and make the temple a heap if they forsake him, leaving passersby astonished, anticipates the destruction Jesus foresees. The conditional ruin-of-house-and-city coheres with the visitation-judgment theme. Low and contested.

pericopes.text: He entered into the temple, and began to drive out those who bought and sold in it, saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house is a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a ‘den of robbers’!” He was teaching daily in the temple, but the chief priests and the scribes and the leading men among the people sought to destroy him. They couldn’t find what they might do, for all the people hung on to every word that he said.

echoes.text: even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
echoes.note: Jesus quotes 'My house shall be a house of prayer' from Isaiah's oracle promising that foreigners' offerings will be accepted in a house of prayer for all peoples. The citation grounds the temple's intended purpose against its corruption. High volume; an explicit, marked quotation introduced by 'it is written.'

echoes.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Jesus brands the temple traffickers as making it 'a den of robbers,' quoting Jeremiah's temple sermon that asks whether the Lord's house has become a den of robbers in the people's eyes. The citation imports Jeremiah's threat of the temple's destruction for covenant infidelity. High volume; explicit quotation fused with Isaiah 56:7.

echoes.text: Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to Yahweh of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Zechariah's eschatological vision ends with 'there shall be no more a trader (Canaanite) in the house of the Lord,' coheres with Jesus expelling the buyers and sellers from the temple. The purified end-time temple free of commerce supports the cleansing act. Low confidence; the prophetic-cleansing background is suggestive but uncited.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and […]
echoes.note: Malachi foretells the Lord suddenly coming to his temple to purify the sons of Levi and the offerings, an oracle of temple purgation that coheres with Jesus's cleansing entry. The Lord-comes-to-purify-the-temple pattern undergirds the scene though no words are quoted. Low confidence.

echoes.text: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
echoes.note: The zeal for God's house that consumes the psalmist faintly informs Jesus's forceful purging of the temple, a connection John makes explicit. In Luke the link is at most an echo of the zealous-for-the-house motif. Low confidence and contested.

pericopes.text: On one of those days, as he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the Good News, the priests and scribes came to him with the elders. They asked him, “Tell us: by what authority do you do these things? Or who is giving you this authority?” He answered them, “I also will ask you one question. Tell me: the baptism of John, was it from heaven, or from men?” They reasoned with themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why didn’t you believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us, for they are persuaded that John was a prophet.” They answered that they didn’t know where it was from. Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: The challenge 'by what authority?' / 'who made you ruler?' echoes the perennial Israelite question put to a divinely commissioned but unrecognized agent (Moses rebuffed: 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?'). Coherent with Luke's Moses-typology of Jesus but volume is faint and the wording is not distinctive.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: The crowd's conviction that 'John was a prophet' whom it would be deadly to dishonor draws on the deuteronomistic theme that God repeatedly sent prophets whom the people rejected, setting up the tenants parable that follows. Volume is moderate; recurrence is strong across the OT prophet-rejection tradition, and it coheres tightly with 20:9-16.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]
echoes.note: The framing of John's baptism as 'from heaven' and the people's reckoning of John as a true prophet trades on the Deuteronomic test of the authentic prophet sent by God. Availability and coherence are good, but the link to John specifically is inferential and contested.

pericopes.text: He began to tell the people this parable. “A man planted a vineyard, and rented it out to some farmers, and went into another country for a long time. At the proper season, he sent a servant to the farmers to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. But the farmers beat him, and sent him away empty. He sent yet another servant, and they also beat him, and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty. He sent yet a third, and they also wounded him, and threw him out. The lord of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. It may be that seeing him, they will respect him.’ “But when the farmers saw him, they reasoned among themselves, saying, ‘This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him, that the inheritance may be ours.’ They threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. What therefore will the lord of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy these farmers, and will give the vineyard to others.” When they heard it, they said, “May it never be!”

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The parable is structurally built on the Song of the Vineyard: a man plants a vineyard, expects its fruit, is disappointed, and the owner finally acts in judgment. Volume is high (the LXX of Isaiah 5:2 supplies 'planted a vineyard' and the verb for letting/hedging), recurrence pervades the vineyard-Israel tradition, and coherence with Luke's polemic against the leaders is total.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The transplanted vine that God planted and then exposes to ravagers reinforces the vineyard-as-Israel image and the motif of the owner withdrawing protection. Moderate volume; strongly coherent and recurrent with Isaiah 5, though it is the secondary vineyard text behind the parable.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'I will send my beloved son' (ton huion mou ton agapeton) verbally echoes the LXX of the Aqedah, where Isaac is the 'beloved son' whom the father gives up. Volume rests on the distinctive phrase agapetos huios, shared with Luke's baptism/transfiguration; coherent with Luke's Son Christology, though some read it merely as 'only/dear son.'

echoes.text: They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. They said one to another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”
echoes.note: The tenants' deliberation 'Come, let us kill him' over the heir verbally mirrors the brothers' plot against Joseph ('Come now, let us kill him... and we shall see what becomes of his dreams'). The shared conspiratorial formula is suggestive but the wording is conventional and the connection is contested.

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house. Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his […]
echoes.note: The escalating beating and killing of successive servants (prophets) sent to the vineyard reflects the murder of Zechariah son of Jehoiada and the broader chronicle of slain prophets, the canonical endpoint of prophet-rejection in the Hebrew Bible. Coherent and recurrent with the deuteronomistic theme, supplying the parable's 'servants.'

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: God's persistently sending his servants the prophets 'rising up early,' only to have them met with stiff-necked refusal, underlies the parable's repeated dispatch and abuse of servants. Recurrence is high across Jeremiah's 'servants the prophets' formula; moderate volume and strong coherence.

pericopes.text: But he looked at them, and said, “Then what is this that is written, ‘The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the chief cornerstone?’ Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, but it will crush whomever it falls on to dust.”

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This is Yahweh’s doing. It is marvelous in our eyes.
echoes.note: Explicit 'what is this that is written' citation: 'The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone.' Verbatim LXX quotation (Ps 117:22), highest volume, and a recurrent early-Christian testimonium, perfectly coherent with the rejected-then-vindicated Son of the parable.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: 'Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken' draws on Isaiah's 'stone of stumbling and rock of offense' on which many shall fall and be broken. Volume is high (shared falling/breaking imagery), it recurs in the NT stone-catena, and it coheres with the judgment turn of v.18.

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: 'It will crush whomever it falls on to dust' echoes the stone cut without hands that strikes the image and grinds it to chaff/dust, scattered like summer threshing. Distinctive crushing-to-powder imagery (Dan 2:44-45 adds the kingdom that shall never be destroyed) gives high volume and strong eschatological coherence.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The tested cornerstone God lays in Zion belongs to the same stone-testimonia cluster and may inform 'cornerstone' here, reinforcing Psalm 118. Recurrence in the NT stone-catena is strong, but for Luke the Psalm 118 citation carries the load, so the Isaiah 28 contribution is secondary.

pericopes.text: The chief priests and the scribes sought to lay hands on him that very hour, but they feared the people—for they knew he had spoken this parable against them. They watched him, and sent out spies, who pretended to be righteous, that they might trap him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the power and authority of the governor. They asked him, “Teacher, we know that you say and teach what is right, and aren’t partial to anyone, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, “Why do you test me? Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” They answered, “Caesar’s.” He said to them, “Then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” They weren’t able to trap him in his words before the people. They marveled at his answer, and were silent.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: 'Whose image (eikon) and inscription?' / 'give to God the things that are God's' plays on the human person as bearer of the divine image: the coin bears Caesar's image, but the human bears God's, owed wholly to God. The eikon wordplay gives moderate volume and the saying coheres with a creation-theology reading widely recognized in interpretation.

echoes.text: Render a recompense to the Gentiles, and take heed to the commandments of the law.
echoes.note: Mattathias's charge to 'pay back the Gentiles what they deserve' and the Maccabean refusal to render to pagan kings what belongs to the law of God forms a Second-Temple backdrop to the tribute question's loaded politics. Availability and coherence are plausible but verbal volume is faint and the link is contested.

echoes.text: My son, fear Yahweh and the king. Don’t join those who are rebellious:
echoes.note: 'Fear the LORD and the king' supplies a wisdom precedent for distinguishing yet ordering obligations to God and to civil authority, coherent with 'give to Caesar... and to God.' Volume is low and the connection is inferential, hence contested.

pericopes.text: Some of the Sadducees came to him, those who deny that there is a resurrection. They asked him, “Teacher, Moses wrote to us that if a man’s brother dies having a wife, and he is childless, his brother should take the wife, and raise up children for his brother. There were therefore seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died childless. The second took her as wife, and he died childless. The third took her, and likewise the seven all left no children, and died. Afterward the woman also died. Therefore in the resurrection whose wife of them will she be? For the seven had her as a wife.” Jesus said to them, “The children of this age marry, and are given in marriage. But those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry, nor are given in marriage. For they can’t die any more, for they are like the angels, and are children of God, being children of the resurrection. But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed at the bush, when he called the Lord ‘The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ Now he is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for all are alive to him.” Some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you speak well.” They didn’t dare to ask him any more questions.

echoes.text: If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies, and has no son, the wife of the dead shall not be married outside to a stranger. Her husband’s brother shall go in to her, and take her as his wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her. It shall be that the firstborn whom she bears shall succeed in the name of his brother who is dead, that his name not be blotted out of Israel.
echoes.note: The Sadducees cite 'Moses wrote to us' the levirate law: if a man dies childless his brother must take the wife and raise up offspring for the brother. This is a near-verbatim paraphrase of the Deuteronomic statute, high volume, and load-bearing for the whole dispute.

echoes.text: Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her, and raise up seed to your brother.”
echoes.note: Judah's command to Onan to 'raise up offspring for your brother' is the narrative enactment of levirate duty and the closest verbal parallel to 'raise up children for his brother.' Moderate volume, coherent with the Deuteronomy citation as the precedent case the Sadducees invoke.

echoes.text: Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.
echoes.note: Jesus' clinching proof: 'Moses showed at the bush, when he called the Lord the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' Verbatim LXX quotation with the bush setting named, highest volume, the keystone of the resurrection argument ('not of the dead but of the living').

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'Children of the resurrection... like the angels' draws on Daniel's resurrection hope, where the wise shine like the stars and the dead awake to everlasting life, a key Second-Temple text affirming bodily resurrection over against the Sadducees. Coherent and recurrent in resurrection discourse; moderate volume.

echoes.text: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations. Go, and gather the elders of Israel together, and tell them, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying, “I have surely visited you, and […]
echoes.note: The patriarchal naming 'the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' as the LORD's everlasting name extends just beyond 3:6 into the surrounding self-revelation, reinforcing the living-God argument. Largely the same citation, so listed as a faint extension rather than a separate echo.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The hope that the righteous will become 'companions of the host of heaven' / shine and be made like the angels parallels 'they are like the angels, children of the resurrection.' A pseudepigraphal analogue warranted by the angelomorphic-resurrection motif, but volume is faint and the dependence is contested.

echoes.text: they who believe that to God they die not; for, as our forefathers, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, they live to God.
echoes.note: 'They live to God, as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live' anticipates Jesus' very logic that the patriarchs are alive to God, joined to the Exodus 3:6 naming. A strikingly coherent Second-Temple parallel (also 4 Macc 16:25), though as a likely independent reading of the same text it is marked low/contested.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “Why do they say that the Christ is David’s son? David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.”’ “David therefore calls him Lord, so how is he his son?”

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: Explicit citation 'David himself says in the book of Psalms, The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' Verbatim LXX quotation (Ps 109:1), highest volume, the single most-cited royal psalm in the NT, fully coherent with the Davidic-Lord puzzle.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: The premise that 'the Christ is David's son' rests on the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting offspring/son for David's throne, which Jesus' question both presupposes and transcends. Coherent and recurrent in messianic expectation; moderate volume as the unstated scriptural basis of 'David's son.'

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.
echoes.note: 'The LORD swore to David... one of your own offspring I will set on your throne' is a further scriptural warrant for the 'son of David' messianism the riddle interrogates. Low volume, secondary to 2 Samuel 7, and inferential.

pericopes.text: In the hearing of all the people, he said to his disciples, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces, the best seats in the synagogues, and the best places at feasts; who devour widows’ houses, and for a pretense make long prayers: these will receive greater condemnation.”

echoes.text: “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
echoes.note: Condemnation of those who 'devour widows' houses' invokes the covenant prohibition against afflicting widows, with God's threat to answer their cry in wrath, grounding the 'greater condemnation.' Recurrence of widow-protection law is strong; moderate volume and tight coherence with Luke's concern for the vulnerable.

echoes.text: Woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees; to deprive the needy from justice, and to rob the poor among my people of their rights, that widows may be their plunder, and that they may make the fatherless their prey!
echoes.note: The prophetic woe against those who frame unjust decrees to rob the widow of her right and make the poor their prey parallels scribes who 'devour widows' houses' under a pretense of piety. Coherent with the long-robed religious oppressors here; moderate volume from the shared widow-spoliation indictment.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh concerning the prophets who lead my people astray; for those who feed their teeth, they proclaim, “Peace!” and whoever doesn’t provide for their mouths, they prepare war against him:
echoes.note: Micah's denunciation of greedy religious leaders who 'cry Peace' while devouring the people supports the picture of pretense-pious exploiters facing judgment. Low volume; one node in the broad prophetic-injustice tradition behind v.47, hence contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: You shall not deprive the foreigner or the fatherless of justice, nor take a widow’s clothing in pledge;
echoes.note: The law forbidding the perversion of justice due the widow and the taking of her garment in pledge stands behind the 'widows' houses' charge. Faint volume on its own, listed as part of the Torah widow-protection backdrop alongside Exodus 22:22.

pericopes.text: He looked up, and saw the rich people who were putting their gifts into the treasury. He saw a certain poor widow casting in two small brass coins. He said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow put in more than all of them, for all these put in gifts for God from their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, put in all that she had to live on.”

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: The widow of Zarephath gives Elijah her last handful of meal and oil, surrendering all she had to live on, and is then sustained. Luke's poor widow likewise gives 'all she had to live on' (bios), and Luke elsewhere pairs Zarephath's widow with the temple critique (4:25-26). The shared figure of the destitute widow whose total self-gift outweighs the abundance of others gives this real coherence, though there is no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one comes into Yahweh’s house: and the priests who kept the threshold put therein all the money that was brought into Yahweh’s house. It was so, when they saw that there was much money in the chest, that the king’s scribe and the high priest came up, and they put up in bags and counted the money that was found in Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: Jehoiada bores a hole in a chest set beside the altar so the people cast (Greek LXX: emballein) their money into it as the temple treasury. Luke uses the same image of people 'casting in' (ballontas/eballen) their gifts into the temple treasury (gazophylakion), the institution Second-Temple readers would recognize. Availability and the shared treasury vocabulary support a faint echo of the temple-offering institution.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them, ‘When a man consecrates a person to Yahweh in a vow, according to your valuation, your valuation of a male from twenty years old even to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver, after the shekel of the sanctuary. If she is a female, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels. If the person is from five years old even to twenty years old, then your valuation shall […]
echoes.note: The Levitical vow-valuation code scales required offerings to a person's ability, anticipating the principle that the poor are assessed according to their means. Jesus' verdict that the widow gave 'more' precisely because she gave from poverty rather than abundance inverts and fulfills this proportional logic. The connection is thematic and contested rather than verbal.

echoes.text: When you reap your harvest in your field, and have forgotten a sheaf in the field, you shall not go again to get it. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow; that Yahweh your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. When you beat your olive tree, you shall not go over the boughs again. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow. When you harvest your vineyard, you shall not glean it after […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy repeatedly singles out the widow alongside the orphan and sojourner as the paradigm of the vulnerable whom God watches over. The widow's appearance as the moral exemplar against the rich foregrounds this Torah category. Faint, atmospheric availability rather than a specific citation.

pericopes.text: As some were talking about the temple and how it was decorated with beautiful stones and gifts, he said, “As for these things which you see, the days will come, in which there will not be left here one stone on another that will not be thrown down.”

echoes.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: Micah prophesies that Zion will be plowed as a field and Jerusalem become heaps, the temple mount a wooded height, the classic oracle of the temple's destruction quoted at Jeremiah 26:18. Jesus' prediction that not one stone will be left on another draws directly on this prophetic tradition of the sanctuary leveled for the people's injustice. High coherence with Luke's broader judgment-on-Jerusalem theme.

echoes.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.
echoes.note: Jeremiah threatens to make the temple like Shiloh and the city a curse, citing Micah's Zion-plowed oracle in a temple sermon that nearly costs him his life. Luke frames Jesus' temple-destruction saying in the same setting (teaching in the temple, opposed by leaders), echoing the prophet who foretold the first temple's fall. Strong recurrence of the temple-doom motif.

echoes.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh. “But go now to my place which was in Shiloh, where I caused my name to dwell at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel. Now, because you have done all these works,” says Yahweh, “and I spoke to you, rising up early and speaking, but you didn’t hear; and I called you, but you didn’t answer: […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon warns that God will do to this house, called by his name, as he did to Shiloh, because the people made it a den of robbers. Luke has just narrated Jesus quoting Jer 7:11 in the temple cleansing (19:46), so the threatened destruction of the desecrated house carries forward here. Coherence and recurrence within Luke's temple sequence.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The Lord warns Solomon that if Israel turns away he will cast off the house he has hallowed and it will become a heap of ruins, an astonishment, with passersby hissing. The admiration of the temple's beautiful stones immediately before the announcement of its fall mirrors this conditional doom on the very house just dedicated. Thematic coherence with the temple-destruction prophecies.

echoes.text: ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,’ says Yahweh of Armies; ‘and in this place will I give peace,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”
echoes.note: Haggai promises the latter glory of this house, adorned with the wealth of nations, will exceed the former. The disciples' marveling at the temple's beautiful stones and votive gifts evokes that anticipated splendor, which Jesus then declares doomed. Faint ironic counterpoint rather than citation.

pericopes.text: They asked him, “Teacher, so when will these things be? What is the sign that these things are about to happen?” He said, “Watch out that you don’t get led astray, for many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and, ‘The time is at hand.’ Therefore don’t follow them. When you hear of wars and disturbances, don’t be terrified, for these things must happen first, but the end won’t come immediately.” Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes, famines, and plagues in various places. There will be terrors and great signs from heaven.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.
echoes.note: Daniel speaks of what 'must happen' (dei genesthai) in the latter days, language Jesus reuses verbatim in 'these things must happen first.' Daniel's apocalyptic framework of divinely-decreed end-time events shapes the whole discourse's logic of necessity. Strong verbal coherence with Danielic apocalyptic.

echoes.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
echoes.note: Azariah's oracle: 'nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every distress.' Jesus' 'nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' is the closest verbal parallel in the OT, framing political chaos as divine eschatological distress. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.
echoes.note: Isaiah's oracle against Egypt: 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, everyone against his brother and against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom.' The kingdom-against-kingdom formula and the picture of internecine collapse map directly onto Jesus' words. Strong verbal recurrence.

echoes.text: Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place in the wrath of Yahweh of Armies, and in the day of his fierce anger.
echoes.note: In the Day-of-the-Lord oracle against Babylon, the heavens tremble and the earth is shaken out of its place in God's wrath. Jesus' great earthquakes and 'terrors and great signs from heaven' draw on this Day-of-the-Lord seismic and celestial imagery. Coherence with the prophetic eschatological catalog.

echoes.text: For in my jealousy and in the fire of my wrath have I spoken, Surely in that day there shall be a great shaking in the land of Israel; so that the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the animals of the field, and all creeping things who creep on the earth, and all the men who are on the surface of the earth, shall shake at my presence, and the mountains shall be thrown down, and the steep places shall fall, and every wall shall fall to the […]
echoes.note: In the Gog oracle a great earthquake shakes the land, with pestilence, bloodshed, famine, and signs of God's judgment. The clustering of earthquake, plague, and famine as eschatological signs parallels Jesus' list closely. Recurrence of the standard Day-of-the-Lord disaster catalog.

echoes.text: When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and meal offering, I will not accept them; but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence.
echoes.note: Jeremiah names sword, famine, and pestilence (plague) as the triad by which God consumes the people, a formula repeated dozens of times in the prophet. Jesus' famines and plagues echo this fixed prophetic triad of covenant curse. Strong recurrence across Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

echoes.text: But news out of the east and out of the north shall trouble him; and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and utterly to sweep away many.
echoes.note: Rumors and reports of war from east and north alarm the eschatological king and provoke great fury. Jesus' 'when you hear of wars and disturbances, don't be terrified' echoes the apocalyptic motif of unsettling war-reports that must not panic the faithful. Faint Danielic coloring.

echoes.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Joel promises wonders in heaven and on earth as portents of the Day of the Lord. Jesus' 'great signs from heaven' belongs to this Joel tradition of celestial portents, developed more fully later in the discourse. Coherence with Joel's sign vocabulary.

pericopes.text: But before all these things, they will lay their hands on you and will persecute you, delivering you up to synagogues and prisons, bringing you before kings and governors for my name’s sake. It will turn out as a testimony for you. Settle it therefore in your hearts not to meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to withstand or to contradict. You will be handed over even by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends. They will cause some of you to be put to death. You will be hated by all men for my name’s sake. And not a hair of your head will perish. “By your endurance you will win your lives.

echoes.text: They will fight against you; but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you”, says Yahweh, “to deliver you.”
echoes.note: God assures the prophet that kings and officials will fight against him but 'shall not prevail against you, for I am with you to deliver you.' Jesus' promise that adversaries 'will not be able to withstand or to contradict' the wisdom he gives mirrors this prophetic commissioning against hostile authorities. High coherence with the persecuted-prophet pattern.

echoes.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
echoes.note: God tells Moses, 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.' Jesus' 'I will give you a mouth and wisdom' directly evokes this divine endowment of speech to a reluctant spokesman before a hostile king. Strong verbal and situational coherence.

echoes.text: You shall speak to him, and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth, and with his mouth, and will teach you what you shall do. He will be your spokesman to the people; and it will happen, that he will be to you a mouth, and you will be to him as God.
echoes.note: The Lord promises to be with the mouth of both Moses and Aaron and to teach them what to do, the divine-rhetoric motif extended. The doubling of mouth-and-teaching reinforces the Exodus background of God supplying words to those summoned before rulers. Recurrence strengthens the Mosaic echo.

echoes.text: Then answered they and said before the king, That Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah, doesn’t respect you, O king, nor the decree that you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day. Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored until the going down of the sun to rescue him. Then these men assembled together to the king, and said to the king, Know, […]
echoes.note: Daniel is brought before the king and delivered up on account of his fidelity, a model of the faithful Jew arraigned before pagan authority who is nonetheless preserved. Jesus' 'bringing you before kings and governors for my name's sake' as occasion for testimony evokes the Danielic court-confessor tradition. Coherence with Daniel's witness motif.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: The little horn wears out the saints of the Most High, who are given into his hand for a time. Jesus' forecast of persecution, betrayal, and death of his followers fits the Danielic pattern of the saints handed over before final vindication. Recurrence within the apocalyptic source of the discourse.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: Micah laments that son dishonors father, daughter rises against mother, and a man's enemies are those of his own household. Jesus' 'you will be handed over even by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends' draws on this prophetic image of eschatological family betrayal. Strong coherence and recurrence in Synoptic tradition.

echoes.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
echoes.note: The people swear that not one hair of Jonathan's head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day, sparing his life. Jesus' 'not a hair of your head will perish' is a near-verbatim proverbial assurance of divine preservation. High volume on the distinctive idiom.

echoes.text: Then she said, “Please let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood destroy not any more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth.”
echoes.note: The wise woman of Tekoa secures David's oath that 'not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground,' the same idiom of total protection. The recurrence of the hair-of-the-head formula across Samuel reinforces its proverbial status behind Jesus' saying. Coherence with the OT preservation idiom.

echoes.text: Solomon said, “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of him shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness be found in him, he shall die.”
echoes.note: Solomon declares that if Adonijah proves worthy, 'not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth.' A third occurrence of the hair-preservation formula, confirming it as a fixed Hebrew idiom Jesus deploys. Faint but corroborating recurrence.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.
echoes.note: Daniel is told, 'blessed is he who waits' and to stand in his lot at the end of days, framing endurance as the path to eschatological reward. Jesus' 'by your endurance you will win your lives' resonates with this Danielic call to persevere to the resurrection-end. Thematic coherence with apocalyptic endurance.

pericopes.text: “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is at hand. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let those who are in the midst of her depart. Let those who are in the country not enter therein. For these are days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled. Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in those days! For there will be great distress in the land, and wrath to this people. They will fall by the edge of the sword, and will be led captive into all the nations. Jerusalem will be trampled down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

echoes.text: After the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One shall be cut off, and shall have nothing: and the people of the prince who shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and its end shall be with a flood, and even to the end shall be war; desolations are determined. He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who […]
echoes.note: Daniel foretells that after the anointed one is cut off, the people of a coming prince destroy the city and sanctuary, with war and decreed desolations to the end. Jesus' Jerusalem surrounded by armies whose 'desolation is at hand' draws directly on Daniel's desolation-of-the-city oracle, the discourse's structural key. High coherence with the Danielic eremosis.

echoes.text: Then I heard a holy one speaking; and another holy one said to that certain one who spoke, How long shall be the vision about the continual burnt offering, and the disobedience that makes desolate, to give both the sanctuary and the army to be trodden under foot?
echoes.note: Daniel asks how long the vision of the transgression that makes desolate, the sanctuary and host trampled underfoot, will last. Jesus' 'desolation' plus 'Jerusalem trampled by the Gentiles until... fulfilled' fuses this trampling-of-the-sanctuary imagery with a temporal limit. Strong conceptual overlap of trampling and desolation.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all the peoples. All who burden themselves with it will be severely wounded, and all the nations of the earth will be gathered together against it.
echoes.note: Zechariah pictures all the nations of the earth gathered against Jerusalem, the city made a burdensome stone. Jesus' image of Jerusalem encircled by Gentile armies belongs to this Zion-besieged-by-the-nations tradition. Coherence with the eschatological siege motif, though Zechariah's outcome differs.

echoes.text: For I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to battle; and the city will be taken, the houses rifled, and the women ravished. Half of the city will go out into captivity, and the rest of the people will not be cut off from the city.
echoes.note: The Lord gathers all nations against Jerusalem; the city is taken, houses plundered, and half go into captivity. Jesus' falling by the sword and being led captive into all nations closely tracks Zechariah's siege-and-exile sequence. Strong recurrence of the captivity-of-Jerusalem theme.

echoes.text: Your holy people possessed it but a little while: our adversaries have trodden down your sanctuary.
echoes.note: Israel laments that adversaries have trodden down the sanctuary. Jesus' 'Jerusalem will be trampled down by the Gentiles' echoes this lament over the Gentile trampling of the holy place. Coherence with the trodden-sanctuary lament tradition.

echoes.text: Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.”
echoes.note: In the Song of Moses, 'vengeance is mine, and recompense,' the day of calamity that comes upon the faithless. Jesus' 'these are days of vengeance' invokes this Mosaic-covenant lawsuit and its appointed day of retribution. High coherence with the covenant-curse framework.

echoes.text: The days of visitation have come. The days of reckoning have come. Israel will consider the prophet to be a fool, and the man who is inspired to be insane, because of the abundance of your sins, and because your hostility is great.
echoes.note: Hosea announces, 'the days of punishment (vengeance) have come, the days of recompense have come; Israel shall know it,' against a faithless people. Jesus' phrase 'days of vengeance' is the closest verbal echo, applied likewise to Israel's judgment. Strong volume on the distinctive plural idiom.

echoes.text: Yahweh will bring a nation against you from far, from the end of the earth, as the eagle flies; a nation whose language you will not understand; a nation of fierce facial expressions, that doesn’t respect the elderly, nor show favor to the young, and they will eat the fruit of your livestock, and the fruit of your ground, until you are destroyed. They also won’t leave you grain, new wine, or oil, the increase of your livestock, or the young of your flock, […]
echoes.note: The covenant curses describe a distant nation swooping like an eagle, besieging the cities, with horrors falling especially on the nursing mother and the tender woman. Jesus' woe to pregnant and nursing women, great distress, sword, and captivity dramatizes these Deuteronomic siege-curses. High coherence and recurrence with the covenant-curse catalog.

echoes.text: Samaria will bear her guilt; for she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.”
echoes.note: Samaria's guilt brings the sword, infants dashed in pieces and pregnant women ripped open. Jesus' woe to the pregnant and nursing in the day of wrath echoes this prophetic horror of judgment falling on mothers and children. Coherence with the siege-atrocity motif.

echoes.text: Afterward, says Yahweh, I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, and his servants, and the people, even such as are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword, and from the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life: and he shall strike them with the edge of the sword; he shall not spare them, neither have pity, nor have mercy.
echoes.note: Jeremiah foretells Zedekiah and the people falling by the edge of the sword, with no pity, given into the hand of the enemy. Jesus' 'they will fall by the edge of the sword' reproduces the prophet's stock formula for Jerusalem's military doom. Recurrence of the sword-and-captivity language.

echoes.text: “but I will scatter them with a whirlwind among all the nations which they have not known. Thus the land was desolate after them, so that no man passed through nor returned: for they made the pleasant land desolate.”
echoes.note: God scatters the disobedient among all the nations, leaving the pleasant land desolate. Jesus' being 'led captive into all the nations' with a desolate Jerusalem echoes this dispersal-and-desolation outcome. Faint coherence with the exile motif.

echoes.text: Go into Media, my child, for I surely believe all the things which Jonah the prophet spoke of Nineveh, that it will be overthrown, but in Media there will rather be peace for a season. Our kindred will be scattered in the earth from the good land. Jerusalem will be desolate, and the house of God in it will be burned up, and will be desolate for a time. God will again have mercy on them, and bring them back into the land, and they will build the house, but […]
echoes.note: Tobit foresees Jerusalem and the temple laid desolate for a time until the times are fulfilled, after which the exiles return and the house is rebuilt. Jesus' 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' shares the structure of a measured desolation with an appointed terminus. Second-Temple availability supports a faint conceptual echo.

echoes.text: Now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will take away its hedge, and it will be eaten up. I will break down its wall of it, and it will be trampled down.
echoes.note: In the vineyard song the Lord breaks down the hedge so the vineyard is trampled down. The trampling-down of God's chosen plot resonates with Jerusalem 'trampled by the Gentiles' as the consequence of covenant unfaithfulness. Thematic and faint.

pericopes.text: There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars; and on the earth anxiety of nations, in perplexity for the roaring of the sea and the waves; men fainting for fear, and for expectation of the things which are coming on the world: for the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. But when these things begin to happen, look up, and lift up your heads, because your redemption is near.”

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Daniel sees 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds of heaven, given dominion, glory, and a kingdom. Jesus' 'they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory' is the climactic appropriation of this throne-vision, the most important OT reference in the discourse. Highest volume, recurrence, and coherence.

echoes.text: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.
echoes.note: In the Day-of-the-Lord oracle the stars, constellations, sun, and moon withhold their light. Jesus' 'signs in the sun, moon, and stars' draws directly on this prophetic darkening of the heavenly bodies. High coherence with the standard cosmic-collapse catalog.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: The host of heaven rots away, the heavens roll up like a scroll, and all their host falls. Jesus' 'powers of the heavens will be shaken' echoes this dissolution of the celestial host on the day of judgment. Strong recurrence within the Day-of-the-Lord tradition.

echoes.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
echoes.note: Joel's day of the Lord: the earth quakes, the heavens tremble, sun and moon darken, the stars withdraw their shining. Jesus' combination of cosmic signs and shaken heavenly powers maps closely onto Joel's portrait. High coherence and recurrence.

echoes.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Wonders in the heavens and on earth, the sun turned to darkness and moon to blood before the great and terrible Day. Jesus' celestial signs as harbingers of the coming day belong to this Joel sign-tradition, cited at Acts 2:19-20. Coherence reinforced by Lukan usage.

echoes.text: Ah, the uproar of many peoples, who roar like the roaring of the seas; and the rushing of nations, that rush like the rushing of mighty waters! The nations will rush like the rushing of many waters: but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far off, and will be chased like the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like the whirling dust before the storm.
echoes.note: Isaiah likens the raging nations to the roaring of many waters, the tumult of the seas, before God rebukes them. Jesus' 'anxiety of nations, in perplexity for the roaring of the sea and the waves' fuses the nations' distress with the sea's roar exactly as Isaiah does. Strong conceptual coherence.

echoes.text: who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the turmoil of the nations.
echoes.note: God 'stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the tumult of the peoples,' linking sea-roar and nations' tumult. Jesus' pairing of the roaring sea with the perplexity of nations echoes this psalmic juxtaposition. Coherence on the distinctive sea-and-nations parallel.

echoes.text: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas; though its waters roar and are troubled, though the mountains tremble with their swelling. Selah.
echoes.note: Though the earth gives way, the mountains fall into the sea, and its waters roar and foam, the faithful need not fear. Jesus' roaring sea and shaken heavens amid which disciples lift up their heads in confidence mirror this psalm of cosmic upheaval and trust. Coherence with the tehom-chaos imagery.

echoes.text: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;
echoes.note: God promises 'yet once more I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land,' and the kingdoms. Jesus' shaken 'powers of the heavens' draws on Haggai's eschatological cosmic shaking. Coherence with the shaking-of-creation motif.

echoes.text: The earth is utterly broken. The earth is torn apart. The earth is shaken violently. The earth will stagger like a drunken man, and will sway back and forth like a hammock. Its disobedience will be heavy on it, and it will fall and not rise again.
echoes.note: In the apocalypse of Isaiah the earth is utterly broken, staggering like a drunkard, its transgression heavy upon it. The men 'fainting for fear' before a reeling cosmos belongs to this Isaian universal-judgment scene. Coherence with the proto-apocalyptic dissolution.

echoes.text: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.
echoes.note: The Lord appears over his people, his arrow goes forth like lightning, marching in the whirlwinds. The theophanic coming with power amid cosmic disturbance faintly colors Jesus' glorious Son-of-Man advent. Faint and atmospheric.

pericopes.text: He told them a parable. “See the fig tree, and all the trees. When they are already budding, you see it and know by your own selves that the summer is already near. Even so you also, when you see these things happening, know that the Kingdom of God is near. Most certainly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all things are accomplished. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will by no means pass away.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.
echoes.note: Joel's restoration: the fig tree and vine yield their fruit as a sign the land is renewed after the day of the Lord. Jesus' fig tree budding as a sign that the Kingdom is near may echo this prophetic use of the fig tree as harbinger. Faint thematic link to seasonal-sign imagery.

echoes.text: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: Isaiah declares, 'the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.' Jesus' 'heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will by no means pass away' applies this contrast of transient creation and abiding divine word to his own speech. High coherence on the enduring-word theme.

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.
echoes.note: Isaiah: 'the heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment... but my salvation will be forever.' The passing of heaven and earth set against an everlasting divine word/salvation is exactly Jesus' antithesis. Strong recurrence within Isaiah of the perishing-cosmos vs. abiding-word motif.

echoes.text: Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end.
echoes.note: The heavens and earth perish and wear out like a garment, but God remains the same and his years have no end. Jesus' 'heaven and earth will pass away' draws on this psalmic contrast between the perishable creation and the unchanging God/word. Coherence with the creation-perishes tradition.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: The heavens roll up like a scroll and the host falls like a leaf from the fig tree (LXX). The fig-tree image and the passing heavens cluster in Isaiah's judgment, faintly underlying Jesus' fig-tree parable juxtaposed with heaven and earth passing. Faint compositional echo.

pericopes.text: “So be careful, or your hearts will be loaded down with carousing, drunkenness, and cares of this life, and that day will come on you suddenly. For it will come like a snare on all those who dwell on the surface of all the earth. Therefore be watchful all the time, praying that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that will happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”

echoes.text: Fear, the pit, and the snare, are on you who inhabitant the earth.
echoes.note: Isaiah's apocalypse: 'terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth.' Jesus' warning that the day will come 'like a snare on all those who dwell on the surface of all the earth' reproduces both the snare and the inhabitants-of-the-earth phrasing. High volume on the distinctive double image.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: The Lord becomes a snare and a trap to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and many stumble and are taken. The snare that suddenly catches the unprepared resonates with Jesus' sudden snare on the earth-dwellers. Faint recurrence of the snare-of-judgment image.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;
echoes.note: The Lord will suddenly come to his temple, and who can stand (endure) the day of his coming? Jesus' call to be watchful so as to be able to 'stand before the Son of Man' on the suddenly-arriving day echoes Malachi's question of who can stand at the Lord's advent. Coherence with the standing-at-judgment motif.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: The day comes burning like an oven against the arrogant and evildoers. The sudden, inescapable arrival of 'that day' against the unwary colors Jesus' warning, though the imagery differs. Faint thematic link to the Day-of-the-Lord suddenness.

echoes.text: Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully. He shall receive a blessing from Yahweh, righteousness from the God of his salvation. This is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek your face—even Jacob. Selah.
echoes.note: The psalm asks who may stand in God's holy place, answering with the clean of hands and pure of heart. Jesus' exhortation to watchful, sober readiness so as to stand before the Son of Man evokes the worthiness-to-stand theme. Faint and contested.
