echoes.text: Don’t be among ones drinking too much wine, or those who gorge themselves on meat: for the drunkard and the glutton shall become poor; and drowsiness clothes them in rags.
echoes.note: Wisdom warns against being among drunkards and gluttons, for drunkenness and carousing bring poverty and ruin. Jesus' caution that hearts not be weighed down by carousing and drunkenness draws on this sapiential warning against dissipation. Faint wisdom-tradition coloring.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: Standing 'before the Son of Man' recalls the Danielic court scene where the saints are vindicated before the one like a son of man given dominion. The closing exhortation ties the paraenesis back to Daniel 7, the discourse's controlling vision. Coherence by inclusio with 21:27.

pericopes.text: Every day Jesus was teaching in the temple, and every night he would go out and spend the night on the mountain that is called Olivet. All the people came early in the morning to him in the temple to hear him.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: On the Day of the Lord his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, the eschatological theater of judgment and kingship east of Jerusalem. Luke's note that Jesus lodged each night on the Mount of Olives, having just delivered the end-time discourse, faintly invokes this prophetic Olivet locale. Faint geographical-typological echo.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory went up from the midst of the city, and stood on the mountain which is on the east side of the city.
echoes.note: The glory of the Lord departs the city and rests on the mountain east of Jerusalem (the Mount of Olives). Jesus teaching by day in the temple but withdrawing each night to Olivet, after pronouncing the temple's doom, faintly mirrors the glory's removal to the eastern mount. Very faint and contested.

pericopes.text: Now the feast of unleavened bread, which is called the Passover, drew near. The chief priests and the scribes sought how they might put him to death, for they feared the people. Satan entered into Judas, who was also called Iscariot, who was numbered with the twelve. He went away, and talked with the chief priests and captains about how he might deliver him to them. They were glad, and agreed to give him money. He consented, and sought an opportunity to deliver him to them in the absence of the multitude.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: The narrative is dated by 'the feast of unleavened bread, which is called the Passover,' directly invoking the institution of Passover and Unleavened Bread in Exodus 12. The framing controls the whole chapter's typology (the lamb, the meal, the deliverance), giving high volume and thematic coherence as Luke maps Jesus' death onto Israel's foundational redemption.

echoes.text: Observe the month of Abib, and keep the Passover to Yahweh your God; for in the month of Abib Yahweh your God brought you out of Egypt by night. You shall sacrifice the Passover to Yahweh your God, of the flock and the herd, in the place which Yahweh shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there. You shall eat no leavened bread with it. You shall eat unleavened bread with it seven days, even the bread of affliction; for you came out of the land of Egypt […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's Passover/Unleavened-Bread regulations supply the calendrical language ('the feast of unleavened bread... the Passover') Luke uses to set the scene. Coherent with Luke's interest in Jerusalem-centered, temple-regulated feast observance, though the volume is lower than Exodus 12.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Satan entering Judas and his secret bargain to betray begins the betrayal-by-an-intimate motif that crystallizes at 22:21 in clear dependence on Psalm 41:9. Here the echo is anticipatory and faint, marked low until the table scene makes it explicit.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: 'Satan entered into Judas' personifies the accuser/adversary who, in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3, acts against the faithful with divine permission. The figure of ha-satan as an agent moving human actors gives availability and coherence with Luke's wider Satan theme (cf. 22:31), though the lexical link is thin.

echoes.text: I said to them, “If you think it best, give me my wages; and if not, keep them.” So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver. Yahweh said to me, “Throw it to the potter, the handsome price that I was valued at by them!” I took the thirty pieces of silver, and threw them to the potter, in Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: Judas being 'glad' to receive money for handing over the shepherd-figure resonates with Zechariah's thirty pieces of silver weighed out for the rejected shepherd. Luke lacks the price detail (unlike Matthew), so the echo is faint and contested, carried mainly by the betrayal-for-silver motif.

pericopes.text: The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover must be sacrificed. He sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat.” They said to him, “Where do you want us to prepare?” He said to them, “Behold, when you have entered into the city, a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you. Follow him into the house which he enters. Tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, “Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?”’ He will show you a large, furnished upper room. Make preparations there.” They went, found things as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: 'The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover must be sacrificed' and the command to 'prepare the Passover' directly enact Exodus 12's prescription for slaughtering and eating the lamb. High volume and recurrence within Luke 22 make Exodus 12 the controlling subtext for the meal Jesus is about to transform.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: The detail that the Passover is eaten in a furnished room with prepared provisions echoes the Exodus stipulation to eat the roasted lamb with unleavened bread that night. Coherent with the meal's redemptive typology, though the lexical contact is general.

echoes.text: You may not sacrifice the Passover within any of your gates, which Yahweh your God gives you; but at the place which Yahweh your God shall choose, to cause his name to dwell in, there you shall sacrifice the Passover at evening, at the going down of the sun, at the season that you came out of Egypt. You shall roast and eat it in the place which Yahweh your God chooses. In the morning you shall return to your tents.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy requires the Passover to be eaten at the place the LORD chooses (Jerusalem), not in private towns; Jesus' insistence on preparing the meal inside the city aligns with this centralization. The coherence with Luke's Jerusalem focus supports a medium-confidence allusion.

pericopes.text: When the hour had come, he sat down with the twelve apostles. He said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer, for I tell you, I will no longer by any means eat of it until it is fulfilled in the Kingdom of God.” He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, “Take this, and share it among yourselves, for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until the Kingdom of God comes.” He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and gave to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.” Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: The Last Supper is staged as a Passover meal ('I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you'), so the sacrificed lamb of Exodus 12 stands behind the bread-and-cup words. High volume and coherence: Jesus reinterprets the paschal elements around his own body and blood-deliverance.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' depends on Moses' covenant ratification, 'Behold the blood of the covenant which the LORD has made with you,' sprinkled to seal Israel to God. Strong verbal and conceptual contact (blood + covenant) makes this a primary subtext for the cup-word.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they broke, although I was a husband to them, says Yahweh. But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in […]
echoes.note: The phrase 'the new covenant in my blood' explicitly takes up Jeremiah's promise of a 'new covenant' that the LORD will make with Israel. The adjective 'new' (kainos) keys directly to Jeremiah 31:31, the only OT text promising a covenant so named, giving high volume and distinctiveness.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'My blood, which is poured out for you' echoes the Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and bore the sin of many. The vicarious 'for you/for many' sense coheres with Isaiah 53's substitutionary suffering, a Servant text Luke cites explicitly at 22:37.

echoes.text: As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the pit in which is no water.
echoes.note: 'By the blood of the covenant I have set your prisoners free' supplies a prophetic combination of covenant-blood and liberation that resonates with Jesus' cup-word. Recurrence of the 'blood of the covenant' phrase (also Exodus 24:8) supports a medium-confidence echo.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand.
echoes.note: 'This is my body which is given for you' coheres with the Servant whose life is made 'an offering for sin,' framing Jesus' self-gift as sacrificial. The 'given for' language overlaps the Servant's self-offering, reinforcing the Isaianic atonement subtext of the meal.

echoes.text: I will take the cup of salvation, and call on Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: The 'cup of salvation' lifted with thanksgiving in the Passover Hallel (Ps 116, sung at the meal) may stand behind Jesus' cup of blessing. Availability is strong (Hallel liturgy), but the lexical link is indirect, so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: This day shall be to you for a memorial, and you shall keep it a feast to Yahweh: throughout your generations you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever.
echoes.note: 'Do this in memory of me' transposes the Passover's standing command, 'this day shall be a memorial,' onto the new rite. The memorial (zikkaron) logic of the feast is coherently redirected to Jesus, supporting a deliberate allusion.

pericopes.text: But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. The Son of Man indeed goes, as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed!” They began to question among themselves, which of them it was who would do this thing.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: 'The hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table' draws on 'my own familiar friend... who ate my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.' The shared image of betrayal by a table companion gives strong volume and coherence as a Davidic/righteous-sufferer prototype Luke applies to Judas.

echoes.text: For it was not an enemy who insulted me, then I could have endured it. Neither was it he who hated me who raised himself up against me, then I would have hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend. We took sweet fellowship together. We walked in God’s house with company.
echoes.note: The betrayal by a close companion who shared sweet fellowship ('we took counsel together, and walked to the house of God') reinforces the table-betrayal motif alongside Psalm 41:9. Recurrence of the intimate-betrayer theme in the Psalter supports a medium-confidence echo.

echoes.text: After the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One shall be cut off, and shall have nothing: and the people of the prince who shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and its end shall be with a flood, and even to the end shall be war; desolations are determined. He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who […]
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man indeed goes, as it has been determined' coheres with Daniel's apocalyptic sense of decreed events ('what is determined shall be done'). The vocabulary of divine determination is faint and could derive from broader Jewish providence-language, so it is marked low.

pericopes.text: There arose also a contention among them, which of them was considered to be greatest. He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’ But not so with you. But one who is the greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves. For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am in your midst as one who serves. But you are those who have continued with me in my trials. I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Jesus' conferral of a kingdom and a heavenly banquet table draws on the Son of Man receiving dominion and an everlasting kingdom in Daniel 7. The 'I confer on you a kingdom' language coheres with the Danielic transfer of rule, given Luke's repeated Son-of-Man framing in this chapter.

echoes.text: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel' echoes 'the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom' and possess it forever. The reign-of-the-saints motif undergirds the apostles' eschatological enthronement, a recurring Danielic theme in Luke 22.

echoes.text: until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.
echoes.note: Daniel 7:22's 'judgment was given to the saints of the Most High' supplies the specific note of the saints exercising judgment that Luke renders as the Twelve 'judging the twelve tribes of Israel.' The verbal contact ('judging' + 'saints reign') strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: where the tribes go up, even Yah’s tribes, according to an ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to Yahweh’s name. For there are set thrones for judgment, the thrones of David’s house.
echoes.note: 'Thrones for judgment' set in Jerusalem for 'the tribes of the LORD' resonates with the apostles' thrones judging the twelve tribes. The combination of thrones + tribes + judgment in a single Psalm gives a coherent and reasonably distinctive subtext.

echoes.text: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his blessing.
echoes.note: 'The twelve tribes of Israel' as a fixed totality derives from the Jacob/twelve-sons tradition formalized in Genesis 49. This supplies the conceptual backdrop for the restored Israel the Twelve will govern, though it is a stock phrase rather than a pointed citation.

echoes.text: He said, “This will be the way of the king who shall reign over you: he will take your sons, and appoint them to him, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and they shall run before his chariots; and he will appoint them to him for captains of thousands, and captains of fifties; and he will assign some to plow his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and the instruments of his chariots. He will take your daughters to be […]
echoes.note: Jesus' contrast with kings of the nations who 'lord it over' may echo Samuel's warning about the oppressive ways of kings who 'take' from the people. The critique-of-domineering-rulers theme is coherent but generic, so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: Eating and drinking 'at my table in my Kingdom' resonates with Isaiah's eschatological feast on the mountain for all peoples. The messianic-banquet image is available and coherent, though the lexical link is loose.

pericopes.text: The Lord said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” He said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!” He said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will by no means crow today until you deny that you know me three times.”

echoes.text: “For, behold, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is sifted in a sieve, yet not the least kernel will fall on the earth.
echoes.note: 'Satan asked... that he might sift you as wheat' draws on Amos's image of Israel shaken 'as grain is shaken in a sieve.' The distinctive sifting-in-a-sieve metaphor for testing God's people gives a coherent and fairly specific OT prototype for Peter's trial.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: 'Satan asked to have you' precisely mirrors the heavenly-court scene where the accuser requests permission to test Job, and God grants it within limits. The structure (Satan demands, God permits, the faithful is tested but not destroyed) maps closely onto Job 1-2, giving strong coherence.

echoes.text: Again, on the day when the God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan came also among them to present himself before Yahweh. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and […]
echoes.note: The second Job council, where Satan again seeks and is granted leave to afflict, reinforces the permitted-testing pattern behind Jesus' intercession for Peter ('I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn't fail'). Recurrence of the accuser-demands motif strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: Satan standing to accuse Joshua the high priest, with the LORD rebuking him, parallels Jesus' protective intercession against Satan's demand for Peter. The accuser-versus-advocate dynamic coheres well with the scene's logic.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “When I sent you out without purse, and wallet, and shoes, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.” Then he said to them, “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a wallet. Whoever has none, let him sell his cloak, and buy a sword. For I tell you that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: ‘He was counted with transgressors.’ For that which concerns me has an end.” They said, “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” He said to them, “That is enough.”

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: Jesus explicitly cites 'He was counted with transgressors' (kai meta anomon elogisthe) as Scripture that 'must still be fulfilled in me.' This is a formal, marked quotation of Isaiah 53:12, the clearest OT citation in the chapter, with maximal volume.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: The surrounding Servant context ('by his knowledge shall the righteous one justify many') reinforces that Jesus reads his impending death through the whole fourth Servant Song, not just the cited line. Recurrence of Isaiah 53 across 22:20 and 22:37 supports the wider echo.

pericopes.text: He came out, and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him. When he was at the place, he said to them, “Pray that you don’t enter into temptation.” He was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw, and he knelt down and prayed, saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him. Being in agony he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground. When he rose up from his prayer, he came to the disciples, and found them sleeping because of grief, and said to them, “Why do you sleep? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”

echoes.text: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.
echoes.note: 'Remove this cup from me' draws on the prophetic 'cup' of God's wrath/judgment, which in Psalm 75:8 the LORD makes the wicked drink to the dregs. The cup as a vessel of divine judgment to be drained gives a coherent OT background for Jesus' prayer.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: Jerusalem having drunk 'the cup of his wrath... the cup of staggering' supplies the wrath-cup imagery behind Jesus' petition. Coherent with the Gethsemane cup as the suffering Jesus is asked to drink, with reasonable verbal distinctiveness ('cup').

echoes.text: Thus says your Lord Yahweh, and your God who pleads the cause of his people, “Behold, I have taken out of your hand the cup of staggering, even the bowl of the cup of my wrath; you shall no more drink it again:
echoes.note: The LORD's promise to take 'the cup of staggering' out of Jerusalem's hand resonates inversely: Jesus asks the cup be removed yet drinks it. Recurrence of the cup-of-wrath motif across Isaiah 51 strengthens the allusion cluster.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it. They shall drink, and reel back and forth, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them.
echoes.note: The 'cup of the wine of wrath' that the nations must drink and stagger reinforces the OT 'cup' as judgment that Jesus invokes. The widespread prophetic recurrence of this image supports its presence behind the Gethsemane cup.

echoes.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty […]
echoes.note: 'An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him' echoes the angel who twice strengthens the despairing Elijah with food for his journey. The angelic-strengthening-of-a-suffering-prophet motif is a coherent and fairly specific prototype.

echoes.text: Then there touched me again one like the appearance of a man, and he strengthened me. He said, “Greatly beloved man, don’t be afraid: peace be to you, be strong, yes, be strong.” When he spoke to me, I was strengthened, and said, “Let my lord speak; for you have strengthened me.”
echoes.note: The heavenly figure who touches and strengthens the exhausted, fearful Daniel ('be strong... and he strengthened me') parallels the angel strengthening Jesus in agony. The vocabulary of an angelic visitor imparting strength to one overwhelmed supports the allusion.

echoes.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him for the saving help of his presence. My God, my soul is in despair within me. Therefore I remember you from the land of the Jordan, the heights of Hermon, from the hill Mizar.
echoes.note: Jesus' agony and sorrow-unto-prayer resonate with the lament 'why are you cast down, O my soul,' a Davidic distress prototype. Coherent with Luke's righteous-sufferer portrayal, though lexically diffuse and so marked low.

pericopes.text: While he was still speaking, behold, a multitude, and he who was called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He came near to Jesus to kiss him. But Jesus said to him, “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” When those who were around him saw what was about to happen, they said to him, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” A certain one of them struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear. But Jesus answered, “Let me at least do this”—and he touched his ear, and healed him. Jesus said to the chief priests, captains of the temple, and elders, who had come against him, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you in the temple daily, you didn’t stretch out your hands against me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.”

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Judas, 'one of the twelve,' approaching to kiss Jesus consummates the familiar-friend betrayal already keyed to Psalm 41:9 at 22:21. The recurrence within the chapter strengthens reading the kiss through the table-companion-betrayer subtext.

echoes.text: Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand. So he struck him with it in the body, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and didn’t strike him again; and he died. Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.
echoes.note: Joab's treacherous kiss and greeting before killing Amasa supplies a biblical type of the murderous kiss of a feigned friend. The image of betrayal-by-kiss makes this a coherent, fairly specific prototype for Judas.

echoes.text: His mouth was smooth as butter, but his heart was war. His words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords.
echoes.note: 'His mouth was smoother than butter, but war was in his heart' captures the hypocrisy of an intimate's deadly greeting that fits Judas's kiss. The echo is thematic rather than verbal, so it is marked low.

echoes.text: He uncovers deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shadow of death.
echoes.note: 'This is your hour, and the power of darkness' resonates faintly with OT contrasts of God uncovering deep darkness; the darkness/light dualism is broadly available in the Psalms and Job. The link is thematic and weak.

pericopes.text: They seized him, and led him away, and brought him into the high priest’s house. But Peter followed from a distance. When they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard, and had sat down together, Peter sat among them. A certain servant girl saw him as he sat in the light, and looking intently at him, said, “This man also was with him.” He denied Jesus, saying, “Woman, I don’t know him.” After a little while someone else saw him, and said, “You also are one of them!” But Peter answered, “Man, I am not!” After about one hour passed, another confidently affirmed, saying, “Truly this man also was with him, for he is a Galilean!” But Peter said, “Man, I don’t know what you are talking about!” Immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed. The Lord turned, and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, “Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.” He went out, and wept bitterly.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Peter's threefold denial, like Judas's betrayal, plays on the failure of an intimate companion, the broader righteous-sufferer-abandoned motif behind Psalm 41:9. The connection is thematic and faint, marked low.

echoes.text: Because of all my adversaries I have become utterly contemptible to my neighbors, A fear to my acquaintances. Those who saw me on the street fled from me. I am forgotten from their hearts like a dead man. I am like broken pottery. For I have heard the slander of many, terror on every side, while they conspire together against me, they plot to take away my life.
echoes.note: The righteous sufferer shunned and denied by acquaintances ('I am... a reproach... my acquaintances are afraid of me') resonates with Jesus abandoned even by Peter. Luke draws elsewhere on Psalm 31 for the passion, lending some availability, but the link here is diffuse.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: 'Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered' undergirds the scattering/failure of the disciples that Peter's denial dramatizes. Luke lacks the explicit shepherd citation (unlike Mark/Matthew), so the echo is faint and contested.

pericopes.text: The men who held Jesus mocked him and beat him. Having blindfolded him, they struck him on the face and asked him, “Prophesy! Who is the one who struck you?” They spoke many other things against him, insulting him.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The mocking, beating, and striking of the blindfolded Jesus enacts the Servant who gave 'my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I did not hide my face from shame and spitting.' The cluster of striking + insult + the Servant's non-resistance gives strong coherence.

echoes.text: Now you shall gather yourself in troops, daughter of troops. He has laid siege against us. They will strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek.
echoes.note: 'They will strike the ruler/judge of Israel on the cheek with a rod' supplies a prophetic image of the ruler humiliated by blows that fits the soldiers striking Jesus' face. The smiting-of-the-ruler motif coheres with the mockery scene.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: 'Despised and rejected... and we esteemed him not' resonates with the men insulting and reviling Jesus. Given Isaiah 53's explicit citation at 22:37, the wider Servant context plausibly colors the mockery as well.

echoes.text: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him; let him be filled full with reproach.
echoes.note: 'Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with insults' echoes the patient endurance of blows and reproach that Jesus exemplifies. The link is thematic and secondary to Isaiah 50:6, so it is marked low.

pericopes.text: As soon as it was day, the assembly of the elders of the people was gathered together, both chief priests and scribes, and they led him away into their council, saying, “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you won’t believe, and if I ask, you will in no way answer me or let me go. From now on, the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” They all said, “Are you then the Son of God?” He said to them, “You say it, because I am.” They said, “Why do we need any more witness? For we ourselves have heard from his own mouth!”

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God' takes up 'Sit at my right hand,' the LORD's enthronement of David's lord. The session-at-the-right-hand language is a near-verbatim appropriation of Psalm 110:1, the most cited OT verse in the NT, with high volume.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The title 'the Son of Man' combined with exaltation before the council fuses Psalm 110 with Daniel 7's 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to receive dominion. This Daniel-Psalm 110 conflation is recurrent in the passion tradition and coheres with Luke's Son-of-Man Christology.

echoes.text: Let your hand be on the man of your right hand, on the son of man whom you made strong for yourself.
echoes.note: 'Let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you made strong' loosely joins 'son of man' with the right-hand of God's favor. The verbal overlap is suggestive but thin, so it is marked low and contested.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The council's question 'Are you then the Son of God?' resonates with the royal decree 'You are my Son,' the Davidic sonship Luke applies to Jesus elsewhere. The divine-sonship background is available, though here the link is conceptual rather than cited.

pericopes.text: The whole company of them rose up and brought him before Pilate. They began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man perverting the nation, forbidding paying taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” He answered him, “So you say.” Pilate said to the chief priests and the multitudes, “I find no basis for a charge against this man.” But they insisted, saying, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee even to this place.”

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: Jesus brought before Pilate and accused, answering only the laconic 'So you say.' Luke is sounding the Servant who 'opened not his mouth' before his accusers; the reticence theme recurs through the whole trial sequence (vv. 9, 14). Volume is modest here but coherence with the Servant pattern is high.

echoes.text: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: Rulers and the 'whole company' rise up and accuse the one charged with being 'a king,' the Lord's anointed. Acts 4:25-27 explicitly reads Psalm 2 onto exactly this Lukan scene (Herod, Pilate, peoples of Israel gathered against the Christ), confirming the availability and the author's own intertextual habit.

echoes.text: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.
echoes.note: 'Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I know not' — the righteous sufferer falsely accused of crimes (here perverting the nation, forbidding tribute). A stock element of the lament-psalm pattern Luke weaves; faint individually but coherent with the cluster.

pericopes.text: But when Pilate heard Galilee mentioned, he asked if the man was a Galilean. When he found out that he was in Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who was also in Jerusalem during those days. Now when Herod saw Jesus, he was exceedingly glad, for he had wanted to see him for a long time, because he had heard many things about him. He hoped to see some miracle done by him. He questioned him with many words, but he gave no answers. The chief priests and the scribes stood, vehemently accusing him. Herod with his soldiers humiliated him and mocked him. Dressing him in luxurious clothing, they sent him back to Pilate. Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before that they were enemies with each other.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: Before Herod Jesus 'gave no answers' though questioned with many words — the clearest Lukan instance of the Servant who, 'as a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.' Volume (verbal silence under interrogation) and coherence with the Passion-Servant reading are both strong.

echoes.text: But I, as a deaf man, don’t hear. I am as a mute man who doesn’t open his mouth. Yes, I am as a man who doesn’t hear, in whose mouth are no reproofs.
echoes.note: 'I am like a deaf man who does not hear, like a mute who does not open his mouth' — the righteous sufferer's deliberate silence before mockers. Reinforces the silence motif alongside Isaiah 53; part of the suffering-psalm matrix Luke deploys.

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying,
echoes.note: Herod with his soldiers 'humiliated him and mocked him,' dressing him in finery as a mock-king. The scorn/mockery of the righteous sufferer ('all who see me mock me') is the Psalm 22 keynote that Luke develops at the cross (vv. 35-37). The Herodian mockery prefigures it.

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: Herod and Pilate, formerly enemies, become friends 'that very day' — the kings of the earth and rulers taking counsel together against the Lord's anointed. Acts 4:26-27 names both Herod and Pilate explicitly from Psalm 2:1-2, making this Luke's own reading.

pericopes.text: Pilate called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them, “You brought this man to me as one that perverts the people, and see, I have examined him before you, and found no basis for a charge against this man concerning those things of which you accuse him. Neither has Herod, for I sent you to him, and see, nothing worthy of death has been done by him. I will therefore chastise him and release him.” Now he had to release one prisoner to them at the feast. But they all cried out together, saying, “Away with this man! Release to us Barabbas!”— one who was thrown into prison for a certain revolt in the city, and for murder. Then Pilate spoke to them again, wanting to release Jesus, but they shouted, saying, “Crucify! Crucify him!” He said to them the third time, “Why? What evil has this man done? I have found no capital crime in him. I will therefore chastise him and release him.” But they were urgent with loud voices, asking that he might be crucified. Their voices and the voices of the chief priests prevailed. Pilate decreed that what they asked for should be done. He released him who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus up to their will.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: Pilate three times declares the innocent ('no basis for a charge,' 'nothing worthy of death') yet hands him over — the 'righteous Servant' (Isa 53:11 LXX 'the just one') condemned with the guilty. Luke's triple innocence verdict frames Jesus as the blameless sufferer.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'He delivered Jesus up to their will' — 'the Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all' / 'was delivered up' (LXX paradidomi). The handing-over verb knits the narrative to the Servant who is given up for the people; faint at the lexical level in WEB but strong in the Greek tradition.

echoes.text: He shall take the two goats, and set them before Yahweh at the door of the Tent of Meeting. Aaron shall cast lots for the two goats; one lot for Yahweh, and the other lot for the scapegoat. Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for Yahweh, and offer him for a sin offering. But the goat, on which the lot fell for the scapegoat, shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement for him, to send him away for the scapegoat into the […]
echoes.note: The crowd choosing between two: Barabbas released and Jesus condemned has been read figurally against the Day of Atonement pairing of the goat for the Lord (slain) and the goat released (Azazel/scapegoat). The pairing is structurally suggestive but Luke gives no textual signal; offered as a contested figural reading.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: A murderer and insurrectionist (Barabbas) is preferred while the innocent is condemned, anticipating Jesus 'numbered with the transgressors.' The substitution of the guilty for the just resonates with the Servant's vicarious place; faint here, fuller at v. 33.

pericopes.text: When they led him away, they grabbed one Simon of Cyrene, coming from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it after Jesus.

echoes.text: Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire and the knife. They both went together.
echoes.note: The condemned bears the wood of his own death — Isaac 'carried the wood for the burnt offering' as Simon carries the cross 'after Jesus.' The Aqedah typology (beloved son, the wood laid on him) is an old figural reading; Luke gives no explicit marker, so it is offered low and contested.

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
echoes.note: Simon compelled to 'carry' (bastazo/airo) the cross faintly mirrors the Servant who 'bore our griefs and carried our sorrows' — the burden-bearing motif. The verbal link is thin and the literal scene is about Roman compulsion; offered as a faint echo.

pericopes.text: A great multitude of the people followed him, including women who also mourned and lamented him. But Jesus, turning to them, said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, don’t weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. For behold, the days are coming in which they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed.’ Then they will begin to tell the mountains, ‘Fall on us!’ and tell the hills, ‘Cover us.’ For if they do these things in the green tree, what will be done in the dry?”

echoes.text: The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, will be destroyed. The thorn and the thistle will come up on their altars. They will tell the mountains, “Cover us!” and the hills, “Fall on us!”
echoes.note: 'They will begin to tell the mountains, Fall on us, and the hills, Cover us' reproduces Hosea 10:8 ('they shall say to the mountains, Cover us, and to the hills, Fall on us') almost verbatim — a near-quotation of judgment on Israel transferred to Jerusalem's coming destruction. Highest volume in the pericope.

echoes.text: “Sing, barren, you who didn’t bear; break out into singing, and cry aloud, you who did not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed' inverts the Isaianic 'Sing, O barren one' — but more directly draws on the prophetic topos that in days of judgment childlessness becomes a mercy. Coherent with Luke's Jerusalem-doom oracle; the barren-woman language is availably scriptural.

echoes.text: and tell the forest of the South, Hear Yahweh’s word: Thus says the Lord Yahweh, Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour every green tree in you, and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be burnt thereby.
echoes.note: 'If they do these things in the green tree, what will be done in the dry?' draws on Ezekiel's fire that 'devours every green tree and every dry tree' — judgment that spares neither. The green/dry wood proverb is rooted in this prophetic imagery of indiscriminate burning; coherence is strong.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh of Armies, Consider, and call for the mourning women, that they may come; and send for the skillful women, that they may come: and let them make haste, and take up a wailing for us, that our eyes may run down with tears, and our eyelids gush out with waters. For a voice of wailing is heard out of Zion, How are we ruined! we are greatly confounded, because we have forsaken the land, because they have cast down our dwellings. Yet hear […]
echoes.note: The 'daughters of Jerusalem' wailing and the call to mourn echo Jeremiah's summons to the mourning-women over a doomed Jerusalem ('teach your daughters wailing'). Thematically apt for Luke's lament oracle; verbal contact is modest.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn. In that day there will be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of […]
echoes.note: Mourning by the inhabitants of Jerusalem 'family by family' over the one they pierced may color the weeping daughters of Jerusalem. The link is thematic (Jerusalem's mourning) rather than verbal; offered faintly.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son. In that day the lamentation in Jerusalem shall be very great, as the mourning for the pomegranate grove cut down in the plain. And the land shall lament in separate families, the […]

echoes.text: My eyes do fail with tears, my heart is troubled; My liver is poured on the earth, because of the destruction of the daughter of my people, Because the young children and the infants swoon in the streets of the city.
echoes.note: The 'daughter of Jerusalem' weeping over the city's ruin, with infants and sucklings fainting, supplies the lament-over-Zion register Luke evokes. Lamentations is the canonical genre-source for Jerusalem-grief; contact is atmospheric.

echoes.text: Men shall go into the caves of the rocks, and into the holes of the earth, from before the terror of Yahweh, and from the glory of his majesty, when he arises to shake the earth mightily.
echoes.note: People hiding 'in the caves of the rocks' from the terror of the Lord in the day of judgment parallels the cry to mountains and hills; a possible secondary source alongside Hosea 10:8 for the day-of-wrath flight motif.

pericopes.text: There were also others, two criminals, led with him to be put to death. When they came to the place that is called The Skull, they crucified him there with the criminals, one on the right and the other on the left. Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: Crucified between 'two criminals' fulfills 'he was numbered with the transgressors' (Isa 53:12), a verse Luke quotes explicitly at 22:37 and here enacts narratively. The 'forgive them' intercession likewise renders the Servant who 'made intercession for the transgressors.' Both Servant clauses converge on this scene with high volume and recurrence.

echoes.text: They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.
echoes.note: 'Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots' directly enacts Psalm 22:18, 'they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.' Verbal correspondence is exact; this is the most secure Psalm-22 echo in the chapter.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' embodies the Servant who 'bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.' The dying intercession for the executioners is the narrative form of Isaiah 53:12's final clause; high coherence within Luke's Servant Christology.

echoes.text: In return for my love, they are my adversaries; but I am in prayer.
echoes.note: 'In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer' colors the dying intercession 'forgive them.' The righteous sufferer who prays for his persecutors is a psalm topos; faint verbal contact, coherent with the lament cluster.

echoes.text: ‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him. His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.” Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God […]
echoes.note: Joseph forgiving brothers who 'did not know' the good God intended frames the 'they know not what they do' ignorance-forgiveness pattern. A thematic Second-Temple resonance (cf. Acts 3:17 'you acted in ignorance'); offered low.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘If anyone sins unintentionally, in any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, and does any one of them:
echoes.note: Forgiveness for those who 'know not what they do' aligns with the Torah category of unintentional/inadvertent sin (sins of ignorance) which is atoneable. Luke may be invoking the legal distinction that makes intercession fitting; faint but available.

pericopes.text: The people stood watching. The rulers with them also scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others. Let him save himself, if this is the Christ of God, his chosen one!” The soldiers also mocked him, coming to him and offering him vinegar, and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” An inscription was also written over him in letters of Greek, Latin, and Hebrew: “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
echoes.note: The rulers scoff 'He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Christ' — a close rendering of Psalm 22:8, 'He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him, let him rescue him, for he delights in him,' framed by 22:7's mocking head-shakers. Volume and recurrence (Luke's sustained Ps 22 use) make this high.

echoes.text: They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.
echoes.note: The soldiers 'offering him vinegar' enacts Psalm 69:21, 'for my thirst they gave me vinegar (sour wine) to drink' — the mocking drink of the righteous sufferer. Direct lexical correspondence (oxos); a core Passion-psalm fulfillment.

echoes.text: Let us see if his words be true, And let us try what shall befall in the ending of his life. For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries. With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong. Let us condemn him to a shameful death; For he will be visited according to his words.
echoes.note: 'Let us see if his words are true... if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him and deliver him' — the wicked taunting the righteous one to prove divine sonship maps precisely onto 'if this is the Christ of God, his chosen one... save yourself.' Deuterocanonical and demonstrably available, this taunt-of-the-righteous text is a strong source for the mockery's logic.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'the Christ of God, his chosen one' (ho eklektos) echoes Isaiah 42:1, 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights,' the Servant designation Luke favors (cf. the transfiguration 'my Chosen'). The title brings the Servant frame into the mockery scene.

echoes.text: But you have rejected and spurned. You have been angry with your anointed. You have renounced the covenant of your servant. You have defiled his crown in the dust.
echoes.note: God's anointed rejected and scorned ('you have renounced... cast off your anointed') resonates with the mocking of the Christ/chosen one. A royal-lament background to the messianic mockery; faint verbal contact.

echoes.text: All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying,
echoes.note: 'The people stood watching... the rulers scoffed' realizes Psalm 22:7, 'all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me, they wag their heads.' The watching-and-deriding tableau is the psalm's own scene; recurrence with v. 35 mockery is strong.

pericopes.text: One of the criminals who was hanged insulted him, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!” But the other answered, and rebuking him said, “Don’t you even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward for our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong.” He said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.” Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The dialogue with the two criminals continues the 'numbered with the transgressors' enactment; the penitent's confession 'this man has done nothing wrong' restates the Servant's innocence (Isa 53:9 'he had done no violence'). Luke turns the transgressor-companions into witnesses to the just sufferer.

echoes.text: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
echoes.note: 'This man has done nothing wrong' echoes 'he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth' — the criminal's verdict confirms the Servant's blamelessness even among the condemned. Coherent with Luke's innocence motif (vv. 4, 14, 22, 47).

echoes.text: For Yahweh has comforted Zion; he has comforted all her waste places, and has made her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of Yahweh; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.
echoes.note: 'Today you will be with me in Paradise' draws on Isaiah's promise that the LORD will comfort Zion and 'make her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden (paradeisos) of the LORD.' The eschatological-Eden 'paradise' is the availably scriptural term Luke uses for restored blessedness.

echoes.text: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed. Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
echoes.note: 'Paradise' (paradeisos, the LXX word for the Eden garden) frames Jesus' promise as the regained Eden — readmission to the garden and the tree of life forfeited in Genesis 3. The figural Eden-restoration reading is well grounded in the LXX vocabulary; medium because Luke does not cite Genesis directly.

echoes.text: You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, emerald, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and beryl. Gold work of tambourines and of pipes was in you. In the day that you were created they were prepared.
echoes.note: 'Eden, the garden of God' (paradeisos in LXX) supplies another availability for the restored-paradise hope. Secondary to the Genesis/Isaiah Eden language; offered as a faint lexical support.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Remember me when you come into your Kingdom' invokes the bestowal of an everlasting kingdom on one like a son of man (Dan 7:14). The kingdom-coming hope draws on Danielic enthronement language; thematic rather than verbal here.

pericopes.text: It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour. The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn in two.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord Yahweh, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.
echoes.note: 'Darkness came over the whole land' at midday fulfills Amos 8:9, 'I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in clear day' — Amos' day-of-the-Lord judgment over mourning Israel. The noon-darkness (sixth hour) verbal and temporal match is strong; the surrounding Amos context (mourning as for an only son, v. 10) reinforces it.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.” Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.
echoes.note: 'Darkness over the whole land' recalls the ninth plague, 'thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days,' a darkness 'that may be felt.' The exodus-plague resonance casts the crucifixion as a moment of judgment/new exodus; coherent though Amos is the closer noon-darkness source.

echoes.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
echoes.note: 'The sun was darkened' echoes Joel's day-of-the-LORD signs, 'the sun and moon are darkened' (Joel 2:10; 3:15), language Luke himself cites in Acts 2:20. Availability is confirmed by Luke's own use; the cosmic-portent register fits the crucifixion's apocalyptic framing.

echoes.text: “You shall make a veil of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cherubim. The work of the skillful workman shall it be made. You shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold; their hooks shall be of gold, on four sockets of silver. You shall hang up the veil under the clasps, and shall bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil: and the veil shall separate the holy place from the most holy for you.
echoes.note: 'The veil of the temple was torn in two' presupposes the Exodus curtain (katapetasma) that screens the Holy of Holies. The tearing dramatically signifies access/judgment upon the sanctuary; the cultic referent is unambiguously the Tabernacle/Temple veil of Exodus 26.

echoes.text: That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,
echoes.note: 'A day of darkness and gloom' as the day of the LORD's wrath supplies further prophetic backing for the noon darkness. Secondary to Amos/Joel; offered as a faint convergent witness.

pericopes.text: Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” Having said this, he breathed his last.

echoes.text: Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth.
echoes.note: 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit' is a direct quotation of Psalm 31:5, 'into your hand I commit my spirit,' the explicit dying word. Luke makes the righteous sufferer's prayer of trust the climactic utterance, replacing Mark's cry of dereliction; verbatim and unmistakable.

echoes.text: In you, Yahweh, I take refuge. Let me never be disappointed. Deliver me in your righteousness. Bow down your ear to me. Deliver me speedily. Be to me a strong rock, a house of defense to save me. For you are my rock and my fortress, therefore for your name’s sake lead me and guide me. Pluck me out of the net that they have laid secretly for me, for you are my stronghold. Into your hand I commend my spirit. You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth. I hate those […]
echoes.note: The whole psalm of the trusting righteous sufferer ('you redeem me, O LORD, faithful God,' surrounded by enemies yet committing himself to God) frames the death-cry beyond the single quoted line. Recurrence of Psalm 31's confidence motif throughout Luke's calm passion supports a wider allusion.

echoes.text: They fell on their faces, and said, “God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?”
echoes.note: 'God of the spirits of all flesh' / the giving-up of spirit may faintly evoke the biblical idiom of the breath/spirit returning to God (cf. Eccl 12:7). Thematic background for the 'breathed his last'; not a specific Lukan target.

pericopes.text: When the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying, “Certainly this was a righteous man.” All the multitudes that came together to see this, when they saw the things that were done, returned home beating their breasts. All his acquaintances, and the women who followed with him from Galilee, stood at a distance, watching these things.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: The centurion's verdict 'Certainly this was a righteous man' (dikaios) crowns Luke's Servant-as-righteous-one theme — 'my righteous servant shall make many righteous.' Luke's distinctive dikaios (vs Mark's 'Son of God') points to Isaiah 53:11 LXX; medium-high coherence with the chapter's innocence refrain.

echoes.text: For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries.
echoes.note: The vindicated 'righteous man' (dikaios) recalls Wisdom's persecuted just one whom God acknowledges as son. The centurion's confession answers the mockers' Wisdom-styled taunt (v. 35); thematic inclusio rather than quotation.

echoes.text: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.
echoes.note: 'All his acquaintances, and the women... stood at a distance, watching' enacts Psalm 38:11, 'my friends and companions stand aloof from my affliction, and my kinsmen stand far off.' The distant-onlookers detail is a precise lament motif of abandonment; strong verbal/situational match.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: The multitudes 'beating their breasts' over the crucified one resonates with the mourning of Zechariah 12:10-12, 'they shall look on him whom they pierced and mourn.' Luke's repentant breast-beating crowd (cf. 18:13) faintly draws on this Jerusalem-mourning prophecy.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

echoes.text: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them. I am confined, and I can’t escape.
echoes.note: 'You have caused my companions to shun me' parallels the acquaintances standing at a distance, doubling Psalm 38:11. A secondary lament witness to the friends-kept-far motif; offered low.

pericopes.text: Behold, a man named Joseph, who was a member of the council, a good and righteous man (he had not consented to their counsel and deed), from Arimathaea, a city of the Jews, who was also waiting for the Kingdom of God: this man went to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body. He took it down, and wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb that was cut in stone, where no one had ever been laid. It was the day of the Preparation, and the Sabbath was drawing near. The women, who had come with him out of Galilee, followed after, and saw the tomb, and how his body was laid. They returned, and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

echoes.text: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
echoes.note: Burial by Joseph, a rich council member, in an unused rock-cut tomb realizes Isaiah 53:9, 'they made his grave... with a rich man in his death,' the Servant honored in burial despite dying among criminals. The 'rich and righteous man' and the new tomb make this Luke's enactment of the Servant's burial; high coherence.

echoes.text: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
echoes.note: Taking the body down and burying it the same day, before the Sabbath, observes Deuteronomy 21:22-23, 'his body shall not remain all night... you shall bury him the same day,' lest the land be defiled by one 'hanged on a tree.' The same-day burial urgency is governed by this law; strong availability and coherence.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
echoes.note: 'On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment' directly invokes the Decalogue Sabbath law, Exodus 20:10 ('you shall not do any work'). Luke's editorial 'according to the commandment' is an explicit appeal to Torah; the rest also frames the third-day timing.

echoes.text: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
echoes.note: The Sabbath rest after the finished work of the cross resonates figurally with God resting on the seventh day after creation — the new creation's Sabbath repose before resurrection. A theological-figural reading; Luke signals only the commandment, so it is offered low.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic form of the Sabbath commandment is an equally available source for 'rested according to the commandment.' Listed alongside Exodus 20 as the alternative Decalogue text Luke's phrase could intend.

pericopes.text: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they and some others came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away from the tomb. They entered in, and didn’t find the Lord Jesus’ body. While they were greatly perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling clothing. Becoming terrified, they bowed their faces down to the earth. They said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee, saying that the Son of Man must be delivered up into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again?” They remembered his words, returned from the tomb, and told all these things to the eleven, and to all the rest. Now they were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James. The other women with them told these things to the apostles. These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn’t believe them. But Peter got up and ran to the tomb. Stooping and looking in, he saw the strips of linen lying by themselves, and he departed to his home, wondering what had happened.

echoes.text: I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz: his body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches, and his arms and his feet like burnished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
echoes.note: The 'two men in dazzling clothing' at the tomb echo Daniel's angelic figure clothed in linen with a face/body 'like lightning' and 'like the gleam of beryl.' Luke's verb 'astraptousē' (flashing/dazzling) matches the Danielic theophanic vocabulary for angelic interpreters who appear at moments of eschatological revelation. Volume and coherence are strong; Daniel is Luke's apocalyptic template.

echoes.text: Two other also appeared to him, young men notable in their strength, and beautiful in their glory, and splendid in their apparel, who stood by him on either side, and scourged him unceasingly, inflicting on him many sore stripes.
echoes.note: The two young men of 'splendid' appearance who appear in the Jerusalem temple to Heliodorus furnish a close Second-Temple parallel to Luke's two men in dazzling clothing. The doubling of radiant angelic figures (cf. also 2 Macc 3:33-34) was a recognizable Hellenistic-Jewish topos for divine vindication and intervention. Availability and coherence support it.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'The third day rise again' draws on Hosea's 'after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up,' the most cited prophetic warrant for third-day resurrection in early Christian and rabbinic exegesis. Luke makes the 'third day' a fixed kerygmatic formula (cf. 24:7, 21, 46), and Hosea supplies the schematic Scriptural pattern. Contested as the precise source but high recurrence.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: Jonah's 'three days and three nights' in the fish is invoked elsewhere in the Gospel tradition as the sign of resurrection (the 'sign of Jonah'), and stands behind the third-day pattern Luke repeats here. The link is typological rather than verbal in Luke 24, so confidence is low and the connection is contested.

echoes.text: On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place far off.
echoes.note: 'On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes' (the Aqedah) was read in early Jewish and Christian tradition as a deliverance-on-the-third-day pattern, the deliverance of the bound son. As a faint contributor to the rabbinic/Christian web of 'third day' rescue texts it may color Luke's formula, though there is no verbal contact. Contested and low volume.

echoes.text: and be ready against the third day; for on the third day Yahweh will come down in the sight of all the people on Mount Sinai.
echoes.note: 'Be ready for the third day, for on the third day the LORD will come down' supplies another 'third day' theophany-and-covenant text feeding the Jewish pattern of decisive divine action on the third day. Its contribution to Luke's resurrection formula is figural and faint, lacking verbal correspondence. Marked contested.

echoes.text: God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day.
echoes.note: Luke dates the resurrection to 'the first day of the week' (mia tōn sabbatōn), and early Christian reading saw new-creation overtones in the resurrection on the day light was first made. The echo is figural and depends on canonical placement rather than wording, so confidence is low and it is contested.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The angels recall Jesus' words that 'the Son of Man must be delivered up... and the third day rise again.' The Son of Man title and his vindication/exaltation derive from Daniel 7, where the one like a son of man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion. The vindication-after-suffering motif coheres with Luke's whole chapter.
