pericopes.text: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem. They talked with each other about all of these things which had happened. While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?” One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things which have happened there in these days?” He said to them, “What things?” They said to him, “The things concerning Jesus, the Nazarene, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. Also, certain women of our company amazed us, having arrived early at the tomb; and when they didn’t find his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of us went to the tomb, and found it just like the women had said, but they didn’t see him.” He said to them, “Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?” Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: The risen Jesus joins the travelers unrecognized and is pressed to stay and share a meal, recalling the LORD/angels appearing to Abraham as a wayfarer who is welcomed with hospitality and food. The pattern of unrecognized divine visitor received with hospitality is a Scriptural type Luke evokes, though there is no verbal quotation. Contested, low volume.

echoes.text: He went to seek a man, and found Raphael who was an angel; and he didn’t know it. He said to him, “Can I go with you to Rages of Media? Do you know those places well?” The angel said to him, “I will go with you. I know the way well. I have lodged with our brother Gabael.” Tobias said to him, “Wait for me, and I will tell my father.” He said to him, “Go, and don’t wait. And he went in and said to his father, “Behold, I have found someone who will go with […]
echoes.note: The angel Raphael travels incognito with Tobias as an unrecognized companion whose true identity is disclosed only at the end (Tob 12). The Emmaus narrative's structure of a hidden divine guide on a journey parallels Tobit's traveling-angel motif, a recognizable Second-Temple type. Faint and structural rather than verbal, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: Jesus' rebuke that the Christ 'had to suffer these things and enter into his glory' presupposes the Suffering Servant who is 'despised and rejected' yet afterward exalted (Isa 52:13; 53:11-12). Luke roots the necessity (dei) of messianic suffering in the Servant Songs, which he cites explicitly elsewhere (Lk 22:37). Coherence with the chapter's exegetical climax is strong.

echoes.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning? My God, I cry in the daytime, but you don’t answer; in the night season, and am not silent. But you are holy, you who inhabit the praises of Israel. Our fathers trusted in you. They trusted, and you delivered them. They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed. But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of […]
echoes.note: The motif of the righteous one who suffers grievously and is then vindicated, which Jesus expounds 'beginning from Moses and all the prophets,' draws on the Passion psalm Luke uses in the crucifixion scene. The suffering-and-glory pattern of Psalm 22 (lament turning to praise/vindication) is a primary text in the Scriptural 'things concerning himself.' Coherence high.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Enter into his glory' echoes the enthronement of the one like a son of man who is given glory and dominion before the Ancient of Days. Luke pairs suffering with glorification, and Daniel 7 supplies the vindicated-and-glorified figure central to his messianic reading. Recurrence across the chapter supports it.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The travelers describe Jesus as 'a prophet mighty in deed and word,' and the exposition 'beginning from Moses' invokes the prophet-like-Moses whom God would raise up and to whom Israel must listen. Luke elsewhere applies this text to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37), making it a likely component of the Mosaic witness here. Coherence and recurrence support medium confidence.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: The report that the chief priests 'delivered him up to be condemned to death' resonates with the Servant who was 'led like a lamb to the slaughter' and handed over. As part of the Servant subtext Jesus is about to expound, it colors the travelers' summary, though without quotation. Low and somewhat contested.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despises, to him whom the nation abhors, to a servant of rulers: “Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall worship; because of Yahweh who is faithful, even the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you.”
echoes.note: The hope that Jesus 'would redeem Israel' sits within the Servant's mission to restore and redeem Israel before he is given as a light to the nations. Luke's redemption-of-Israel language (cf. Lk 1:68; 2:38) draws on Deutero-Isaiah's restoration vocabulary. Faint here, hence low.

pericopes.text: They drew near to the village, where they were going, and he acted like he would go further. They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.” He went in to stay with them. When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave to them. Their eyes were opened, and they recognized him, and he vanished out of their sight. They said one to another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.

echoes.text: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
echoes.note: 'Their eyes were opened, and they recognized him' deliberately inverts 'the eyes of both were opened' in Eden, where opened eyes brought shame and exile; here opened eyes at the breaking of bread bring recognition of the risen Lord. The verbal correspondence (eyes opened) plus reversal is a coherent Lukan new-creation motif. Volume is moderate; the allusion is widely recognized.

echoes.text: He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
echoes.note: The shared meal at which the divine guest is recognized recalls the LORD/angels eating with Abraham at Mamre, where hospitality discloses the visitor's identity. The Emmaus meal as the locus of revelation parallels the Mamre table-fellowship type. Structural and faint, so low and contested.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: The breaking of bread that opens their eyes carries Passover/Eucharistic overtones, the meal at which deliverance is remembered and made present. Given Luke's Passover framing of the Last Supper, the Emmaus bread figurally recalls the Passover bread of redemption. Typological rather than verbal, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: Elisha prayed, and said, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.
echoes.note: Elisha's prayer that the servant's eyes be opened to see the unseen heavenly reality offers a parallel for the divinely granted opening of eyes to perceive the risen Christ. The motif of God opening human eyes to spiritual sight is a recurring OT pattern Luke taps. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: Jesus 'vanished out of their sight' faintly echoes the sudden removal of righteous figures who are 'taken' by God (Enoch 'was not, for God took him'). As a marker of a translated/heavenly figure no longer subject to ordinary presence, it anticipates the ascension. Very faint, contested.

pericopes.text: As they said these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace be to you.” But they were terrified and filled with fear, and supposed that they had seen a spirit. He said to them, “Why are you troubled? Why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is truly me. Touch me and see, for a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. While they still didn’t believe for joy, and wondered, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?” They gave him a piece of a broiled fish and some honeycomb. He took them, and ate in front of them.

echoes.text: All these days I appeared to you. I didn’t eat or drink, but you all saw a vision.
echoes.note: Raphael's disclosure, 'I appeared to you, but I did not eat or drink; it was a vision that you saw,' frames the Second-Temple assumption that angelic/spirit visitants only seem to eat. Luke counters precisely this by having the risen Jesus eat real food to prove he is 'not a spirit' but has flesh and bones, engaging Tobit's category. Coherence and availability are strong.

echoes.text: He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
echoes.note: Jesus eating broiled fish before them to prove corporeal reality parallels the angels who 'ate' before Abraham at Mamre, the locus classicus for heavenly visitors sharing human food. Luke uses the eating motif as physical proof against the disciples' supposition of a spirit. Recurrence of the 'divine visitor eats' type supports it.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them.
echoes.note: The disciples suppose they see a disembodied 'spirit' (pneuma), reflecting a current view that the righteous dead exist as souls 'in the hand of God.' Luke's insistence on flesh and bones engages and corrects such a discarnate-soul expectation. Conceptual and faint, so low and contested.

echoes.text: After my skin is destroyed, then in my flesh shall I see God,
echoes.note: 'In my flesh I shall see God' anticipates an embodied vindication beyond death that resonates with Luke's emphasis on the risen Jesus' flesh and bones. As a faint OT witness to bodily hope it may color the scene, but there is no verbal contact. Contested, low.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “This is what I told you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled.” Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures. He said to them, “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things. Behold, I send out the promise of my Father on you. But wait in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high.”

echoes.text: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you.
echoes.note: That repentance and forgiveness be proclaimed 'to all the nations' fulfills the Psalter's vision that 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD,' part of the Writings (psalmoi) Jesus names as bearing witness to him. Luke roots the universal mission in the Psalms he has just cited. Coherence with the tripartite-canon statement supports it.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The Servant given 'as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' is the programmatic text behind 'repentance and remission of sins... to all the nations.' Luke quotes Isa 49:6 explicitly at Acts 13:47 and alludes to it at Acts 1:8, making it the key prophetic warrant for the worldwide mission launched here. Volume and recurrence are high.

echoes.text: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'Beginning at Jerusalem' enacts the eschatological pattern whereby 'out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem,' the nations streaming to and the word streaming from Zion. Luke reverses the centripetal pilgrimage into a centrifugal mission from Jerusalem. Coherence is strong.

echoes.text: Many nations will go and say, “Come, and let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For the law will go out of Zion, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem;
echoes.note: Micah's parallel oracle that 'the word of the LORD' goes forth 'from Jerusalem' to instruct the nations reinforces the Jerusalem-origin of the universal proclamation. The doubled prophetic witness (with Isa 2:3) strengthens the case that Luke draws on the Zion-mission tradition. Recurrence supports medium.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The herald who proclaims good news of salvation from Zion underlies Luke's commissioning of witnesses to preach forgiveness beginning at Jerusalem. Luke's vocabulary of proclaiming (kēryssō) good news echoes the Isaianic herald, a text central to his mission theology. Coherence good.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: 'Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved... in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape' underwrites repentance/forgiveness proclaimed 'in his name' beginning from Jerusalem. Luke cites Joel 2 at Pentecost (Acts 2:21), making it a strong intertext for the commission. Recurrence in Luke-Acts supports it.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: 'I send out the promise of my Father on you... until you are clothed with power from on high' anticipates Joel's outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, which Luke fulfills explicitly at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, quoting Joel). The Spirit as the Father's promise is the bridge from Luke 24 to Acts. Volume and recurrence are high.

echoes.text: Until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is considered a forest.
echoes.note: 'Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high' supplies the very phrase 'power from on high' (ex hypsous) for the promised Spirit-endowment. Luke's 'clothed with power from on high' draws on this Isaianic image of the Spirit poured out to renew. Verbal contact ('from on high') gives medium-strong confidence.

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: 'I will pour my Spirit upon your descendants' reinforces the promised-Spirit theme of being clothed with power, an OT pattern of the Spirit poured out as gift and blessing. Together with Joel and Isa 32 it forms the cluster behind the Father's promise. Recurrence within the cluster supports it.

echoes.text: But the Spirit of Yahweh came on Gideon; and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered together after him.
echoes.note: 'Clothed with power' (enedysasthe) recalls the idiom that the Spirit of the LORD 'clothed itself with' Gideon, the standard OT metaphor for divine empowerment of a chosen agent. Luke's clothing-with-power language may draw on this Spirit-clothing idiom. Faint verbal idiom, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: When Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished, Moses commanded the Levites, who bore the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, saying, “Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God, that it may be there for a witness against you.
echoes.note: 'All things written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms... must be fulfilled' names the threefold Hebrew canon (Torah, Prophets, Writings), and the Law of Moses as a written witness placed beside the ark to testify is the Torah pole of that witness. Luke frames the whole of Scripture, beginning with Moses' written law, as testifying to Christ. Coherence with the canon formula supports it.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The prologue to Sirach repeatedly names 'the Law and the Prophets and the others/the rest of the books,' the earliest explicit witness to the tripartite division of Hebrew Scripture that Luke 24:44 presupposes ('law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms'). It supplies the Second-Temple canonical framework, not a content-quotation. Availability and coherence support medium.

pericopes.text: He led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. While he blessed them, he withdrew from them, and was carried up into heaven. They worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.

echoes.text: Then he went down, and lifted up his hands Over the whole congregation of the children of Israel, To give blessing to the Lord with his lips, And to glory in his name. And he bowed himself down in worship the second time, To declare the blessing from the Most High. And now bless you the God of all, Which everywhere does great things, Which exalts our days from the womb, And deals with us according to his mercy.
echoes.note: Jesus 'lifted up his hands and blessed them' as he departs reproduces the climactic scene of Simon the high priest who 'lifted up his hands over the whole congregation... to pronounce the blessing of the LORD,' after which the people worship. Luke casts the ascending Jesus as the great high priest performing the Aaronic benediction. Volume, coherence, and the worship response all align strongly.

echoes.text: Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people, and blessed them; and he came down from offering the sin offering, and the burnt offering, and the peace offerings.
echoes.note: 'Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and came down' is the priestly prototype for Jesus' parting gesture of lifted hands and blessing. The lifting-hands-to-bless is the defining act of the Aaronic priesthood, which Luke transfers to the ascending Christ. Verbal and gestural correspondence is high.

echoes.text: “Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.’ You shall tell them, ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’ “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.”
echoes.note: The Aaronic blessing ('The LORD bless you and keep you...') is the content of the priestly benediction Jesus enacts with lifted hands. Luke evokes the priest putting the divine name on the people as the risen Christ blesses them at his departure. Coherence with the Lev/Sirach cluster supports it.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Jesus 'was carried up into heaven' while his disciples watch, closely paralleling Elijah taken up into heaven before Elisha, whose witnessing disciple then receives a double portion of his spirit. Luke's ascension-then-Spirit sequence is modeled on the Elijah-Elisha succession, and Luke uses Elijah typology throughout. Volume and coherence are high.

echoes.text: When they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” He said, “You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be so for you; but if not, it shall not be so.”
echoes.note: Elisha's request to inherit Elijah's spirit, granted 'if you see me taken,' parallels the disciples who witness Jesus' ascent and then await the promised Spirit. Luke ties the seeing of the departure to the bestowal of the Spirit, mirroring the Elijah-Elisha transfer. Recurrence with the prior verse supports medium.

echoes.text: God has gone up with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a trumpet.
echoes.note: 'God has gone up with a shout' supplies the enthronement-ascent motif of God ascending to his throne amid praise, fitting the disciples who 'worshiped him and returned... with great joy, praising God.' Luke's ascension-to-worship sequence draws on the Zion enthronement psalms. Coherence with the joyful praise response supports it.

echoes.text: Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is the King of glory? Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in battle. Lift up your heads, you gates; yes, lift them up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in. Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.
echoes.note: The 'gates lift up your heads' entry of the King of glory was read in early tradition as the ascent of the exalted Lord into the heavenly sanctuary, paralleling Jesus carried up into heaven. Faint and traditional rather than verbal in Luke, so low and contested.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: Enoch who 'walked with God, and was not, for God took him' is an OT type of the righteous one assumed into heaven, contributing to the assumption pattern Luke narrates. As one of the canonical assumption figures (with Elijah) it faintly informs the ascension. Low, contested.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The ascent into heaven and the disciples' worship enact the giving of dominion and the service/worship of all peoples to the one like a son of man who comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days. Luke's exalted Christ receiving worship realizes the Danielic enthronement. Coherence with the Son of Man framing of the chapter supports it.

echoes.text: Moses and Aaron went into the Tent of Meeting, and came out, and blessed the people: and Yahweh’s glory appeared to all the people. Fire came out from before Yahweh, and consumed the burnt offering and the fat upon the altar. When all the people saw it, they shouted, and fell on their faces.
echoes.note: After Aaron's blessing the glory of the LORD appears and the people fall down/worship; Luke's sequence of priestly blessing followed by worship in the temple mirrors this Levitical pattern of blessing-then-glory-then-worship. Structural echo reinforcing the priestly reading, so low and supportive.
